studies.title: Fulfil Your Bonds
studies.meaning: The surah opens with one command and then shows what it costs. Fulfil your bonds. The classical scholars read the word broadly. It covers the covenant with God, the treaties a community signs, and the ordinary agreements of trade and marriage. What follows tests that breadth at once. Livestock is permitted, with exceptions to come. Game is set aside while a person is in the state of pilgrimage. The closing clause names the authority behind all of it. God decides as He wills.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the later part of the Medinan period. Surah five is generally placed among the last long surahs to come down. The community was governing itself by then. It held treaties with neighbouring tribes and managed access to the pilgrimage. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this opening. They read its placement as a heading for the whole surah. The surah returns again and again to covenants kept and broken, by the community addressed and by those before it.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a knot tied tight. Arabic uses the same root for fastening a rope and for concluding an agreement, so the word carries the physical image of something bound rather than merely stated.
The verb means to pay in full, with nothing shaved off. It is the same root used for weights and measures given honestly, so keeping an agreement is framed as settling a debt exactly.

A state, not a place. The word marks a person who has entered the consecrated condition of pilgrimage, in which ordinary permissions are suspended for a time and the desert itself becomes off limits to the hunter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian trade ran on spoken agreement in front of witnesses. A caravan share, a grazing right, a marriage settlement, a truce between tribes: none of it was filed anywhere. The only enforcement was reputation. A man known to break his word could not raise a partner or a loan. Herds were the money of that world. So a rule about which animals may be eaten touched the household accounts directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah takes its name, The Table, from a scene that does not arrive until its final pages. There the disciples of Jesus ask for a table set from heaven. Several long surahs are named this way, for one scene rather than a theme. So a reader who opens at the first ayah meets contracts and covenants long before anything like the title.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting a command about contracts at the head of a surah makes agreement a religious matter, not a civil one. The duty is not owed to the other party alone. It is owed upward. That is why the ayah ends with God's authority rather than with a penalty. It also explains the shape of the ayah. Permission and restriction come from the same voice. What is allowed and what is withheld are equally acts of one will.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction and adds that every agreement will itself be brought forward and asked about.
Extends the bond to oaths sworn in God's name and warns against untying what was deliberately tied.
Continues directly, naming the sacred months and the pilgrimage offerings that the closing clause here has just touched.

studies.applyIt: Think of one small agreement you made this month and have quietly let slide, a reply you promised, a sum you said you would send, a time you said you would arrive. Do not renegotiate it in your head. Settle it today, and notice that the discomfort of finishing it is smaller than the discomfort of carrying it.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers to keep their promises. Farm animals are allowed as food, except the ones He names later. Wild game is not on that list while you are on pilgrimage. God decides what He wants.

studies.title: Sacred Signs And Old Grudges
studies.meaning: A list of things not to violate, and all of them are markers rather than rules. The rites themselves, the sacred month, the offering animals, the garlands hung on them to show what they were, and the people travelling towards the House. Each is a sign that something stands under protection. The verse then turns to the feeling that would make a person ignore such a sign. Old hatred is named and refused. Cooperation is defined by what it is for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from one of the last surahs revealed. The reference to being barred from the Sacred Mosque points back to the year the Muslims were turned away at Hudaybiyya without performing the pilgrimage. Within a few years the same people who had turned them back would be travelling under their protection. The verse speaks into that window, when the grievance was recent and the power had shifted.

keyTerms.note: From a root for perceiving and for a mark that makes something recognisable. The word covers both the rites and the physical signs by which they were known, which is why animals and months appear in one list.
Necklaces of bark or hide hung on an animal set aside for offering. They worked as public notice: anyone seeing the collar knew that the beast and the person driving it were not to be touched.
A word for lasting dislike rather than a flare of anger. It names a grudge that has had time to become part of a person, and it comes back in the verse about testimony a few lines later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months were the breathing space of the economy. For four months a year weapons were put down across Arabia. The great fairs ran under that truce. Poetry contests, debt settlements and marriage deals were all timed to it. A collared animal walking a trade road could not be touched. Breaking any of these customs did more than offend. It made travel impossible for everyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning about letting hatred for a people carry you into wrong appears twice in this surah. It comes here and again six verses later. Here it is applied to attacking those who barred the way. There it is applied to giving fair testimony. Repetition this close together is unusual. Early scholars read the second as widening the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a grievance from what it makes you do, without denying the grievance. The people who barred the way are described as having done exactly that. So the wrong is named in the same sentence that refuses to allow revenge. Cooperation is then defined by content, not by loyalty. The question asked of any alliance is what it is for. That cuts across the tribal assumption that you help your own.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same warning about hatred, applying it to the giving of testimony.
Describes the barring from the Sacred Mosque that this verse refers back to.
Sets the limit of hostility, allowing kindness towards those who did not fight you.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you deal with while carrying an old grievance. Check whether it has started deciding small things: how fast you reply, whether you pass on what they need. Fix one of those this week, without announcing it. The concern here is not the feeling. It is what the feeling has quietly begun to allow.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people not to harm the things that keep pilgrims and their gifts safe. An old grudge against the people who once shut you out is no reason to do wrong. Help each other do good, not harm.

studies.title: The Day The Religion Was Completed
studies.meaning: A long list of what is set aside opens the ayah. Animals found dead, blood, swine, and anything offered to another name. Then beasts killed by a fall or by wild animals, unless reached alive. Divining arrows follow. Then the register changes completely. The ayah says the religion has been brought to completion and the favour finished. Those who reject it have given up hope of its collapse. The last clause returns to the list and lifts it for anyone driven by real hunger.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the closing years of the mission of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The classical scholars place the central declaration very late. Most put it on the plain of Arafat during his final pilgrimage. They also note that the reports about its exact setting do not agree, and they keep more than one account. The material around it speaks to a community that now governed itself. That community needed its practice stated plainly rather than worked out.

keyTerms.note: The verb points to a whole that lacks nothing further, distinct from the verb used a clause later for a favour poured out to the brim. Completeness of form and fullness of measure are named separately.
A passive form: the person does not choose the situation, it forces itself on them. The word governs the whole concession, which is why the exception is read narrowly and tied to genuine compulsion.
Headless arrow shafts marked with instructions and drawn from a bag to settle a decision. Naming them alongside food places a way of seeking knowledge, not only a way of eating, inside the same list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat was scarce and rarely wasted. A carcass found on a trail, an animal that had fallen from a ledge, one gored in a fight over grazing: all of it was food to a hungry camp, and much of it was slaughtered at a stone altar with a name spoken over it. The arrows were drawn before a journey or a raid, at the same shrines. What the ayah lists is not exotic; it is the ordinary week.
studies.didYouKnow: The address to those who believe occurs sixteen times in surah five. That is more than in any other surah. It is more than in the whole of the second surah, which is over twice as long. This ayah falls inside that run of direct address. That is part of why its central declaration reads as spoken to a gathered community rather than about one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Completion is claimed for the religion, not for the community. The difference matters. Nothing further will be added to the guidance. Everything after this is the work of understanding it and living it. The clause about despair casts the opposition as spent, not as a standing threat. A concession for hunger comes right after a statement of perfection. That says the completed thing bends for a starving person without being made less.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same short list and the same concession for necessity, in the earlier Medinan surah.
States the list again in a Meccan setting, showing it was in place long before this declaration.
Repeats the exception for the one driven by hunger, with the same insistence on no intent to transgress.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your own eating is done without a thought given to where the food came from or who it passed through. Once today, before a meal, pause long enough to name it: what this is, how it reached you, who grew or carried it. The pause takes ten seconds and changes very little except your attention.
studies.explainEasier: Some foods are not allowed. Animals that died on their own, blood, pork, and meat offered to other names. God says He has now finished giving this religion. If someone is starving, God forgives them.

studies.title: What The Trained Hawk Brings
studies.meaning: A question is asked and the answer widens rather than narrows. Instead of a list, the reply gives a category: the good and wholesome things are open to you. Then it handles the specific case behind the question, the catch brought back by a trained bird or hound, which the hunter did not kill with his own hand. The training itself is credited to God, who taught the human being the skill that the animal is now taught. The name is to be spoken over what is caught.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It follows directly on the list of what is set aside in the ayah before. Early scholars report that the question came from inside the community. People who had lived by hunting with dogs and falcons wanted to know where the new list left them. The wording keeps the question rather than dissolving it. That is a pattern across this surah, where instruction often arrives as an answer to something actually asked.

keyTerms.note: The root covers what is pleasant, clean and beneficial at once, so the word resists being reduced to a single test. It answers a question about categories with a quality rather than a catalogue.
From a root meaning to wound or to earn, used of animals that take game and of the limbs that acquire. The double sense makes the trained hunter an extension of the hand.
A participle built on the word for dog but applied to any creature schooled to hunt. It describes the handler, not the animal, so the passage credits the discipline rather than the instinct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hunting with a saluki or a hawk was not sport in that world. It was how a household ate in a lean season. A well-trained dog was worth more than a camel to a family at the desert's edge. Training took months of patient work and a bond that survived hunger. The bird came back to the wrist with the catch whole rather than eating it. That restraint was the whole skill.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah closes by calling God Swift in reckoning. That name usually ends passages about accounting and judgement, not passages about food. Placing it here, after a concession, is the surah's habit. A warm allowance is followed by a name that keeps the allowance from being taken as a free hand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims sit inside a practical answer. The first is that skill is handed down. What the handler teaches the animal, God taught the handler. So ability is traced upward rather than owned. The second is that a category can do the work of a list. By answering with the good things rather than an inventory, the reply leaves room for foods and cases nobody in that audience had yet met. That is how a text of fixed length speaks to an open future.

crossReferences.why: Describes the Messenger as making good things open and lifting burdens, the same movement from restriction to relief.
Uses the same word for the good things, addressed to all people rather than to believers alone.
Returns later in this surah to the same principle, warning against declaring off limits what has been left open.

studies.applyIt: Someone taught you the thing you are best at. Today, take two minutes to name them to yourself, and if they are reachable, send them a message that says what specifically you learned and where you have used it since. Not gratitude in general. One skill, one sentence about what it made possible.
studies.explainEasier: People asked what food is allowed. God says all good things are. That includes what your trained dogs and birds catch for you. Say God's name over it before you eat.

studies.title: The Shared Table And The Dowry
studies.meaning: The permission of the ayah before is restated, then stretched in two directions that touch daily life. The food of those who received earlier scripture is open to this community, and theirs to them. The traffic runs both ways, and that is the point. Marriage to chaste women of those communities is placed within reach too. The condition is that the dowry is given and the bond is a marriage, not an arrangement kept quiet. A warning closes the ayah. Rejecting faith empties the work that came before.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Muslims, Jews and Christians lived as neighbours in the city. They traded in the same markets and often shared kinship lines. Early scholars attach no particular occasion to the ayah. They read it against the practical question it settles: whether ordinary social life across those lines was possible at all. The answer given is that eating together and marrying are not the boundary. Belief is.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for what is eaten, without qualification. Its bareness is doing work here: the ayah does not carve out categories of dish or occasion, it names the whole ordinary business of feeding one another.
From a root meaning to fortify. The word carries the sense of a woman whose life is guarded and settled, and the same root supplies the word for a fortress, so honour and security share one image.
Literally their wages or recompense, the same word used elsewhere for reward. Naming the dowry with it makes the payment a right owed to her, not a price paid to her family.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's households were laced together. A date grove might be worked by one family and watered under an agreement with another of a different faith. A wedding drew in cousins on both sides of a religious line. Meals were the visible test. A shared dish was the sign that two families recognised each other. Refusing food was how a community drew a boundary. So opening the table was a public statement, not a private allowance.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for today opens this ayah. It also opens the central clause of the ayah before, two sentences apart. The classical scholars noticed the repetition. They read the two as one moment. That is why the completion of the religion and the opening of the shared table are often discussed together. The two belong to quite different subjects.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah settles a boundary question by moving it. A difference of religion is not treated as something unclean. So food and marriage cross the line. Faith itself is left as the thing that actually marks people apart. The closing warning keeps the openness from reading as not caring. The passage is generous about shared social life and firm about belief. Holding those two together is the position it takes.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same tone toward those who have not fought you: fairness and kindness are not withheld for difference.
Addresses marriage across religious lines from a different angle, in the earlier Medinan surah.
Uses the same word for the dowry, naming it as a right given to the woman herself.

studies.applyIt: Think of one household near you that keeps a different faith or none at all, and whom you have never fed. Invite them for something small this month, tea, or a plate of whatever you were cooking anyway. The point is not a conversation about religion. It is the ordinary act this ayah treats as unremarkable and most of us have quietly stopped doing.
studies.explainEasier: God says good food is allowed for you. The food of Jews and Christians is allowed too, and your food is allowed for them. Marriage to chaste women from those groups is open, as long as the dowry is given.

studies.title: Water, Earth, And No Burden
studies.meaning: The washing before prayer is set out plainly. Face, arms to the elbows, a wipe over the head, the feet. Then the exceptions arrive in order. The state after intimacy, illness, travel, the ordinary needs of the body. Last comes the case where no water can be found, and clean earth stands in for it. The closing sentence explains the whole passage. What is intended is not hardship but cleansing and a favour completed, so that thankfulness follows.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars connect the concession about earth to an incident on a journey. A search for a lost necklace delayed the company and left it without water at prayer time. Reports about the details vary, and more than one occasion is recorded. The general setting is a community often on the move. For them the absence of water was a practical certainty, not a case that never happened.

keyTerms.note: The word covers the surface of the earth broadly, dust and soil and stone, rather than one substance. Choosing a wide word keeps the concession usable wherever a traveller happens to stop.
The same adjective used of permitted food earlier in the surah. Applying it to the ground ties purity of the body to a quality the passage has already been using for what is eaten.
A narrowness, the feeling of a space too tight to move in. The denial is physical in flavour: the passage says the intent is not to close a person in, but to open them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the axis of desert life. Wells were owned, guarded, and sometimes fought over; a caravan planned its stages by them and a miscalculation was fatal. Travellers carried skins that went sour and ran dry, and a party could easily pass a day and a night with none to spare for washing. The permission to use the ground was addressed to people who had already stood at an empty well.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage lists the washing, then spends its final third explaining the intention behind it. That is unusual. Most passages of instruction in the Quran close with a name of God rather than a stated purpose. Here the purpose comes in the negative first: no burden intended. Then the positive is named. Thankfulness is placed last.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Cleansing is presented as something done to the person, not achieved by them. The verbs at the end have God as their subject. That makes the washing a matter of receiving rather than qualifying. Putting earth in place of water sharpens the point. If the material can change entirely without the act being lost, then what is sought is not the water. It is the turning. The passage says so outright.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same concession in almost the same words, in the surah revealed shortly before this one.
States the same principle in another setting: ease is intended for you, and not hardship.
Says outright that no constriction has been laid on you in religion, using the same word.

studies.applyIt: Before your next prayer, slow the washing down by ten seconds. Feel the water on the back of your hands rather than getting through it. Most of us have made this the fastest part of the day, a thing done while thinking about something else. Notice, once, what it is like to arrive at prayer already paying attention.
studies.explainEasier: Before you pray, wash your face, your arms, your head and your feet. If there is no water, you can use clean earth instead. God does not want to make things hard for you. He wants to make you clean.

studies.title: We Hear And We Obey
studies.meaning: Two things are placed together and asked to be held in mind at once: a favour received and a pledge given. The pledge is quoted rather than described, in the words the community itself used. Then the closing clause moves inward. God knows what the chests contain, which turns a public undertaking into something audited privately. The ayah does not repeat the pledge's terms at all. It repeats the moment of saying it, which is a different kind of reminder.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars differ on which pledge is meant. Some read it as the undertaking given at the two meetings before the migration, when delegations from the city committed themselves. Others read it more widely, as the commitment implied in accepting faith at all. The tradition records the range without settling it. The wording is broad enough to hold both readings.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to bind fast, the same family as a tether and a thing relied on. It names an agreement with weight behind it, not an intention stated and then left alone.
An idiom for the innermost content of a person, phrased as a possession of the chest rather than a thought in a mind. It reaches what the speaker themselves may never have examined.
The verb has a reciprocal form, which places God and the community at the two ends of one tie. The pledge is not simply received from above; it is entered into from both sides.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath in Arabia was performed, not filed. Hands were clasped. A formula was spoken aloud before witnesses. The memory of the gathering was the record. Breaking one carried a shame that followed a man's name into other towns. Poets kept the tally. A tribe's good name was largely a list of pledges honoured or betrayed. Those lists were recited at gatherings and remembered long after everyone involved had died.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase quoted here, we hear and we obey, appears elsewhere in the Quran as the answer of believers. It also appears in an altered form, as the reported refusal of an earlier community who said they heard and disobeyed. The same two verbs carry both sentences. So the whole contrast turns on a single word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah pairs memory with answering for what you do. The pairing is the argument. A favour recalled and a pledge recalled are the same act of attention, pointed two ways. The ayah ends with God's knowledge of the chest rather than with a consequence. That puts the honesty of the pledge inside the person. What was said aloud in company is checked somewhere no company can reach.

crossReferences.why: Records the same words as the believers' response to what was sent down to them.
Gives the phrase again as the answer of those called to have a matter judged between them.
Describes those who kept what they pledged to God, and those among them still waiting.

studies.applyIt: Recall a commitment you made out loud, to a person or in prayer, that nobody else remembers. Do not judge how you have done with it. Just say it again to yourself in the same words you used, and notice which part of you flinches. That flinch is the ayah's subject, and it is more useful than a fresh resolution.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to remember what He gave them, and the promise they made to Him. They said they would listen and obey. He knows what is really inside people's hearts.

studies.title: Justice Is Nearer To Awe
studies.meaning: The instruction comes with its own obstacle attached. Hatred of a people is named as the pressure that bends judgement. The verse does not ask for the hatred to be settled first. It repeats the command bare. Then it gives a comparison rather than an absolute: acting justly is nearer to awareness of God. Early scholars note how modest that phrasing is. It measures an act by the direction it is heading, not by calling it enough.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah. The passage begins with the standing of agreements and moves on to how people hostile to the community are treated. By this point relations with several groups had broken down, after years of raids and broken terms. Early scholars record no single occasion. They read the warning as addressed to a community that now had the power to be unfair.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word whose root meaning is presence. A witness is one who was there, so testimony is described as reporting what you actually have rather than as arguing for a side.

From the root for balancing two weights. The same consonants can also mean to turn aside, so the word holds fairness and straying together. The verse uses that, commanding one and warning of the other.

A comparative, not a superlative. Just conduct is placed nearer to awareness of God than the alternative, rather than made the same as it. That keeps the statement measured and leaves room for the difficulty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia was a group act. Witnesses were not strangers but the men of a clan. Their word carried the weight of the group behind it. So an honest witness could be accused of betraying his own people. Feuds ran for decades, and everyone could recite the injuries. Being asked to testify accurately about a tribe that had killed your relatives was not a test on paper.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and 4:135 form a pair, and the pairing is exact. Each begins by calling believers to stand. Each names a temptation. The two temptations are opposites. One warns against being pulled by love of yourself and your family. This one warns against being pushed by hatred of an enemy. Between them they cover both ways a witness can lean.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is presented as something that survives hostility. It does not depend on the other side deserving it. The passage assumes a settled dislike and asks for accuracy anyway. Fairness is cut loose from goodwill. Calling it nearer to awareness of God, rather than the same as it, makes a further point. The act is no stand-in for an inner state. But it is the closest thing within reach of a person who is not there yet.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same demand with its terms reversed, naming desire rather than hatred as the pressure.
Uses the same warning about hatred a few verses earlier, applied to revenge.
Extends fairness to those who have not fought you, describing God as loving the equitable.

studies.applyIt: Pick a person or a group whose views reliably irritate you and find one thing they have got right. Say it plainly, without the softening clause that takes it back. You are not endorsing anything. The verse assumes the dislike stays and asks only that it stop editing what you are willing to admit is true.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to be fair and to tell the truth when they speak up, even about people they cannot stand. Hating someone is not a reason to treat them unfairly. God knows what you do.

studies.title: A Promise And Its Opposite
studies.meaning: Two sentences, built as a matched pair, close the section. The first is a promise made by God, and the word for promise is used rather than a conditional: forgiveness and a great reward are stated as owed. The second describes those who refused and denied the signs, and promises nothing at all; it simply names where they belong. The asymmetry is deliberate. Reward is framed as a commitment God has taken on, while the other outcome is left as a description.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes a passage about fairness toward people one has reason to resent. The instruction just before it says not to let hostility push a person into injustice. The pair here supplies the horizon that makes such restraint bearable. Early scholars note no separate occasion for these two ayat. The placement does the work. It turns a moral demand into something with a stated outcome on both sides.

keyTerms.note: The verb of a binding undertaking, used in Arabic for what a person can be held to. Applied to God it makes the following clause an obligation He has placed on Himself, rather than a possibility.
The first word is a wage for labour done, not a gift. Pairing it with an adjective of magnitude keeps the sense of something earned while removing any proportion between the work and the payment.
A name built from a root for a fire kindled fiercely and heaped high. The Quran uses several names for the fire, and this one carries intensity rather than depth or duration.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wages in that economy were usually paid late. A herdsman worked a season and was paid at its end. A caravan hand was paid on the return, a harvester at the threshing floor. Trust that payment would come was the whole basis of hiring. A master known to withhold could not hire again. Promises of later payment were the ordinary money of work. That is why a promise named as a promise carried weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat are close to the same length in Arabic and share one shape in the grammar. That is why they are commonly recited together and treated as a single movement. The pattern of a matched promise and warning runs through this surah. It tends to arrive at the close of a section rather than at its opening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a promise beside a description says something about how the two outcomes are held. One is guaranteed by an undertaking. The other follows from what a person has done. It is stated without any language of obligation on God's part. The classical scholars point to that imbalance. They read it as mercy built into the grammar, not added later as a softening.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical promise formula and adds that God's word is the truest there is.
Sets the same two outcomes as a pair in a Meccan surah, keeping the same order.
Names forgiveness and gardens as the reward, using the same word for a wage earned.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you did this week that nobody noticed and that cost you something, a temper held, a favour done quietly, an honest answer that was inconvenient. Do not tell anyone about it. Sit with the fact that it was recorded anyway. Then do one more of the same kind today, deliberately unwitnessed.
studies.explainEasier: God has made a promise to people who believe and do good. They will be forgiven and given a great reward. People who turn away and call His signs lies will end up in the Fire.

studies.title: The Hands That Were Held Back
studies.meaning: A rescue is recalled without being described. A group meant to reach out their hands against the community, and the hands were held back. Nothing is said about who they were, when it happened, or what stopped them. The classical scholars offer several possible episodes without settling on one. That openness leaves the ayah usable by anyone. What follows is not gratitude but reliance. The memory is given as a reason to place trust where it has already proved sound.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Reports name more than one occasion. There is a planned attack while the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) sat with a delegation. There is an ambush prepared on an expedition. There is a raider who found him resting and was disarmed. Early scholars record several and do not agree. That is why the ayah is usually read for its principle rather than its incident. The setting is a community under threat off and on.

keyTerms.note: The verb of spreading something open, used of a hand offering as readily as of a hand seizing. The menace lies entirely in the object of the sentence; the gesture itself is neutral.
To restrain by withholding, as one keeps a hand from falling. The verb does not describe destroying the threat, only stopping it, which is a smaller and far more common kind of rescue.
A command in the third person, softer than a direct order. The form states what should follow rather than instructing an individual, which suits a conclusion drawn from something already witnessed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raid in Arabia was decided quickly and carried out at dawn. Camps posted watches. But the real defence was knowing which tribes had reason to come, and which had given their word not to. Everyone had a story of a night that could have gone differently. A horse that shied. A scout who lost the trail. A plan dropped for reasons nobody on the receiving end ever learned.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as intended describes a plan formed and nearly acted on, not a passing wish. Arabic marks the difference between settled resolve and idle thought. The Quran uses this verb sparingly. Its best known use is of Joseph's moment of near-yielding. So its appearance signals an intention that had already hardened into a decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is described as a hold on someone else's hand. It is not a shield around the protected. That places God's action inside another person's choice. That is the harder claim. It also means most rescues are never seen. If the help comes at the level of an intention never acted on, the protected party cannot count how often it has happened. The instruction to rely follows from not knowing.

crossReferences.why: Records another moment when a threatened people answered with reliance and came away untouched.
Describes a plot to seize or expel the Prophet, and God's planning set against it.
Names another occasion when God turned back those who had come, without the community fighting.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing that could have gone badly for you this year and did not: an illness caught early, a journey you missed, a person who changed their mind about you. You will never know the full list. Take the one you can name and say something for it tonight, out loud, before you ask for anything else.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to remember a time when some men planned to attack them. He stopped their hands before they could. So keep God in mind, and trust Him.

studies.title: Twelve Chiefs And A Loan
studies.meaning: A covenant is recalled in its first form, with its terms listed. Twelve representatives were appointed, one for each tribal division. The pledge was given a condition and a consequence in one sentence. Prayer, alms, belief in the messengers, support for them, and a loan made to God: five terms. Against them stands a promise. Wrongs will be covered over and they will be let into gardens. The final clause says plainly what happens if the covenant is dropped after all that.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It opens a long section addressed to communities who had received earlier scripture. The Quran takes the story as known and does not tell it. That suits an audience in the city which included people who could supply the details. The recall serves the surah's argument about covenants. It has just told the believers to remember their own pledge. Now it shows an earlier one and what became of it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to bore through or to investigate. The word names someone who looks into a group's affairs on another's behalf, closer to an inspector than a ruler, and carries responsibility rather than rank.
A loan, not a gift, and the adjective means good in the sense of well made. The image places God in the borrower's position, which is startling enough that the early scholars pause on it.
The verb means to cover, from the same root as a farmer covering seed with soil. Wrongs are not erased in the picture; they are buried, which is a different promise from never having done them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lending in Arabia was a serious social act. A loan without interest to a man in difficulty marked a generous house. It was kept in memory. It was repaid in loyalty as much as in coin. Tribes appointed spokesmen for talks. Those men carried their group's word and answered for it. So both the twelve overseers and the loan would have read as familiar arrangements, not as images.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of lending to God appears six times in the Quran, always with the same two words. It always carries a promise of multiplying or of forgiveness. It never promises repayment in kind. This is one of very few places where a trading verb is used of God, with God on the receiving side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The covenant is conditional and says so. That marks it off from a guarantee of status. God's presence, I am with you, comes before the conditions rather than after. So being accompanied is not the reward for keeping the terms. It is the setting in which the terms are kept. The closing clause makes clear that a covenant can be entered and lost. That is this surah's steady theme, applied here to an earlier community.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of a loan made to God, and answers the question the image provokes.
Mentions the same division into twelve, in the account of the years in the wilderness.
Recalls the community's own pledge a few ayat earlier, which this covenant is set beside.

studies.applyIt: Lend something this week without keeping a record of it: time, money, a tool, an hour of listening. Then deliberately do not follow up. Most of us lend with a quiet ledger running in the background. Try one transaction where you close the ledger at the start, and notice how differently the giving feels.
studies.explainEasier: God made a deal with the Children of Israel. He chose twelve leaders from them. He said He would be with them if they prayed and gave to the poor. They also had to trust His messengers. Then He would forgive them and give them gardens.

studies.title: Pardon Them And Overlook
studies.meaning: A hard description ends in an unexpected instruction. A broken covenant produced hardened hearts. Words were moved out of their places. Part of the reminder was simply let go. The passage then says that betrayal will keep surfacing, with a small exception noted: except a few of them. Instead of allowing a response, it tells the Prophet to pardon and to turn away from the matter. The closing clause gives the reason. It concerns God's love, not what the other party deserves.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, during a time of strained relations between the young community and some of the older communities of the city. Early scholars do not tie the ayah to a single episode. They read it against the general situation instead. The exception clause is not decoration. It marks that the description does not cover everyone. The classical commentaries keep it carefully whenever they sum up the passage.

keyTerms.note: Used of stone that has lost any give, and of a heart in the same way. The image is not of a heart turned evil but of one that no longer registers pressure, which is a subtler failure.
From a root for an edge or a margin. The verb suggests moving something to one side rather than destroying it, so what is described is displacement of meaning more than deletion of text.
Built on the word for a broad flat surface, which includes the page of a book and the flat of a sword. It asks for more than pardon: to present a smooth face and let the matter drop.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grievances in Arabia were stored in poetry. A wrong done to a tribe was put into verse. It was learned by heart and recited at every gathering. So a feud could outlive everyone who started it by generations. A man who let an injury go risked his standing. The give and take that protected a tribe rested on one certainty: nothing was ever simply dropped. An instruction to overlook cut against that whole machinery.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs at the end of this ayah, pardon and overlook, occur together several times in the Quran. They always come as a pair aimed at the wronged party, not at the wrongdoer. The second shares a root with the word for a page. That is why the English idiom about turning a page lands close to the Arabic image.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction to pardon is not grounded in the other party's innocence. The ayah has just spent four clauses denying it. It is grounded in what God loves. That moves the reason for mercy entirely. Mercy becomes a statement about the one forgiving, not a verdict on the one forgiven. The ayah also refuses to condemn a whole group, and it does so in a single phrase. That refusal sits inside the charge rather than after it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to pardon and overlook to the same community in the earlier surah.
Asks whether you would not love to be forgiven, and makes that the ground for forgiving.
Continues immediately with a parallel account of another community's neglected pledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of the grievance you retell most often, the one with a polished version you have told several people. Notice how much of the retelling is maintenance. This week, when the opening comes to tell it again, let it pass. You do not have to forgive anything yet. Just stop keeping the account current.
studies.explainEasier: They broke their promise, so their hearts grew hard. They moved words around and forgot part of what they were told. God still tells the Prophet to forgive them and let it go.

studies.title: The Forgotten Portion
studies.meaning: The frame of the ayah before returns, with a different community and a different outcome. A pledge was taken. A portion of what had been given as a reminder was let go. The consequence named is not punishment arriving from outside. It is division within: enmity and hatred set among them, and lasting. The classical scholars read the forgotten portion as the part that would have held them together. The last clause puts off the accounting rather than delivering it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The community addressed here had a long history of division within it by the seventh century. Arabian audiences knew of it through trade contacts to the north. They knew of it too through Christian communities in the south and east of the peninsula. The Quran does not list the disputes. It names the mechanism instead. That lets the ayah work as a general warning rather than as a report.

keyTerms.note: A share allotted, as of an inheritance or a division of spoils. Calling the neglected part a portion implies the reminder came apportioned, so letting one share go leaves a gap rather than a smaller whole.
From a root meaning to fasten glue to a thing, hence to make something stick. The verb pictures enmity adhering between people, difficult to separate once it has been applied.
An intensive form well beyond ordinary dislike, paired here with a separate word for open hostility. Naming both keeps the inward feeling and its outward expression distinct from one another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian merchants travelled north to Syria and south to Yemen. They met Christian communities that differed sharply from one another and knew it. Monasteries dotted the trade roads. Travellers brought back arguments along with goods. A caravan hand could describe more than one kind of church without being able to explain the difference. That ordinary awareness is the background against which the ayah's claim landed.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it are built on the same frame: a pledge taken, a portion neglected. Only the consequence changes. The Quran uses such close repetition sparingly. Here the effect is to make the difference between the two outcomes stand out against a sentence that is otherwise nearly the same.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division is presented as a consequence, not an accident. The mechanism given is neglect, not rebellion. Nothing is described as denied outright. Something was simply allowed to slip. That makes the warning harder to escape, since neglect needs no decision at any point. The verdict is put off to the last day rather than issued here. That also keeps the passage from being used to judge any living person.

crossReferences.why: Names holding together to the rope of God as precisely what prevents the outcome described here.
Says division came after knowledge arrived, out of rivalry between them rather than ignorance.
Sets up the frame this ayah repeats, using the same words for the neglected portion.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you learned once and know you have let go: a language, a practice, a discipline you were good at. Do not try to restore it. Just spend fifteen minutes with it this week and notice how much is still there. This ayah is about portions dropped quietly, and most of ours are dropped without a decision.
studies.explainEasier: God also took a promise from people who called themselves Christians. They forgot part of what they were told. So He let anger and hate grow between them. One day He will show them what they did.

studies.title: A Light And A Clear Book
studies.meaning: An address is made directly to those who hold earlier scripture, and it is framed as arrival rather than accusation. The messenger clarifies much of what had been kept concealed and, this is the striking half, passes over much else. Deliberate silence is named as part of the mission. Then the sentence turns to what has come: a light, and a book that makes things plain. The two are given without an explicit link, and the early scholars differ on whether the light names the messenger or the revelation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the section of the surah addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. Early scholars report no specific occasion. The setting is a city where learning in scripture was present. Questions about what a text said, and what had been left out of public teaching, were live and often argued. The ayah enters that conversation as a claim about what is disclosed, not as a demand.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite in the Arabic, so a light rather than the light. The early scholars read it as the messenger or as the revelation, and the indefiniteness is part of why the question stays open.
An active participle, so the book is not merely clear but clarifying: it does something to what it touches. The same root supplies the verb used two clauses earlier for the messenger's work.

The verb of pardoning, used here of information rather than of offence. It describes leaving something undisclosed as an act of forbearance, which is unusual to praise in a passage about clarification.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in seventh-century Arabia was mostly heard, not read. Texts lived with the scholars who held them. They were recited in gatherings. They reached ordinary people through teachers who chose what to pass on. Reading was rare and manuscripts rarer. So what a community knew of its own book leaned heavily on a small number of people. A claim about what had been kept back was, in that setting, a claim about those people.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and one four later open with the same address and the same phrase about a messenger who has come. The two form a bracket around the material between them. The surah uses that kind of repeated opening several times. It gives the long middle section a shape you hear in recitation before you see it on a page.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described here as disclosure with restraint. The restraint is credited, not apologised for. That says something about how the Quran understands its own scope. It does not claim to settle every question a reader might bring. It treats some silences as mercy. The ayah also frames the meeting between communities as one about information rather than power. That sets the terms for the passage that follows.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the address and the arrival, moving the emphasis to the long gap that preceded it.
Calls the revelation a light by which God guides whom He wills, using the same image.
Speaks of a covenant to make the scripture clear to people and not to conceal it.

studies.applyIt: There is something you know about someone that you could say and have not said. Check, once, which kind of silence it is: protection, or avoidance. This ayah praises one and not the other, and the difference is usually obvious to you and to nobody else. You do not need to act today. Just name it accurately.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the people who have earlier books that His messenger has come to them. He makes clear much of what they were hiding, and leaves much of it alone. A light and a clear book have come.

studies.title: The Ways Of Peace
studies.meaning: The light of the sentence before is given a job here, and it is movement rather than glow. God guides by it those who follow what pleases Him along the roads of peace. He brings them out of darkness into light. The plural is worth noticing: darknesses, several, against a single light. The passage ends with a straight path. Three images of direction are stacked in one sentence, and none of them is explained.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address to communities holding earlier scripture. No specific occasion is reported. The argument in the surah has been about disclosure and concealment. This passage answers the question left hanging: what the newly arrived light is for. The community in the city had itself just been assembled out of tribes that had fought each other. So roads of peace was not an abstraction.

keyTerms.note: A plural of paths, not one road. The second word covers peace, soundness and safety together, and is also a name of God, so the phrase can be heard as the roads that lead to Him.
Plural in Arabic where English has only a singular. Darkness comes in kinds and layers; light in this sentence stays single, and the imbalance is a regular feature of the Quran's use of the pair.

An intensive form of contentment, used almost exclusively of God's acceptance. What is followed here is not a rule but an inclination, which makes the condition attached to guidance one of orientation rather than performance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A route across Arabia was chosen for safety before speed. Some wadis were held by tribes with a grudge, some wells had a price, and a guide's whole value was knowing which was which this season. Caravans travelled by night under stars they had learned by name, and a wrong turn in the dark meant days lost or worse. Peace and road were practically the same word to a traveller.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran pairs darkness with light thirteen times. In every one of them darkness is plural in the Arabic while light stays singular. The plural form of the word for light never occurs in the text at all. English translations smooth this out, because a plural darkness reads awkwardly. So a reader working from a translation rarely meets the pattern.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as something done to a person who has already turned. That puts human leaning before God's direction, without making it the cause. The clause by His permission sits in the middle. It keeps the movement from running on its own. Peace is named as where the roads end, not as their condition. That reverses the usual assumption that a person has to be at peace before setting out.

crossReferences.why: Describes God as the ally who brings believers out of darkness into light, in the same words.
Opens by naming the book's purpose as bringing people out of darkness into light.
Says God and His angels do this for the believers, adding mercy as the motive.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement you are in that has more than one way forward. List the routes honestly, including the one that costs you something. Then ask which of them ends with everyone still speaking. That is the only test this ayah offers, and it usually rules out the option you had already decided on.
studies.explainEasier: God uses this light to guide anyone who wants to please Him. He shows them roads of peace. He takes them out of the dark and into the light. He puts them on a straight road.

studies.title: Who Could Prevent God
studies.meaning: A specific claim is named and rejected: that God is the Messiah, son of Mary. The refutation is not an argument from scripture but from a single question. If God willed to bring the Messiah to an end, along with his mother and everyone on earth, who could hold Him back? Naming the mother beside the son places both inside the created order. The sentence then widens to sovereignty over the heavens and the earth, and to a creating that answers to nothing outside itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's long address to communities holding earlier scripture. Christian communities were present in Arabia, at Najran in the south and along the northern trade routes. Delegations reached the city. Early scholars do not tie the ayah to one meeting. It takes up a particular wording rather than a whole community. That is why the phrasing is exact about what is being denied.

keyTerms.note: The Quran keeps this title throughout and never disputes it; what it disputes is what the title is taken to mean. The word appears twice in this one sentence, both times with the son of Mary attached.
The verb of ownership rather than of strength. The question asks who possesses anything at all against God, which turns a debate about nature into a question about property and control.

keyTerms.gloss: to destroy, bring to an end
keyTerms.note: A verb used of perishing and of being lost. Applying it to an imagined case tests the claim. It asks what would follow if the one being called God could cease, which is the whole argument packed tight.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia knew Christianity through monks on the caravan roads. It knew it through the church at Najran, which had its own bishops. It knew it through Abyssinia across the sea. A Christian king there had sheltered emigrants from Mecca. Traders carried disputes about doctrine north and south, along with incense and cloth. The wordings argued over in Syrian and Ethiopian churches were not distant ideas. They arrived in the market with the goods.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran. Jesus is nearly always identified as her son rather than through a father's line. That holds even in passages that dispute claims made about him. The nineteenth surah carries her name. It gives her story at greater length than any other passage in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument turns on what can be ended, not on scripture. That makes it available to anyone. Whatever can be brought to an end is not the one who ends things. Whatever entered existence through birth has a beginning. By adding everyone on earth to the same clause, the ayah refuses to single anyone out. The Messiah being created is stated as the shared condition of all created things. It is not a demotion of him in particular.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same claim later in this surah and adds the Messiah's own words about worship.
Compares the creation of Jesus to that of Adam, made from dust by a word.
Gives Jesus describing himself as a servant of God, in his own reported speech.

studies.applyIt: If you have a Christian friend or colleague, ask them sometime what they actually believe. Ask for their own words, not what you have heard about it. Listen without correcting. This ayah is exact about the wording it addresses. Being exact is impossible if you have only ever heard a position described by people who reject it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say God is the Messiah, the son of Mary. The Quran asks who could stop God if He chose to end the Messiah, his mother, and everyone on earth. Everything belongs to God.

studies.title: Then Why Does He Punish You
studies.meaning: A claim of special standing is quoted and answered with a question, not a denial. The ayah asks why, in that case, they are punished for their wrongs. The answer given is short and deflating. You are human beings from among those He created. What follows removes the last footing for the claim. Forgiveness and punishment are placed entirely within God's will. Then the sentence widens to sovereignty and return. Nothing is left resting on inherited status.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's address to communities of earlier scripture. The classical scholars report that a version of the claim was made in the city. It was said in conversation with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The reports differ in their details. The wider setting is a society where group identity was inherited and rarely questioned. There a claim of favour by descent sounded ordinary, not provoking.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the intensive form, so considerably more than fondness. Pairing it with the claim of sonship shows what was at stake: not affection but a standing that no conduct could put at risk.
The word for the human as flesh and skin, distinct from the term that emphasises companionship or forgetting. It is the plainest available way of saying you are made of what everyone else is made of.
A noun of place from a verb meaning to become. It names not simply where one arrives but what one turns into on arriving, which is why it closes passages about answering for what you do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the load-bearing structure of Arabian society. A man's line was recited before his name in formal settings. It decided whom he could marry. It decided what protection he could claim, and where he sat at a gathering. Claims of inherited favour were the ordinary language of status. The reply here is that you are human beings from among those He created. That takes down a whole social structure in one short clause.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah answers a claim with a question and never states the other position directly. The correction arrives entirely through what the listener has to grant. This is a recurring method in the surah. It prefers to argue by asking rather than by declaring. That is part of why several of its passages read as one side of a live conversation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates being loved from being let off. It does not deny that God loves. This surah says elsewhere that He will bring a people He loves and who love Him. What it denies is that love can be inherited, or that it suspends consequence. Placing forgiveness and punishment together under one will keeps both hope and answering for what you do alive. Neither is allowed to harden into a possession.

crossReferences.why: Answers another claim of exclusive entry with a demand for proof rather than a flat denial.
Speaks of a people God loves and who love Him, showing love described but never inherited.
States that outcomes follow deeds rather than the wishes of any community about itself.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where you assume you get some latitude, because of your family, your record, how long you have been doing this, how much you have given. Say the assumption out loud to yourself in one sentence. You do not need to dismantle it today. Most of us have never even heard ours stated plainly.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said they were God's children and the ones He loves. The Quran asks why He punishes them then. They are people He made, like everyone else. He forgives and punishes whom He wants.

studies.title: After A Long Silence
studies.meaning: The address of a few ayat earlier returns, this time with a different emphasis. A messenger has come, and the phrase that matters is the one about a gap: after an interval in which no messenger came. The purpose is stated as pre-emption, so that you cannot say nobody came to us. Then the two functions are named, bringer of good news and warner, and immediately repeated in the affirmative. Nothing is argued here. A gap is closed and the record set straight.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The interval meant is the stretch between Jesus and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The classical sources reckon it at several centuries. The figures the early scholars give differ from one another. Across that period Arabia held prophetic memory but no prophetic presence of its own. That is part of why the region shows up so little in the scriptural histories the surrounding communities kept.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to slacken or fall quiet after activity. It names a pause in something ongoing rather than a simple absence, which frames the gap as an interruption within a sequence.
From the root for skin, because news that pleases shows first in the face. The word names the effect on the hearer rather than the content of what is carried.
One who gives notice of something coming while there is still time to act on it. The Arabic carries urgency without threat; a warner in this sense performs a service rather than a punishment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News in Arabia arrived on foot. A rider reaching an encampment was surrounded before he dismounted, and what he carried, a raid, a death, a market price, a birth, was repeated and turned over for days afterwards. The one who came with good news was rewarded with a gift by custom. Both of the words in this ayah name roles that existed in that society and were paid for.
studies.didYouKnow: The two titles paired here, bringer of good news and warner, recur throughout the Quran. They appear wherever a messenger's role is being defined, and rarely alone. In this ayah they turn up twice inside one sentence. Once inside the objection being headed off, then again in the answer to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah treats the absence of guidance as an argument a person could really make. It takes that argument seriously enough to close it. So answering for what you do is tied to access. Nobody is held to what never reached them. The ayah also frames revelation as a reply to a possible complaint, not as something imposed. That shifts the whole encounter from demand to answer.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle: messengers sent so people have no argument against God afterwards.
Says no community is called to account until a messenger has been sent to it.
Opens with the same address and the same arrival, with its emphasis on disclosure instead.

studies.applyIt: Think of an excuse you keep in reserve: nobody told me, I was never taught, it was not explained. Test one of them honestly this week by finding out whether the information was actually available to you. Sometimes it was not, and that matters. Often it was, and knowing which is which is worth the half hour.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the people who have earlier books that His messenger has come to them. He came after a long time with no messengers. Now no one can say that nobody warned them.

studies.title: Prophets, Kings, And A Land
studies.meaning: Moses counts the favours before making the demand, and the order matters. Prophets among you, kingship, and a gift given to no other people: three items, and none of them the land. Then the instruction arrives. It is framed as entry into something already assigned, not conquest of something new. The warning attached is not about failure but about turning back, which is a different risk entirely. The loss named is what that turning would cost them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the Quran is retelling a history its audience partly knew. The episode belongs to the years after the escape from Egypt, at the edge of the land. In this surah the passage sits directly after the covenant recalled at its opening. So a broken pledge and a refused instruction stand a few ayat apart. Early scholars treat that sequence as the surah's argument rather than as chronology.

keyTerms.note: The early scholars read the plural several ways: rulers in fact, or people freed from serving anyone, or households with a home and a servant of their own. Every reading turns on ownership of one's own life.
A passive participle from a root meaning to be pure and to be set aside. The land is not called holy in itself but made so, which keeps the sanctity a matter of designation.
The verb of a reversal, physically retreating the way one came. It is the same word used elsewhere for abandoning faith, so the image of walking backwards carries both senses at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For an Arabian audience, entering land held by others was a familiar prospect and a frightening one. Settled towns had walls, wells and stored grain. Nomadic groups had mobility and little to defend. A decision to move on a fortified place was taken by consultation. It could split a tribe. The ones who went were rarely the ones who had argued for it. Reluctance here needed no explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places where the Quran gives a speech of Moses to his own people with no confrontation with Pharaoh nearby. Most of the Moses material is built around the contest in Egypt. This passage belongs to the harder, later story. The surah reaches for it because its subject is covenant rather than rescue.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The favour is recited before the demand, and that sets a pattern. What is asked of a community is presented as fitting what it has already received. Naming the land as written for them makes the instruction a matter of taking possession. It is not a gamble. That is exactly what the refusal in the next ayah will not accept. Assurance, the passage implies, does not remove the need to walk.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reply immediately, and the refusal turns on exactly the assurance offered here.
Describes the inheritance of the land promised, within a passage on the same history.
Recalls the same favour, being preferred over the worlds, at the start of the longest surah.

studies.applyIt: Before you next ask someone for something difficult, spend a minute listing what they have already given you. Say one item of it aloud when you ask. Not as technique. The order in this passage is favour first, demand second. Most requests fail because they arrive with the second half only.
studies.explainEasier: Moses told his people to remember what God gave them. God sent prophets among them and made them rulers. Then he told them to go into the holy land God had set aside for them, and not to turn back.

studies.title: Not Until They Leave
studies.meaning: The refusal is careful, and that is what makes it damning. They do not deny the promise or the prophet; they attach a condition. There are overpowering people in it, so we will not enter until they leave, and if they leave we will enter. The logic is impeccable and empty: they will take the land at precisely the moment it needs no taking. Faith is not rejected in this sentence. It is postponed until it costs nothing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a retelling addressed to a community that was itself being asked for difficult things. The Quran gives the episode without dating it. It does not name the people in the land beyond the single word used for them. What the surah wants from the story is its shape. So the details a chronicle would supply are left out, and the reply is quoted at length instead.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to compel, or to set a broken bone by force. The word can describe a giant, a tyrant, or simply one who imposes, and the early scholars note that all three senses were heard here.
The particle that carries the whole refusal. Everything before it is agreement and everything after it is a condition, which is how a postponement is made to sound very much like consent.

A participle rather than a verb, so it states a settled state instead of an act. Choosing this form for a promise about the future makes it sound far more certain than the speakers' behaviour warrants.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every fortified settlement in the region was defended by people who had held it for generations. They knew every approach to it. An attacking force fought uphill against walls, with no supply line behind them. The reluctance this passage records made military sense. The audience hearing it in the city knew what that reasoning felt like from the inside. They had faced decisions of the same shape.
studies.didYouKnow: The refusal in this ayah is quoted at greater length than the instruction that provoked it. A second, blunter refusal is quoted two ayat later. The Quran gives more words here to what the people said than to what the prophet said. That is unusual. It turns the passage into a study of one particular kind of answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a failure that is not disbelief and is much harder to see. Everything the speakers say fits with faith. What is missing is willingness to act while the outcome is still uncertain. That puts the test in timing rather than in doctrine. It also shows that a promise from God does not remove risk from the person who has to move first. The passage does not pretend otherwise.

crossReferences.why: Answers immediately with two men who accept the same facts and draw the opposite conclusion.
Describes another moment of hanging back when the going was hard, and what was said of it.
Records a group who withdrew while others thought about God, and quotes their reasoning back.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you agree with something in principle and attach a condition to it. Write the condition down. Then ask what would have to be true for it to be met, and whether you would still be needed at that point. Some conditions are prudence. Some are a way of saying no while sounding like yes.
studies.explainEasier: The people told Moses that strong men lived in that land. They said they would not go in until those men left. If the men left, then they would go in.

studies.title: Go At Them By The Gate
studies.meaning: Two voices break the consensus, and the passage describes them oddly: two men of those who feared, whom God had favoured. The fear is not denied, it is stated and then set beside the advice. Their counsel is tactical rather than inspiring, go in by the gate, and once you are inside you will prevail, and only after that practical instruction do they name reliance on God. Courage here is presented as a plan plus a trust, in that order.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars identify the two men from the earlier scriptural tradition and differ over the details they report. That is why the Quran's own account leaves them unnamed. They are marked only by their fear and by God's favour on them. The surah is addressing a community that had recently lived through its own moments of shared hesitation. It keeps the account very short.

keyTerms.note: The early scholars read the object of this fear in more than one way: fear of God, or fear of the people holding the land. The Arabic leaves it open, and the ayah carries either reading.

A single definite gate, not gates in general. The advice is concrete enough to be acted on, which is what distinguishes it from encouragement, and the early scholars note the practicality without settling which gate.
From a root for overcoming in a contest. Stated as a participle rather than as a promise verb, so the outcome is described as a condition they will be in rather than as a guarantee issued to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A walled town lived or died at its gate. Walls could not be taken by men on foot, but a gate could be rushed at the right hour, and every raid in that world was planned around one. Those who knew the timing of the gates, when they opened for water carriers and when the watch changed, were worth more than fighters. Advice about a gate was expert advice.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage names the two men only by an attribute and never gives their names. The older tradition supplies them, and the classical commentaries record what it says. The Quran does this often, keeping a figure anonymous while preserving their words exactly. That shifts attention from who was speaking to what was actually said.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance on God is placed after the plan, not instead of it, and the ordering is the passage's argument. The two men do not claim the outcome is assured regardless; they name a specific action, predict what follows it, and only then locate the whole thing in trust. That keeps trust from becoming a substitute for judgement. And the note that they feared makes courage a thing done with fear rather than in its absence.

crossReferences.why: Pairs consultation and decision with reliance on God, arranged in the same order as here.
Instructs preparation of whatever force can be mustered, then turns to reliance in the next breath.
Shows Jacob giving practical instructions to his sons and then naming God as the one relied on.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been praying about and have not planned for. Give it twenty minutes today: write down the first concrete step, the gate. Keep praying about it. The two men in this passage did both, and the passage puts the practical half first without treating it as any less faithful.
studies.explainEasier: Two men who were afraid, but whom God had helped, spoke up. They told the people to go in through the gate. Once inside, they would win. They said to trust God if they really believed.

studies.title: We Are Staying Right Here
studies.meaning: The second refusal drops the pretence. Never, as long as they are in it. Then comes a sentence the early scholars treat as the low point of the whole exchange: you and your Lord go and fight, we are sitting here. The prophet's response is not anger but a statement of limits, I control only myself and my brother, followed by a request to be separated from the people. He does not argue any further. He hands the situation back.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The Quran keeps the words of the refusal without softening them. Early scholars note that this is unusual for a passage recounting an earlier community's failure. The surah is building a case about covenants abandoned, and this is its sharpest illustration. The answer that follows is quoted just as exactly. So a reader gets both the insult and the reply in their original form.

keyTerms.note: A participle of sitting, and the Quran uses the same word elsewhere for those who stay behind when others go out. A physical posture became a standing term for withholding oneself.

The verb of ownership again, applied here to the self. It concedes that a prophet's authority does not extend to compelling anyone, which is a statement about the limits of the office rather than a complaint.
To draw a distinction between two things, from the root that gives the word for a criterion. The request is that a division be made, not that a punishment be sent down.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader in Arabia commanded by consent, not by right. A chief who called for a march and was refused had no way to compel anyone. Men simply stayed at their tents, and the matter was over. Standing in front of a group that had decided not to move was among the most exposed positions in that society. Everyone hearing this passage had either been in it or watched someone be.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sitting used in this refusal comes back in the Quran for those who stayed behind from later expeditions. In one passage it is set directly against those who strive. A term for a body position became one of the text's standard words for a moral choice. That happened through that kind of use.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prophet's answer defines prophethood by what it cannot do. He can deliver the message. He can decline to be counted with a refusal. There the office ends. That protects a reader from two errors at once: expecting a messenger to compel belief, and blaming him for a community's choice. The request to be separated is also not a curse. It asks for a distinction, and what follows is a consequence rather than a punishment sent.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who were glad to sit behind, using the same root for their position.
Contrasts those who sit at home with those who strive, without condemning the seated outright.
States that a prophet cannot compel people into belief, which is the limit named here.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you have been carrying a decision that is not yours to make: a relative's choice, a colleague's work, a friend's direction. Say the sentence this passage models, that you have control only over yourself. Then act on the part that actually is yours, and let the rest be someone else's to answer for.
studies.explainEasier: The people told Moses they would never go in while those men were there. They said he and his Lord should go and fight, and they would stay. Moses asked God to keep him apart from them.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Forty Years Of Wandering
studies.meaning: The answer to the request is a consequence, and it is measured. The land is closed to them for forty years, during which they will wander without bearings. Nothing is destroyed and nobody is struck down; the generation that refused simply does not arrive. The last clause is addressed to the prophet, and it concerns grief: do not sorrow over them. That instruction is easy to miss and is the reason the passage ends where it does rather than with the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The forty years is stated in the Quran itself rather than worked out. Early scholars note the match with the older scriptural account without dwelling on it. The surah places this outcome shortly after the covenant it recalled at its opening. So a reader meets a pledge, a refusal and a consequence within twenty ayat of one another. That is the argument the arrangement is making.
