keyTerms.note: Not simply travelling without arriving, but losing one's bearings; the root gives the word for a trackless waste. The wandering is described as a state of the people rather than of the route.
A number the Quran uses for a period of full maturing, as for the age at which a person reaches their strength. Here the span is long enough for one generation to be replaced by another.
A verb of sorrow bordering on despair, stronger than ordinary sadness. Telling the prophet not to feel it acknowledges that he otherwise would, which is why the instruction is given at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Forty years in that world was effectively a lifetime of adult memory. A man who could recall a drought forty years back was the oldest voice at a gathering. His account of it settled arguments. A generation would circle in open country until it was gone. Told that way, the sentence was measurable by everyone. This particular set of people would never see what they had been offered.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions a period of forty in only four places. Twice it is the nights of an appointment on the mountain. Once it is the age at which a person reaches full strength. The fourth is here. In each case the number marks a completion rather than a stretch of time. That is why early scholars read it as a generation rather than as arithmetic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consequence fits the refusal exactly. People who would not enter are given endless movement without arrival. That is what they chose, extended. The Quran uses that pattern often: outcomes shaped like the acts that produced them rather than imposed from outside. The final instruction about grief adds something else. A messenger is not required to carry sorrow for a decision he argued against and lost.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same history and describes what the people asked for instead of what was offered.
Records Moses asking not to be held responsible for what the foolish among them did.
Asks the Prophet whether he would destroy himself with grief over those who turn away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision someone close to you made against your advice, which you are still carrying. You argued; they chose. The instruction here is not to stop caring but to stop grieving as though the outcome were yours. Put it down for one day, deliberately, and see whether anything you were holding up actually falls.
studies.explainEasier: God said the land would be closed to them for forty years. They would wander about with no home to reach. He told Moses not to feel sad about people who would not obey.

studies.title: Accepted From One Of Them
studies.meaning: The story is introduced as something to be recited in truth, which signals that a version of it is already in circulation. Two offerings; one accepted, one not; and no reason given for the difference. The one refused announces murder rather than asking why. The reply is a single sentence and it does not defend the speaker: God accepts from those who are conscious of Him. The entire quarrel is left resting on that one line, with nothing added to soften it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The Quran gives no names, no place and no period. Early scholars supply names from the older tradition while treating them as material outside the text. The story is placed here because the surah has just recounted a refusal and its consequence. It now goes back to the first human quarrel and shows the same mechanism at its origin, before communities or covenants existed at all.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root for nearness. The word names what is offered by what it is for, so the thing given is defined by the approach it attempts rather than by any value of its own.
A passive in an intensive form, and no agent is named in the sentence. Acceptance is reported as something that happened, and the means by which either man knew of it is left entirely unstated.
From a root meaning to guard oneself, to place a shield between. It names a posture of wariness before God rather than a level of achievement, which is part of why the reply is not a boast.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Offerings at Arabian shrines were public and competitive. A man brought a beast to the sanctuary and the size of it was noticed. Poets recorded generosity and stinginess alike. Whether an offering had been received was read from what followed: rain, a safe journey, a birth. So acceptance could be known. It could be known to differ between two men standing side by side. That idea was not strange to that audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells this story once, in this surah, and nowhere else. Most of its narratives appear in several places with different emphases. This one is given a single time and at length. The instruction to recite it in truth suggests the audience already knew a version. They were being handed the account the text itself vouches for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the act from its acceptance. Then it refuses to explain the gap. Two men do the same outward thing and only one is received. The reason offered is a quality of the person rather than of the offering. That is uncomfortable by design, since it removes any technique for guaranteeing acceptance. The reply also models something else. The response to another's success is examination of oneself rather than resentment.

crossReferences.why: Says neither flesh nor blood reaches God, but the consciousness behind the offering does.
Describes charity emptied by display, another case of an act performed and not received.
Continues the exchange with a refusal to answer the threat of violence with violence.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone in your field gets what you were hoping for, notice the first sentence your mind produces. Do not suppress it. Write it down, and then write what you would have to believe about acceptance for it to be untrue. This ayah puts the whole difference between two men inside that second sentence.
studies.explainEasier: Two sons of Adam each gave an offering. God took one and not the other. The one who was turned down said he would kill his brother. His brother said God accepts from people who keep away from wrong.

studies.title: I Will Not Extend My Hand
studies.meaning: The threatened man answers a promise of murder with a refusal, and the refusal is exact. If you stretch out your hand to kill me, I am not one to stretch mine out to kill you. He does not say he cannot, or that he will flee, or that he forgives. He states what he will not do, and gives one reason: fear of God, Lord of the worlds. The classical scholars are careful to note that this is restraint rather than incapacity.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside a story the Quran gives no date for. The exchange is preserved in direct speech, which is how the text handles its most consequential moments. The surah has been dealing with covenants and their breach at the level of whole communities; here it drops to two individuals and shows the same choice with nothing institutional around it. No specific occasion in the city is reported for the telling.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used earlier in this surah of hands extended against the community. Here it occurs twice in one sentence, once for the aggressor and once refused by the one he is addressing.
A participle governed by a negation, which in Arabic denies the character rather than the single act. He is not saying he will refrain this time; he is saying that is not the kind of person he is.

The title used at the opening of the Quran, naming God's relation to everything that exists. Choosing the widest possible name here makes the restraint answerable to far more than the two men involved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood in Arabia was answered with blood, and the obligation fell on a whole kin group. A killing set a debt payable in camels or in a life, and a man who declined to pursue it exposed his family to being thought unable to defend itself. Refusing to strike back was not read as principle; it was read as weakness, and it invited the next injury. The choice in this passage carried that cost.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of very few passages in the Quran where a person speaks at length in the moment before being killed. The speech contains no appeal for help and no attempt to escape. The narrative gives him three sentences and gives his brother one. So the account is weighted almost entirely toward the one who does not act.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given for restraint is fear of God and nothing else. Not the wrongness of killing. Not the bond of brotherhood. Not consequences in this life. That grounds a moral refusal in a relationship rather than in a principle. It is a different foundation, and one that holds where principles are being argued over. It also means the earliest recorded moral choice in the human story is a choice not to act.

crossReferences.why: Gives the outcome: the refusal did not prevent the killing, and the passage does not pretend otherwise.
Says to repel with what is better, and describes an enemy becoming a close friend.
Describes the servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with words of peace.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship where you are keeping a response in reserve, something you would say or do if they went one step further. Take it off the table today, privately, without telling them. Notice how much attention it was quietly using. That is the difference between deciding in advance and deciding in the moment.
studies.explainEasier: The brother said something back. Even if the other one reached out to kill him, he would not reach out to kill back. He said this was because he feared God, the Lord of all the worlds.

studies.title: His Soul Made It Easy
studies.meaning: Two sentences complete the exchange and then the act. The first is the threatened man's, and it is difficult: I would rather you carry my wrong along with your own. The early scholars read it as accepting the outcome rather than wishing harm, since the alternative on the table was to fight. Then the narration takes over. His soul made the killing of his brother easy for him, so he killed him. The verb is the heart of the ayah: nothing overpowered him, something was smoothed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has been building an argument about how a community loses what it was given. This passage supplies the mechanism at the smallest possible scale. The Quran does not stage the murder or describe it. It gives the inward movement and then a single verb for the act itself. Early scholars note that the brevity is deliberate. It holds attention on what happened inside rather than outside.

keyTerms.note: From the root for willing obedience. The intensive form means to render something pliable, so the soul is described as making the act agreeable rather than as compelling it outright.
The self as the seat of appetite and impulse, named here as the subject of the sentence. The grammar makes it an actor within the man, which is how the Quran usually describes internal persuasion.
A verb of coming back to a place in order to settle in it, used of taking up a dwelling. Wrongdoing is pictured as something one goes home with rather than something one merely incurs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Killing within a family had no remedy in Arabian custom. A death between tribes could be settled with payment worked out by go-betweens. But a man who killed his own brother left his kin with nobody to claim against. There was nobody to pay either. Such cases were remembered as ruptures rather than as disputes. They were spoken of with a particular horror, because the machinery for repair had no place to attach.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing what the soul did has no exact equivalent in English. Translators reach for prompted, seduced, or made easy, without agreeing among themselves. The classical scholars spend more space on this one word than on the killing itself. It locates responsibility precisely: the self persuaded, and the man consented.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evil here is something argued for, not something that takes hold. Nothing outside is blamed in the ayah. There is no whisper and no enemy. The soul makes the act easy and the man does it. That puts the blame exactly where the Quran usually puts it. It also explains how a person reaches something that would once have been beyond them. The result is named without drama: he became one of the losers.

crossReferences.why: Describes the soul as commanding toward wrong, except where God's mercy intervenes.
Names restraining the self from its desire as what leads a person to the garden.
Continues immediately with the regret that arrives far too late to matter.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you did recently that you would have called out of character a year ago. Trace the steps backward, not to excuse them but to find the point where it started feeling reasonable. That point is what this ayah names. Most people can find it in about five minutes, and it is almost never where they expected.
studies.explainEasier: The brother said he would rather the other man carry both their wrongs and end up in the Fire. Then the killer's own self made the deed feel easy. He killed his brother and lost everything.

studies.title: A Raven Digging The Ground
studies.meaning: The murderer is left standing over a body he does not know what to do with, and the passage does not describe his grief. It describes a bird. God sends a raven to scratch at the earth in front of him, and he watches it and understands. His words are self-accusation rather than repentance: was I unable even to be like this raven. The last clause names what he became, one of the regretful, and the Quran does not say the regret was accepted.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the account of the first killing. The Quran keeps the story compressed and then gives unusual space to this final scene. Early scholars read that scene as the point of the whole telling. The audience in the city was living with feuds inherited from before the migration. A passage about a man discovering he has no idea what to do after a killing had an obvious application.

keyTerms.note: A bird that caches food by burying it, so the behaviour shown was ordinary rather than miraculous. The lesson arrives through something the man could have watched on any day and had never thought to learn from.
The verb for putting something out of sight, related to the word for what lies behind. Burial is named as concealment rather than as ritual, which is the plainest possible description of it.
Regret in Arabic is close to the sense of biting one's own hand. The word describes a feeling rather than a turning, which is why the early scholars are careful not to read it as repentance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ravens were everywhere in Arabia, at camps and battlefields and rubbish heaps. Their habits were common knowledge. Poets used them as omens of separation, since they were seen picking over an abandoned campsite after a tribe had moved on. A listener would have had no trouble picturing the bird. The image of a man learning from one carried a sting the Quran does not need to spell out.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of very few places in the Quran where an animal teaches a human being something directly. It is the only one where the lesson is a practical skill rather than a sign to be read. The word for regret used at the end appears only five times in the whole text. It always names a state a person arrives in rather than an act they perform.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Instruction arrives from below rather than above. A man who has just committed the first murder is taught by a scavenging bird, and the humiliation of that is the point of the scene. It also marks a limit: he learns what to do with the body and nothing about what to do with himself. The passage ends on regret precisely because regret, by itself, changes nothing.

crossReferences.why: Draws the general principle about a single life out of this killing, in the very next ayah.
Gives another case of a creature's behaviour prompting a human being to reflect.
Describes God instructing the bee, showing creatures as carriers of instruction.

studies.applyIt: There is something practical you have avoided learning because asking would be embarrassing. How a form works. How to say a word. How something in your own house actually functions. Learn one of them this week from whatever source is nearest, however humbling. The man in this passage had to be shown by a bird, and only because he waited.
studies.explainEasier: God sent a raven to scratch at the ground in front of him. It showed him how to bury his brother. He said he could not even match a bird. Then he was full of regret.

studies.title: As If He Killed Everyone
studies.meaning: The verse reports a decree given to the Children of Israel. It is drawn as the conclusion of the story told a few lines earlier. One life is set equal to all lives, in both directions, killing and saving. The exceptions named stop this from becoming a claim that no killing is ever answered. Early scholars read the comparison as about the character of the act. What a murderer does to one person, he has shown he is willing to do to anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah. The passage follows the account of the first murder, where one brother kills the other over an offering. The decree is introduced as what follows from that story. At this point much of the surah addresses communities holding earlier scriptures. The verse reports what was written for them, then adds that many afterwards went to excess in the land.

keyTerms.note: The verb for writing, used of what is inscribed and settled. Applying it to a moral statement given to an earlier community presents it as recorded and standing, not as advice offered once and left.

keyTerms.gloss: as though, it is as if
keyTerms.note: A particle of comparison, and its presence is the whole grammar of the verse. What follows is stated as a likeness rather than an equation, which is how the classical scholars handle the scale of it.
The causative of the verb to live. Early scholars take it to cover rescuing from death and also lifting someone out of ruin, so the counterpart to killing is any act that restores a person to living.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society built on blood vengeance, one killing was never one killing. A death obliged a clan to answer. The answer obliged the other side. A single incident at a well could set two groups killing each other for a generation. Everyone listening had heard the family lines of such feuds recited aloud. The claim that one murder amounted to all murders described something they had watched happen.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison here has a close parallel in rabbinic writing. The Mishnah's charge to witnesses in capital cases likens saving one life to saving a whole world. The Quran presents the statement as something decreed for the Children of Israel. The two texts stand as separate witnesses to one wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse refuses to do sums with moral judgement. If a life could be weighed against a number, killing one person would be a smaller wrong than killing many. The comparison denies exactly that, by making a single death total. Putting the saving clause in the same sentence gives the reverse an equal scale. So ordinary rescue is not a lesser kind of act. It is the other end of one measure.

crossReferences.why: Tells the story of the two brothers from which this decree is drawn.
Sets out the sanctity of life directly, and limits how an heir may respond.
Places the prohibition of killing among the commands given to every community.

studies.applyIt: Take the news you read this week and find one number in it, a count of people affected by something. Look up a single name from among them if you can. Read that one story instead. The verse works by refusing to let a person become a figure. The smallest way to keep it is to make the figure a person again.
studies.explainEasier: God told the Children of Israel something important. If you kill one person, it is like killing everyone. If you save one person, it is like saving everyone. One life counts that much.

studies.title: Disgrace In This World
studies.meaning: A category is defined before any consequence is named. Those who make war on God and His Messenger, and work to spread ruin in the land. Four outcomes are then listed. The classical scholars differ over what the list is. Some read it as a range matched to the severity of what was done. Others read it as a set of choices left to those who judge. What the ayah states in its own voice is the purpose: disgrace in this life. It adds that a greater accounting lies elsewhere.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars connect the passage to an incident involving a group who came to the city. They were given shelter and provisions, and then killed a herdsman and drove off livestock. Reports of the details vary in the classical sources. The wider setting is a region without policing. Highway robbery was common there, and a single band could close a caravan route for a season.

keyTerms.note: The verb of open warfare rather than of crime. Defining the category this way makes the passage about a state of hostility to a whole order, which is why the early scholars discuss its boundaries at such length.
The spoiling of something that was sound, used of food going bad and of a society coming apart. It names damage done to a shared condition rather than injury to any individual.
Shame that is visible to others, not private guilt. The ayah names this as the aim in this world, which places the whole passage in the register of deterrence and public order.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade in Arabia depended on roads no authority patrolled. A band that took to the passes could shut a route for a season. The losses fell on everyone. The merchant, the households waiting for grain, the tribes whose income was the passage fee. Communities dealt with such bands themselves. The response was public by necessity, since deterrence was the only protection anybody had.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah that follows opens with an exception for those who turn back before being caught. The classical commentaries treat the two as inseparable and read them as one passage. Several of the long surahs use this pattern. A severe statement comes first, then a named exception in the very next sentence rather than pages later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage frames the offence as directed against God and His Messenger, not against a victim. That is a claim about what makes public violence different in kind from private wrong. It also splits the accounting in two. Something visible now. Something afterwards that the ayah calls great without describing. Naming both keeps worldly consequence from being mistaken for a final verdict on anyone.

crossReferences.why: Adds the exception for those who turn back before being taken, and is always read together with this.
Describes the one who works ruin in the land, destroying crops and livestock alike.
Instructs against spreading ruin in the land after it has been set right.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between a wrong that hurts a person and a wrong that damages something everyone relies on. A shared rota, a common fund, a reputation the whole group needs. When you next weigh a small dishonesty, ask which kind it is. This passage rests on that difference, and most of us never make it at all.
studies.explainEasier: People who make war on God and His Messenger and spread ruin in the land face hard punishments. The ayah lists four of them. The point is to shame them in this life. A worse one waits after that.

studies.title: Repentance Before The Arrest
studies.meaning: An exception is cut out of a severe passage, and its timing carries the weight. Repentance counts if it comes before the person is caught. Once capture has happened, a change of heart looks no different from surrender. So the window is placed while the choice still costs something. The verse after it turns from the offender to everyone. It asks for awareness of God and for a means of drawing near. Early scholars read that as any act which closes distance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a passage about violent robbery and what follows from it. That passage itself comes after the account of the first murder. Early scholars link the verses around it with a group who killed after being given hospitality, though the reports vary in detail. What the exception clause records is that the severity and the way out of it were published together. They came in one breath.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to return, and it is used of God turning towards a person as well as of a person turning towards God. One word describes both movements, which is why the two are hard to separate.
From the root for capacity and for measuring out. The clause turns on the moment power passes to the other side, so the timing of the repentance is set by who now holds the situation.
A word for the connection or path by which one reaches something wanted. Early scholars explain it broadly as whatever brings a person nearer to God, and note that the term is left open on purpose.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Highway robbery was the standing danger of caravan travel. The roads between Mecca, Medina and the north ran through country where a small band could take a season's trade in an afternoon, and there was no policing beyond what a clan could mount for itself. A man who had robbed a caravan lived outside anyone's protection until he was caught. The window described here was a real one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the means of approach occurs only twice in the Quran. It is here, and again in surah 17. There it describes those already close to God, competing to come nearer still. The two uses put the same term at opposite ends of a scale. One is for someone looking for a way back. The other is for those who have arrived.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is given a deadline rather than a limit. That is a particular kind of seriousness. The offer stands while it can still be refused. Closing it at the moment of capture keeps repentance from becoming a tactic. The second verse then removes any hint that this is a special arrangement for offenders. The same movement towards God is asked of everyone, in the same words, straight afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same kind of limit, contrasting repentance in time with repentance at the point of death.
Uses the same word for the means of approach, of those already near to God.
Offers those who stop what has already passed, on the same condition of ceasing first.

studies.applyIt: If there is something you have decided to stop doing when circumstances eventually force you to, try moving the date forward by a week. The verse makes the value of a turn depend on whether it still cost something when you made it. Nothing about the act changes; what changes is whether it was yours.
studies.explainEasier: If someone who has done wrong stops and turns back before they are caught, God will forgive them. The next verse speaks to everyone else. It asks them to stay close to God and to keep trying to get closer.

studies.title: Everything On Earth, Twice Over
studies.meaning: An imagined case is built and then dismantled. Suppose someone owned everything on earth, and then the same again alongside it, and offered the whole of it as a ransom on the day of resurrection. The answer is short: it would not be accepted from them. The passage does not say the price is too low. It says the transaction does not exist, which is a different and harder claim, and the sentence closes without offering any alternative currency at all.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a stretch of the surah dealing with judgement and its finality. No specific occasion is reported for it. The community addressed included merchants from Mecca who had left property behind. It also included people in the city whose standing rested on land and date groves. A passage denying that wealth can serve as a ransom spoke straight into a society where almost everything else could be settled by payment.

keyTerms.note: The verb of buying a captive out of captivity, an entirely ordinary transaction in that world. Using it here presents the day of judgement as the one situation where the familiar mechanism has no counterpart.

keyTerms.gloss: the like of it with it
keyTerms.note: A doubling added after the total has already been named. The phrase exists to remove the thought that the figure was simply not high enough, closing that argument before anyone can make it.
The same verb used of the rejected offering earlier in this surah, and again in the passive with no agent named. The two passages are joined by a single word about what God does or does not receive.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Almost every serious problem in Arabia had a price. A killing was settled in camels. A captive was bought back by his tribe. A debt could be transferred, and a man in trouble counted his herd first. Ransom was not an image; it was the standard machinery of dispute, worked out by go-betweens and paid in livestock. The whole society ran on the assumption that enough wealth resolves anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of a ransom that would not be accepted appears in three places in the Quran. In all three the offered price is everything on earth plus the same again, phrased almost identically. That reuse across surahs is a feature of the text's descriptions of judgement. They return to fixed images rather than inventing new ones.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage goes after a specific instinct rather than a doctrine. It is the belief that any situation can eventually be bought out of. The ayah names an impossible sum and refuses it. The problem, it says, is not short resources but a wrong kind of solution. That leaves a reader without a fallback, which is the point. What the surah offers instead, one ayah earlier, is not payment but approach.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same words for the ransom refused, in a Meccan surah on the same theme.
Says an earth full of gold offered as ransom would not be taken from one who died refusing.
Denies that any ransom or intercession will be accepted from a soul on that day.

studies.applyIt: Think of a problem you are quietly assuming money will solve one day. Name it honestly. Then ask what the actual solution is, apart from the money. Sometimes money really is the answer. Often it has been standing in for a conversation, an apology, or a change you would rather pay to avoid making.
studies.explainEasier: Some people turn away from God. Imagine they owned the whole earth twice over. Imagine they offered it all to buy their way out on the last day. It would not be taken from them.

studies.title: What The Hands Have Earned
studies.meaning: Two very different sentences sit together. The first describes people who will want out of the fire and will not get out. The word used for punishment means settled in place, not merely long. The second names a consequence for theft. The classical scholars discuss at length the conditions under which it was understood to apply. They treat it as narrowly bounded. The ayah gives its own reason in two words: a recompense for what was earned, and a deterrent from God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. A caravan, a storehouse or an unguarded flock could be a family's whole survival through a season. There was no police force, no insurance and no prison. Early scholars do not report a single occasion for this passage. They discuss it alongside the conditions and exemptions preserved in the tradition. That is why classical treatments of it run long.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the verb to stand or to reside. The punishment is described as taking up residence rather than as continuing, which is a spatial image where English reaches instead for a temporal one.
From a root meaning to hold back through fear. The word names the effect on those watching rather than on the one punished, which is why the ayah is so explicit about its aim.
The verb of acquisition, used across the Quran for what a person accumulates in deeds. Applying it to theft turns the taking into an earning, which is the sentence's quiet and deliberate irony.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were no locks worth the name and no institutions to appeal to. A tent had no door. A storehouse was guarded by whoever happened to be awake. Theft from a caravan or a flock could end a household, and pursuit was the family's own job. Punishment in that world was necessarily public and immediate. There was nowhere to hold anyone and nothing else that would stop the next attempt.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names the man and the woman clearly and gives them the same consequence. Arabic could have used a single masculine form to cover both. The Quran does this in a number of places. The classical grammarians observed that such doubling is never accidental. It is generally read as insisting the two are addressed equally.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage states its own purpose, which is unusual. The purpose given is deterrence rather than payback. That places it in the register of protecting a community, not of balancing a moral account. The ayah that follows opens the door to repentance and repair in the same breath. So severity and return are set together rather than in sequence. That is how the classical commentaries read the pair.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with repentance and repair, and is always read together with this ayah.
Warns against consuming one another's wealth wrongly, stating the principle behind the passage.
Warns against taking others' property by false means or through the authorities.

studies.applyIt: Look at the small things you have taken and not returned: a book, a tool, time billed generously, a pen from an office. None of it is what this passage is about. Return one of them anyway this week. The point is to feel accurately what it means for a thing to belong to someone who is not you.
studies.explainEasier: People in the Fire will want to get out and will not be able to. Then the ayah turns to stealing. A thief, man or woman, has a hand cut off. God says this is meant to stop others.

studies.title: After His Wrong, He Turns
studies.meaning: The severity of the previous ayah is answered at once. Whoever turns back after his wrongdoing and sets things right, God turns toward him. Two verbs from the same root are used, one for the person and one for God, so the turning is mutual in the Arabic in a way English cannot show. The next sentence widens to sovereignty and puts it as a question rather than a claim: do you not know that the kingdom belongs to God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars treat this ayah and the one before it as a single passage and read them together. They note that the tradition preserves cases in which repentance was accepted. No separate occasion is reported. The placement is itself the argument. A consequence is stated and the way back is opened in the very next sentence, before a reader has time to conclude that the door has closed.

keyTerms.note: The verb means simply to return. It carries no sense of penance or self-punishment, only of reversing direction, which is why the Quran can use the identical word of God turning toward a person.
To repair what was broken, used of mending a relationship or a state of affairs. Pairing it with turning back means the passage asks for a change in the situation as well as in the heart.
The same verb as the person's, with a preposition that changes the direction of travel. God's turning is described as a movement toward, which makes forgiveness an approach rather than a verdict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Making peace in Arabia was a public procedure. Go-betweens walked between two houses. Terms were agreed, and the settlement was announced so everyone knew the matter had ended. A man who had wronged another and wanted back into standing had to repair the damage visibly. Feeling differently about it was not enough. The pairing here of turning and setting right read as the ordinary shape of a settled dispute.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic verb for a person's repentance and the verb for God's acceptance of it are the same word. Only the preposition that follows is different. One of the names of God in the Quran is built on that root. So the one who returns and the one who is returned to are named from the same three letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repentance is presented as a return, not as an appeasement. That removes any suggestion that something is being paid off. The requirement of setting things right keeps it from becoming purely inward. Then comes the question about the kingdom belonging to God. It reframes the whole passage. Forgiveness and punishment sit inside a single will, so neither can be predicted and neither can be presumed upon.

crossReferences.why: Describes wrongs exchanged for good after repentance and reform, using the same pairing.
Sets the limits: repentance for those who act in ignorance and turn back soon afterwards.
Tells those who exceeded against themselves not to despair of the mercy of God.

studies.applyIt: Pick a wrong you have already apologised for and never repaired. The apology was the first verb; this ayah names a second one. Work out what setting it right would actually involve, even partially, and do the smallest version of it this week. Most of us stop after the sentence and consider the matter closed.
studies.explainEasier: Anyone who turns back after doing wrong and puts things right will be forgiven. Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. He punishes whom He wants and forgives whom He wants.

studies.title: Believed With Their Mouths
studies.meaning: The Prophet is told not to grieve, and that grief is the ayah's opening subject. Groups are described by their behaviour rather than named: some who said they believed while their hearts did not, and some who came listening for material to carry elsewhere. A tactic is quoted in their own words, take this ruling if you are given it and be wary if you are not. The passage ends by locating the failure in hearts that were not purified.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars connect the passage to a group who brought a dispute to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They hoped for a lighter outcome than their own scholars would give. They had agreed in advance to accept the judgement only if it suited them. Reports of the case differ in their details. The classical commentaries are explicit that the description applies to those individuals and their conduct.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so habitual and avid listening rather than simply hearing. Repeated twice in one sentence with different objects, it describes people who come to gather material rather than to learn anything.
The phrase is redundant in ordinary Arabic, since saying already implies the mouth. Adding it confines the belief to the organ that produced it, which is the entire point of the clause.
From a root meaning to test metal in fire to separate the pure from the dross. The word covers trial, temptation and turmoil at once, and the early scholars note all three senses here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The city was small enough that a judgement given in one quarter was known in all of them by evening. Legal opinion was a social resource. A man with a dispute would sound out several authorities before committing to one. The choice of judge was itself a move in the dispute. What the ayah describes was a recognisable strategy. It was familiar to anyone who had ever taken a quarrel to a third party.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest single ayat in the surah. It opens with the address O Messenger, which occurs exactly twice in the whole Quran, both times in this surah. The far commoner address is O Prophet, used more than a dozen times elsewhere. So the switch here is noticeable to anyone reading in Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between what a person says, what their heart holds, and what they came for. It treats the last of these as decisive. Coming to revelation with a verdict already chosen is described as a way of not receiving it at all. The comfort offered to the Prophet is not that the situation will improve. It is that the situation is not his to fix. That is the limit this surah drew earlier around Moses.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same description and gives the instruction that follows from it.
Tells the Prophet not to be grieved by those who rush into disbelief, in nearly identical words.
Describes people saying with their tongues what is not in their hearts, using the same distinction.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you ask someone's advice when you have already decided. Everyone does it, and it is not always dishonest. But name it before you ask, at least to yourself, and consider saying it out loud: I think I have made up my mind, but tell me anyway. The conversation changes completely.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said they believed but did not mean it. Others came only to listen and carry stories back. They changed words and only took a ruling if they liked it. God tells the Messenger not to be sad about them.

studies.title: Judge, Or Turn Away
studies.meaning: The description continues and then an instruction follows that is unusual for how much it leaves open. If they come to you, judge between them, or turn away from them. Both are permitted, and the reassurance attached is that turning away costs nothing at all. But if judgement is given, it is to be equitable, and the ayah closes with a statement rather than a command: God loves those who deal in fairness. Choice about whether to act; none about how.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It continues directly from the previous ayah and its account of a dispute brought for judgement. Early scholars read the two as one passage. The setting is a city where the young community's authority was still being worked out with the older communities around it. There a request for judgement was as much a political act as a legal one.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to strip away or destroy utterly. The word describes earnings that consume what they are added to, so the name of the thing already contains a verdict on it.
To present one's side rather than one's face, hence to disengage. It is the same verb used elsewhere for turning from what is worthless, and here it names a legitimate option rather than a failure.
From a root that yields both fairness and, in another form, injustice, since the underlying sense is division. Equity is a matter of dividing correctly, not of feeling well disposed toward anyone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was how disputes ended in a society with no courts. A respected man heard both sides, often in his own courtyard. His judgement held because both parties had agreed in advance to accept it. Declining to arbitrate was normal and carried no shame. An arbitrator who suspected he was being used had every reason to step back. The permission here reflects a real and familiar choice.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for illicit earnings occurs three times in the Quran. All three are in this surah, and all within a short span of one another. Concentrations like that are one of the ways a surah signals its subject. This one deals throughout with what a community takes, consumes and accepts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two questions that are usually run together. Whether to involve yourself, and how to act once you have. Discretion is granted freely on the first and withdrawn entirely on the second. It also grounds fairness in something other than duty. The reason given is what God loves. So equity is presented as an attraction rather than a burden, which is the move this surah made earlier about pardon.

crossReferences.why: Commands standing firm in witness and fairness even toward people you have reason to dislike.
Extends the same demand to testimony given against yourself and against your own family.
Asks why judgement is sought here at all when they have their own scripture to hand.

studies.applyIt: Someone will ask you to weigh in on a dispute this month. Before you do, ask yourself honestly whether you are wanted for your judgement or for your support. If it is the second, you are allowed to decline, and this ayah says so plainly. If you do weigh in, say the part that costs the person who asked.
studies.explainEasier: These people listen to lies and take money they should not. If they come to you, you can judge between them or leave it. Turning them away will not hurt you. If you do judge, be fair. God loves fair people.

studies.title: The Book They Already Have
studies.meaning: A question is asked that answers itself. Why come to you for judgement when they hold the Torah, and God's ruling is in it? The sharper half is what follows: and then they turn away after that. The objection is not that they consulted the wrong authority. It is that they consulted an authority they had already decided not to obey. The closing clause describes what such a person is not, and it is left standing without elaboration.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of the same passage about a dispute brought for judgement. Early scholars tie it to the same case and read the three ayat together. The surah is at a point where it describes how a community relates to a text it already holds. This ayah is the pivot. What is identified is not absence of guidance but unwillingness to be bound by guidance held.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to appoint someone as arbiter. The grammar puts the power in their hands: they are choosing who will decide, which is exactly what the question is probing.
The word covers judgement, wisdom and governance from a single root. Saying it is present in the book they hold is a statement of respect for that scripture, made before any criticism follows.
Literally to turn one's side, or to take charge elsewhere. The verb describes a physical turning away and, in other passages, taking someone else as an ally, so the desertion has a direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Consulting an outside arbiter was ordinary in that world. Moving between arbiters was ordinary too. A dispute might pass through several hands before it settled. Each party pushed for whoever seemed likely to favour them. What made a judgement stick was not the arbiter's office. It was the parties' prior agreement to be bound by it. Without that, the whole procedure was theatre, and everyone knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran says that the Torah contains God's ruling in the very passage where it criticises a group's conduct. It does this repeatedly across this section of the surah. The criticism is never aimed at the earlier scripture. The surah goes on to call that scripture guidance and light in the very next ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah names a failure that needs neither disbelief nor ignorance. Everything needed is present and acknowledged. What is missing is willingness to be bound by an answer before hearing it. That is a condition anyone can be in with any text. The passage also models something about criticism. A scripture is honoured in the same breath as conduct is questioned, and the two are kept carefully apart.

crossReferences.why: States immediately that the Torah holds guidance and light, honouring what has just been invoked.
Describes accepting a judgement without resistance in oneself as the mark of faith.
Describes those who come readily to judgement only when the ruling is likely to suit them.

studies.applyIt: Find the advice you have already been given, by someone qualified, and have not acted on. You do not need a second opinion. Sit with the fact that you already have the answer, and either follow it or say plainly to yourself that you have decided not to. This ayah is about the space between those two.
studies.explainEasier: They come to you to settle their case, but they already have the Torah, and God's ruling is in it. Then they turn away from what it says. People like that are not really believers.

studies.title: Guidance And Light Sent Down
studies.meaning: The Torah is described in the Quran's own voice as a revelation carrying guidance and light. It was applied by prophets who had submitted, and by teachers and scholars entrusted with preserving it. Then the address turns direct. Do not fear people, fear Me. Do not sell My signs for a small price. The final clause is about those who do not judge by what God sent down. The classical scholars read it in more than one way, and set the readings side by side without ranking them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section of the surah that treats the succession of revealed books. The passage arrives right after a question about why a group sought judgement elsewhere while holding their own scripture. Early scholars read the sequence as deliberate. Criticism of conduct is followed at once by respect for the book itself, so the two are never confused with one another.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for Lord, so the term names people defined by attachment to God rather than by an office. The early scholars gloss it as those who teach the lesser matters before the greater ones.
A passive in a form meaning to seek something of another. Preservation is described as a trust placed in them, which makes it a responsibility received rather than a role anyone claimed.
Not a wrong price but a small one. The phrase concedes that something is gained and then measures it, which is sharper criticism than saying the exchange produced nothing at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religious learning in that world was a livelihood as well as a calling. A scholar was supported by his community. He was consulted on disputes, births, contracts and inheritance. His standing depended on being useful to the people who fed him. The pressure to give an answer that pleased was built into the arrangement, not personal. Anyone who had ever sought a ruling understood exactly where it came from.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the two that follow it each end with the same clause about those who do not judge by what God sent down. Each closes on a different word for them. The classical commentaries discuss the three endings together. They read the variation as meaningful rather than as repetition for emphasis.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds the authority of a scripture in its source, not in its keepers. Then it addresses those keepers directly about the pressures that bend them. Fear of people is one. Small prices are the other. Those are the two ways a preserved text quietly stops being applied. That is a description of how guidance is lost without anyone denying it. This surah returns to that worry again and again.

crossReferences.why: Ends with the same clause and a different word, and is read together with this ayah.
Warns against selling the signs of God for a small price, in almost the same phrasing.
Recalls a covenant to make the scripture clear and not conceal it, and what became of it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you softened what you knew to be true because of who was listening. Not a lie, just a rounding down. Identify what you gained by it: comfort, standing, an easier afternoon. This ayah asks you to name the price, and the point of naming it is that it is nearly always smaller than you assumed.
studies.explainEasier: God sent down the Torah, and it holds guidance and light. Prophets and teachers used it to judge. God tells them not to fear people, but to fear Him. They should not sell His signs for a small price.

studies.title: Whoever Forgoes It In Charity
studies.meaning: A principle of exact proportion is recalled from the earlier scripture: a life for a life, and the same for eye, nose, ear and tooth, with wounds requiring equivalence. The list is itemised rather than summarised, deliberately. Then a single clause changes the direction of the whole passage. Whoever gives it up as charity, that is an atonement for him. The right is affirmed and a way of not using it is offered, and the reward is attached to the second.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of what the earlier scripture contained. Early scholars note that the principle of exact requital was itself a restraint in its original setting. It replaced an escalation in which one killing was answered with several. Arabia in the seventh century still worked that way. So an audience hearing this passage understood proportion as a ceiling rather than as a licence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow a track precisely. The word names a matching rather than a punishment, so what it demands is that the response trace the injury exactly and go no further than it.
The verb of voluntary giving, from the root for truthfulness. Applying it to a waived right makes the forgoing itself a gift, which is why a reward follows rather than mere approval.
From the root for covering over. What is covered is the giver's own record, so the passage says that letting go of a claim against another repairs something in the one who lets go.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood money was negotiated in camels, and the talks could take weeks. Elders walked between the families. A figure was reached, and the herd changed hands in public so that everyone knew the matter was closed. A family that waived the payment entirely gained enormous standing. It was rare, because the payment was often what kept the bereaved household fed through the year.
studies.didYouKnow: The list in this ayah names five parts of the body in a fixed order before turning to wounds in general. The classical scholars note that the order moves from the whole person outward to particular faculties. The clause about atonement that follows is a single short sentence. It stands against that entire itemised list.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out a right and then makes giving it up more valuable than using it. The right is never withdrawn. That is a specific structure. Justice is not replaced by mercy; it is left standing while mercy is placed above it. The passage also puts the benefit of forgiveness in the forgiver's own account rather than in the offender's. That changes what forgiving is for.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle and then commends remission by the injured party's own family.
Says the recompense for an injury is its equal, and that pardon is rewarded by God.
Draws out the value of a single life, in this same surah and from the same tradition.

studies.applyIt: There is something you are owed, money or an apology or an acknowledgement, that you could probably still extract. Consider writing it off, deliberately and without telling the other person. Not because you are wrong to be owed. This ayah says the release is credited to you. Holding the claim open costs more attention than the debt is worth.
studies.explainEasier: In the Torah God set a fair match for harm. A life for a life. An eye for an eye. A tooth for a tooth. But anyone who gives up that claim as a gift will have it count for him.

studies.title: In Their Footsteps
studies.meaning: The succession is described as a following of tracks. Jesus, son of Mary, is sent after the prophets just named, confirming what was already in his hands. He is given the Gospel. It is described in exactly the words used for the Torah two ayat earlier: guidance and light. The confirmation is stated twice inside one sentence. The closing phrase adds something the earlier description did not, that it is counsel for those conscious of God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the surah's account of successive revelations. The passage sits between the description of the Torah and the description of the Quran. Early scholars read the three as one continuous argument about a single line of guidance. No specific occasion is reported. The audience included people who held one or another of these books. The sequence is presented as their shared history rather than as a dispute.

keyTerms.note: From the word for the nape or the back of the head, so the image is of one coming immediately behind another. The verb makes the succession physical, a walking in tracks rather than an abstract sequence.
An active participle from the root for truthfulness. Confirmation here means declaring the earlier revelation true, and the word is repeated within the same sentence, which is unusual and deliberate.
Advice given with feeling, meant to move rather than merely to inform. It names a kind of speech that assumes the listener already knows and needs reminding, which is a different task from teaching.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a real skill in Arabia, taught young and highly prized. A man could read from prints in sand how many had passed, how heavily laden, and how long ago. Guides were hired for that ability alone. The image of one prophet sent in another's tracks would have landed as an ordinary and precise picture, not as a figure of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used for the Gospel here, containing guidance and light, is word for word the phrase used two ayat earlier for the Torah. The Quran repeats descriptions across books deliberately. Here the repetition is itself the argument. The same two nouns are applied to each revelation in turn.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as continuous, not as a series of corrections. Each book confirms what came before it. The same words describe them. That makes a difference of community a difference of moment rather than of source. The reading sets up the ayah that follows. There the Quran describes itself in the same sequence. It is also the ground on which the surah asks each community to apply what it holds.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical description, guidance and light, of the Torah two ayat earlier.
Completes the sequence, describing the Quran as confirming and watching over what preceded it.
Describes the sending of Jesus and what was placed in the hearts of those who followed.

studies.applyIt: Read something written by a believer of another tradition this month. A prayer, a page of reflection, a hymn. Not to compare, and not to argue with it. This ayah describes a single line of guidance running through several communities. Reading someone else's part of it is a small way of taking that seriously.
studies.explainEasier: After those prophets God sent Jesus, the son of Mary. He agreed with the Torah that came before him. God gave him the Gospel, and it holds guidance and light too.

studies.title: Let Them Judge By It
studies.meaning: One sentence, and the instruction points away from the speaker. Let the people of the Gospel judge by what God sent down in it. The Quran is not asking them to adopt something new here; it is asking them to apply what they already hold. The closing clause repeats the formula used in the two ayat before it, with a third word for those who do not, and the classical scholars read the variation across the three as meaningful.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The passage completes a sequence: the Torah, then the Gospel, then, in the next ayah, the Quran. Christian delegations reached the city, and Christian communities were established across the peninsula. So the address had actual recipients. Early scholars note that the instruction comes with no demand attached to it. That is the feature of the ayah they most often remark on.

keyTerms.note: A third-person imperative, which in Arabic states what ought to follow rather than commanding someone present. The form keeps the sentence from reading as an order issued to another community.
Named by the book they hold rather than by community or descent. The Quran uses this pattern frequently, which places identity in what a group has received rather than in what it inherited.

From a root describing a date leaving its skin, hence stepping outside a boundary. It names departure from an order rather than denial of it, which is why it differs from the two words used just before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Christian communities in Arabia were real and visible. The church at Najran negotiated its own terms with the city. Monks kept cells along the Syrian road. Abyssinia across the water was a Christian kingdom. It had received refugees. An instruction addressed to the people of the Gospel was not rhetoric in that setting. It named people a merchant might have done business with that year.
studies.didYouKnow: Three ayat in a row here end with the same clause about those who do not judge by what God sent down. Each closes on a different noun. The classical commentaries give considerable attention to why the three differ. They preserve several explanations side by side without settling on any one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah asks a community to be faithful to its own revelation rather than to abandon it. That is a striking thing for a scripture to say about another book. It implies something about the failure addressed across this whole section. The failure is not holding the wrong text. It is not applying the text one holds. That places the burden inside each community rather than between them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction and the same closing formula about the earlier scripture.
Says explicitly that they stand on nothing until they uphold the Torah and the Gospel.
Describes what would have followed if they had upheld what was sent down to them.

studies.applyIt: Consider the practice you have quietly let lapse. Not someone else's, yours. A weekly call, a page read at night, a giving you used to do monthly. Restart it once this week at its smallest possible size. This ayah's whole instruction is to apply what you already have, and that usually turns out to be the harder request.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the people who follow the Gospel to judge by what He put in it. Anyone who will not judge by what God sent down has stepped outside the line. That is what the ayah says.

studies.title: A Law And A Way
studies.meaning: The Quran is described in the same sequence as the two books before it: sent down with truth, confirming what preceded it, and watching over it. Then the passage turns outward in a way nothing before it prepared. Each community has been given a law and a way; had God willed, all of them would have been one; the difference exists as a test. What follows is not tolerance but competition, and the field named is good works.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing the surah's account of successive revelations. Early scholars read this ayah as the summary of the whole section. That is why they treat the three earlier descriptions as building toward it. The city held several communities with distinct laws living side by side and sharing space. So a statement about plural legal traditions addressed a situation, not a theory.

keyTerms.note: A rare word the early scholars gloss as guardian, witness and trusted keeper. It describes a relation of oversight to the earlier books rather than replacement of them, which is why the range of glosses matters.

keyTerms.gloss: a law and an open road
keyTerms.note: The first word names the path worn down to a watering place; the second a broad clear route. Both are images of access rather than of restriction, which colours the whole statement about difference.
The verb of a footrace, in a form meaning to compete to get ahead. It turns a statement about plurality into an instruction, and the finish line named is good deeds rather than agreement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the sharpest boundary in Arabian life. A well belonged to a tribe. The paths worn down to it were known and defended, and a stranger asked permission or fought. The word chosen here for law is the word for that path to water. So a listener heard a claim about survival, access and belonging before hearing anything about law-making.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated as watching over occurs twice in the Quran. Once here, describing the revelation's relation to earlier books, and once as one of the names of God. The early Arabic dictionary writers gathered several glosses for it without settling on one. The commentaries record the range rather than deciding it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The plurality of communities is put down to God's will rather than to human failure. That is a substantial claim. Difference is described as a test, and the passage names what the test is for. It is not proving whose law is right. It is who does more good with what they were given. The final clause hands the disputes themselves to God, so the arguments are not resolved here, only postponed.

crossReferences.why: Repeats that God could have made all people a single community, and states that He did not.
Uses the same instruction to race toward good, with each group having a direction it faces.
Gives the previous step in the sequence, describing the Gospel in exactly these terms.

studies.applyIt: Find someone whose way of practising differs from yours and who does one thing better than you: is more generous, more patient with their parents, more consistent. Name the thing specifically. Then take that one practice as a target for the month. This ayah says the difference is a race, and races are run by improving.
studies.explainEasier: God gave this Book to the Prophet. It agrees with the books before it and keeps watch over them. He gave each group its own law and way. He could have made everyone one people, but He wanted to test them. So they should race in doing good.

studies.title: Beware They Turn You
studies.meaning: The instruction of the previous ayah is repeated and then given a warning it did not carry. Judge by what God sent down; do not follow their inclinations; and be on guard that they do not turn you from some part of what was sent down to you. The word is some, not all. The danger described is erosion at the edges rather than wholesale abandonment. The closing clause reads any turning away as a consequence already under way.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars read this ayah with the two before it as one instruction repeated for emphasis. The repetition is itself what they comment on. The same command is given twice in consecutive ayat, with a different warning attached each time. The setting is a period when the community's decisions were being lobbied for by parties with a direct stake in the outcome.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to fall or to drift downward. The word names wanting that pulls rather than reasoning that persuades, which is why it stands here in contrast with what was sent down.
The same root used earlier in the surah for testing metal by fire. Here it carries the sense of drawing someone off a course, so the danger described is deflection rather than direct opposition.
A small word doing large work. The warning is not about abandoning revelation but about conceding a portion of it, which is how the surah has already described what happened to earlier communities.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every party in the city had reason to lobby. Alliances shifted with the harvest and with news from Mecca. A judgement given in one quarter altered the standing of families in another. Pressure did not usually arrive as an argument. It arrived as a delegation, a favour recalled, a marriage proposed. Resisting it required a fixed reference point, which is what this instruction supplies.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to judge by what God sent down is given twice in two consecutive ayat, each time with a different addition. The ayah after that turns the same idea into a question. Repetition at this density is rare in the Quran. Early scholars treat it as the emphasis of the whole section.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the usual way guidance is lost. Not by rejection but by giving ground, a portion at a time. The pressure always looks reasonable at the moment it arrives. Naming a part rather than the whole makes the warning usable. Nobody feels themselves to be abandoning everything. The surah has already shown two earlier communities losing exactly a portion, using the same word.

crossReferences.why: Describes an earlier community forgetting a portion of what they had been reminded of.
Describes pressure to invent something other than what was revealed, and the steadying against it.
Warns against following the inclinations of those who would not follow the direction given.

studies.applyIt: Identify one commitment you have already renegotiated downward without ever deciding to: a start time, a portion given, a rule you keep for yourself. Restore it exactly, once, this week. Not permanently, and not as a resolution. Just to find out how far the edge has moved while you were not looking at it.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to judge by what He sent down and not follow what these people want. He warns him to watch out. They may pull him away from part of it.

studies.title: The Judgement Of Ignorance
studies.meaning: One question, and then another. Is it the judgement of the age of ignorance that they want? And who is better than God in judgement, for a people who have certainty? The first question names an alternative the audience would have recognised as a whole social order rather than a legal option. The second does not argue; it attaches its answer to a condition. Those who are certain will find the question rhetorical, and the ayah says so without pretending otherwise.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The term used here for the earlier period entered Arabic as a name for the time before the mission. Early scholars apply it to a condition rather than a date: arbitrary custom, tribal precedence, judgements that followed strength. The community hearing this had lived under that system within living memory. Many of them had benefited from it, which is what gives the question its edge.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for not knowing, but the early scholars read it as recklessness and arrogance more than as a lack of information. It names a way of behaving, which is why it can describe an era or a person.

A verb of active pursuit, and in another form the root yields transgression and oppression. Seeking and overstepping share a family, which suits a question about what someone wants a judgement to do for them.

From a root meaning to become still, as sediment settles in water. Certainty in Arabic is a settling rather than an intensity, which is why the ayah makes it the condition for the question landing at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before the mission, a dispute was often decided by whose relatives were more numerous. A weak man with a strong case could expect nothing. A strong man could expect the matter quietly dropped. Soothsayers were consulted, arrows were drawn, and outcomes tracked power rather closely. Everyone in the audience remembered how that had gone for their own family, and the memories were not uniform.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the earlier age appears four times in the Quran. It is never a neutral historical label. Each use names a specific behaviour being set against something better. The term became the standard name for the pre-Islamic period afterwards, but the text itself uses it to describe conduct.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage frames the choice as between two whole systems rather than between two verdicts. That is why the alternative is named by an era and not by a rival ruling. It also makes the argument conditional. God's judgement is called better for people who are certain. That concedes that the question settles nothing for those who are not. The Quran often argues this way, addressing those already listening.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same term for the earlier age, contrasting a way of behaving rather than a date.
Describes accepting a judgement without resistance in oneself as the mark of belief.
Gives the instruction this question follows from, with its warning about being deflected.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you still settle things by weight rather than by merit: who is louder, who is senior, who will make it awkward. Pick one small decision this week and make it the other way, on the facts alone, and watch what it costs you. That cost is the honest measure of what you have been doing until now.
studies.explainEasier: The ayah asks if they really want the old way of judging, from the time before. Then it asks who could judge better than God. For people who are sure, there is no better judge.

studies.title: Do Not Take Them As Protectors
studies.meaning: The word at the centre of this ayah does not mean friend. It names a protector and ally, the party one turns to for security. Early scholars read the instruction in the setting the following ayat supply. People were hedging their alliances during armed conflict, out of fear that the community would not survive. This same surah has already opened shared meals and marriage across these lines. So what is addressed here is the pact, not the neighbour.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a period of active conflict when treaties in and around the city were being broken and remade. The classical scholars connect the passage to individuals who sought protection pacts with parties outside the community. The fighting's outcome was still uncertain. The reports name more than one such case. The three ayat that follow describe those individuals' reasoning in their own words.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for one who is near and has charge of another's affairs. It covers a guardian, a patron and a treaty partner, and its political weight is what the whole passage turns on.
The verb of the same root, meaning to place oneself under someone's protection or to hand one's allegiance over. It describes an act of alignment rather than any feeling of warmth toward anyone.
From a root meaning to put something out of its proper place. The closing clause names a category by conduct rather than by community, which is the pattern this surah keeps to throughout.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Survival in Arabia ran on protection. A man without a patron could be killed on the road with no consequence. A group without allies could be starved out. Pacts were made and broken as the balance shifted. Hedging was ordinary prudence rather than betrayal. The passage addresses that machinery directly, at a moment when the community's survival looked to some like the losing side of a wager.
studies.didYouKnow: The word at the centre of this ayah shares a root with one of the names of God used a few ayat later. There God is named as the protector of the believers. The surah sets the two uses against one another deliberately. The question raised is not whether to have a protector but which one is being relied on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats allegiance as a kind of confession. Where a person turns for safety is presented as a truer statement of belief than what they say. That is why the ayat that follow quote people's reasoning rather than their creed. The standard is uncomfortable in every direction. The surah applies it to the community being addressed. It does not apply it to anyone else.

crossReferences.why: States that God does not forbid kindness and fairness toward those who have not fought you.
Opens shared food and marriage across the same lines, earlier in this same surah.
Names where allegiance belongs instead, only a few ayat later in the passage.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself where you would actually turn if things went badly this year: who you would call, what you would fall back on. Answer honestly, without improving it. This ayah is not asking you to sever anything. It is asking you to notice what your emergency plan reveals about what you are relying on.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers not to take these groups as protectors while they protect each other. Anyone who joins himself to them counts as one of them. God does not guide people who do wrong.

studies.title: We Fear A Turn Of Fortune
studies.meaning: The reasoning behind the hedging is quoted, and it is not hostile. We fear that a turn of events may reach us. It is a calculation about risk, made by people the ayah describes as having a sickness in their hearts, and the sickness is named as that calculation rather than as malice. The response is not an argument. It is a possibility: perhaps God will bring an opening, and then they will regret what they were keeping to themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, during the same period of shifting alliances. Early scholars connect the description to individuals in the city who kept arrangements on both sides while the conflict was unresolved. Reports differ over which cases are meant. What the passage preserves is the reasoning rather than the names. That is why the classical commentaries treat it as a posture available to anyone.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a circle. The image is of fortune coming round, which was how that society understood reversal: not as chance but as a wheel that had already turned for others before them.

The ordinary word for illness, applied here to the heart. The Quran uses it for a condition rather than a decision, which suggests something progressive that the person may not have chosen or even noticed.
To conceal something within oneself, from a root that also yields the word for a private conversation. The regret named at the end attaches to what was hidden, not to what was openly done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hedging was standard practice among the trading families. A merchant with goods on two routes did not put everything on one. A household with several sons might place them in different alliances. Nobody called this treachery. It was how families survived reversals that arrived without warning. The passage describes prudent people making an ordinary calculation, which is what makes its verdict sting.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for regret at the end of this ayah is the same one used earlier in the surah for the man standing over his brother's body. Those are two of only five occurrences in the whole Quran. This surah reaches for it twice. Both times it is a regret that arrives after the moment for acting has passed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is treated here as a position rather than merely an emotion. What the speakers fear is that events will run a certain way, and the passage answers by naming a possibility they had not priced in. That is the whole correction: not that their fear is cowardly, but that their model of how things work has no room in it for God acting. The regret named is for a hidden calculation.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of a sickness in the heart, and says that it increases over time.
Quotes people with sickness in their hearts saying God's promise was only delusion.
Gives the aftermath, and the believers' question once the calculation has been exposed.
