studies.applyIt: Name one arrangement you keep in place purely as insurance against something you say you trust God with. It may be entirely sensible. Look at it anyway and ask which of the two it is: prudence, or a bet placed against your own stated position. Most of us have one of each and have never separated them.
studies.explainEasier: People with sickness in their hearts rush to join those groups. They say they are afraid things may turn against them. But God may bring a win, and then they will be sorry about what they hid.

studies.title: Their Strongest Oaths
studies.meaning: The scene shifts forward to the moment after. Believers look at the people who had sworn by God with their most emphatic oaths that they were with them, and ask a single question: are these the ones. The question is left unanswered, because the answer is the point. Two short clauses close it. Their works came to nothing, and they ended as losers. The oath itself is not condemned; what happened to it is simply reported.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the description of those hedging their alliances. Early scholars read the two ayat as one scene. The second shows the reckoning the first expected. Oaths in the city were public and formal, and swearing by God with emphasis was the strongest assurance available. That is why the passage lets the contrast carry the argument without adding anything to it.

keyTerms.note: The first word means exertion to the very limit of capacity. The phrase describes an oath sworn as forcefully as the language allows, which is what makes the collapse that follows so exact.
Used of livestock that swell after eating a poisonous plant and then die. The image is of something that looks full and is fatally spoiled, which is a very specific picture of worthless works.
A commercial word for a trader whose capital has gone. It measures the outcome against what was staked rather than against a standard, so the loss is theirs before it is anyone's judgement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath sworn by God in front of witnesses was the closest thing that society had to a contract. There was no registry. There was no enforcement beyond reputation. The emphatic oath existed precisely for situations where nothing else would be believed. Using the strongest form and then failing to honour it did more than break an agreement. It spent the only currency a man had for future ones.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for works coming to nothing occurs across the Quran for deeds that are performed and then lost. Its underlying image is agricultural rather than legal. An animal eats what looks like good pasture, swells, and dies. Several of the Quran's words about spiritual failure carry that kind of physical picture beneath them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say the oaths were lies when they were made, and early scholars generally do not either. What it shows is that assurance given in one set of conditions can dissolve in another. The person swearing may not know in advance which they will be. That makes the ayah less about hypocrisy than about the limits of self-knowledge. It is why the question is left open.

crossReferences.why: Describes oaths sworn with the strongest emphasis, and answers that obedience is better known.
Describes charity rendered worthless, using the same verb for works coming to nothing.
Records people swearing by God that they had not said what they in fact said.

studies.applyIt: Think about how emphatically you promise things. Some of us swear hardest when we are least sure. This week, when you next feel the pull to add force to an assurance, drop the force and reduce the promise to what you can actually deliver. Say the smaller thing. It will be believed for longer.
studies.explainEasier: The believers will look at them and ask if these are the same people who swore by God. They had sworn that they were on their side. Their deeds came to nothing, and they lost everything.

studies.title: A People He Loves
studies.meaning: The warning about turning away is answered with a replacement, not a threat. God will bring a people, described in five clauses. Love is named in both directions, and God's love comes first. Then come two opposite bearings: lowered towards believers, firm towards those who reject. Early scholars read them as one temper adjusted to its object. The last clause is the sharpest. They do not fear the blame of anyone who blames.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah. The passage is about alliances, and about people whose loyalty ran elsewhere. Early scholars record several suggestions about who the promised people are, and settle on none. They treat the description as the point, not the naming. By this stage the community was large enough that reputation inside it had become a pressure in its own right.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the word for humbled or lowly, used here of a bearing chosen rather than imposed. Early scholars explain it as making oneself low for believers, the way ground is low enough to be walked on.
From the root for might and for what is rare and hard to reach. Set against the word before it, it describes not harshness but a refusal to be moved, so the pair marks two directions of one strength.

The form names one instance of blame. What is denied is not endurance under long criticism but any flinch at all, including at the single remark that makes a person adjust what they were about to say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Arabia was enforced by poetry. A satirist could damage a man's standing across the peninsula in a few lines. Those lines travelled with every caravan, and families paid to have their honour defended in verse. Shame was the main tool of social control. It worked better than any authority. Describing people who do not flinch at blame named something rare enough to be worth promising.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause in which God loves them and they love Him appears in this exact form nowhere else in the Quran. Elsewhere the text names the kinds of people God loves: the just, the patient, those who rely on Him. Only here is the love returned inside one sentence. God's love is stated first and the human answer second.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine love is stated first. God loves them, and their love follows in the second clause. That puts the first move outside the human being. The passage also treats the community as replaceable. That is a hard thing to say to people just warned about turning back. The message does not depend on any one group carrying it. Courage is then defined socially, as freedom from the fear of what people will say.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the threat of replacement, saying others would be brought who are not like you.
Makes love the axis of the relationship, tying it to following the Messenger.
Describes those who deliver God's messages and fear none but Him.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you did not say this week because of how it would land, and ask whether the reason was kindness or fear of being thought badly of. Those two feel identical from the inside. The verse names the second one specifically, and the way to tell them apart is usually who was being protected.
studies.explainEasier: God says that if some people walk away from their faith, he will bring others in their place. He will love them and they will love him. They will be kind to believers and will not worry about what people say.

studies.title: Your Protector Is God
studies.meaning: The negative instruction a few ayat earlier is answered with its positive. Your protector is God, and His Messenger, and those who believe. Those are the ones who keep up the prayer, give the purifying due, and are bowing. Early scholars differ over the last clause. Some read it as the believers' habitual bearing of humility. Some read it as pointing to a specific act. Reports of an occasion are recorded, and the tradition keeps the readings side by side.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the passage about where allegiance belongs. The classical sources record reports of one occasion for this ayah. Early scholars do not agree about them. That is why the main commentaries set out the reports and the general reading together. Neither is ranked above the other. On any reading the setting is a community deciding whom to rely on while its ties were unsettled.

keyTerms.note: The singular of the word used earlier for allies. Naming God first and in the singular makes protection one thing with a single source, which the rest of the sentence then extends rather than divides.
A participle describing the bowing posture of prayer, and in wider usage a bearing of humility. The early scholars read the clause both ways, as a state the believers are in and as a particular act.
A group bound to one another by a common commitment. The Quran uses the word both of this alignment and of its opposite, so it names a kind of belonging rather than an honorific title.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's patron was the most consequential fact about him. It determined who would avenge him, who would feed his family in a famine, and whether his word carried in a dispute. Changing patrons was possible and public, and the whole town knew when it happened. To be told that protection now ran through one source, and through the people who prayed and gave, was to be told the map had been redrawn.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as the party of God appears twice in the Quran. Both times it is the closing clause of a passage about allegiance, and both times it promises the same outcome. Its opposite, a party belonging to the adversary, appears once. That is in the same surah as the second of those two, which makes the pairing deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is described as a single thing with an order inside it. God, then the Messenger, then the believers. That places human solidarity downstream of a relation with God rather than beside it. The two markers given are prayer and the purifying due. One is vertical and the other horizontal. So belonging is identified by what a person does with God and with other people, not by descent or by a stated position.

crossReferences.why: Gives the negative instruction that this ayah answers, only a few ayat earlier.
Closes another passage on allegiance with the same phrase and the same promise.
Describes believing men and women as protectors of one another, with the same two markers.

studies.applyIt: Look at your week and count the hours you give to the two things this ayah names: standing in prayer, and putting money or effort where it helps someone. Do not judge the number. Just have it. Whatever it turns out to be, add fifteen minutes to the smaller of the two this week and leave the rest alone.
studies.explainEasier: Your real protector is God. Then His Messenger. Then the believers who pray and give to the poor. Anyone who turns to them for help is on God's side. God's side always wins.

studies.title: Those Who Make It A Joke
studies.meaning: The instruction about allies returns with a different test. What is named is not a community but a behaviour. It is taking your religion as mockery and as amusement. The ayah is explicit that such people may be found among those given scripture before you. They may be found among those who reject faith too. That places the category across both lines rather than along them. The closing clause makes it a matter of consciousness of God rather than of grievance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Early scholars connect this ayah and the one after it to people who ridiculed the call to prayer when it was raised in the city. They imitated it and laughed. Reports vary in their detail. The call was new, audible across the whole town, and unavoidable. That is what made it a natural target, and what makes the passage specific rather than general.

keyTerms.note: A noun rather than a verb, so the religion is described as having been turned into a thing of a certain kind. The grammar reports a transformation rather than a single incident of laughter.

The word for children's play, used across the Quran for activity without purpose. Pairing it with mockery separates two failures: treating something as ridiculous, and treating it as merely unserious.

The same word as the earlier instruction, and its placement at the end of a long sentence is deliberate: the criterion arrives before the category it applies to, so behaviour is what determines the outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon in Arabia, and a professional one. Poets were hired to satirise a rival tribe. Their verses travelled further and lasted longer than any raid. A community could be defended against attack and still be ruined by ridicule. Reputation determined who would trade, marry and ally with it. Taking mockery seriously was not thin skin. It was an accurate reading of that society.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words paired here, mockery and play, occur together again in the very next ayah. There they are applied to the call to prayer. The Quran often repeats a phrase across consecutive ayat this way, first as a test and then as the instance that shows it. The pair appears nowhere else in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test given is behaviour. It is said plainly to cut across communities rather than to follow them. That is the passage's structural claim. It matches the surah's practice elsewhere of naming conduct rather than groups. Ending on consciousness of God rather than on the offence also turns the instruction inward. The guard asked for is over one's own alignment, not over anyone else's speech.

crossReferences.why: Gives the specific instance, mockery of the call to prayer, in the very next sentence.
Instructs withdrawal from a gathering where God's signs are ridiculed, until the subject changes.
Says to turn away from those who mock the signs until they enter some other discourse.

studies.applyIt: Notice which rooms you go quiet in. Everyone has one where their practice would be treated as a joke, and everyone manages it somehow. You do not have to leave the room. But this week, in one such conversation, say the ordinary true thing once, without defending it, and see what actually happens.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers not to take as friends the people who turn their faith into a joke. That is true whether those people have earlier books or none. He says to keep God in mind if they really believe.

studies.title: When You Call To Prayer
studies.meaning: The general criterion becomes a specific scene. When you call to the prayer, they take it as mockery and as play. The verb and the nouns are the same as the ayah before, so criterion and instance are matched word for word. Then a reason is given, and it is unexpected: because they are a people who do not use reason. Ridicule is diagnosed as a failure of understanding rather than as hostility, which is a gentler judgement than the tone suggests.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The call to prayer was established in the city and was audible everywhere, which was the point of it. Early scholars report that some who heard it imitated and laughed at it. The reports differ over which individuals were involved. A public, repeated, unignorable summons was a new thing in that town. Reactions to it were part of how the community's presence was worked out.

keyTerms.note: The verb of calling across a distance to someone who may not be looking your way. It suits a summons meant to reach people at work in their houses and fields, which is what the call was for.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, as a camel is hobbled. Reasoning in Arabic is a binding of things together, so the failure named is one of connection rather than of intelligence.

The word for aimless activity, repeated from the previous ayah. Its return in the same phrase joins the criterion to its instance, so the general rule and the particular case are linked by vocabulary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before the call was established, gathering people for prayer was a practical problem. The community discussed using a horn, a bell, or a fire lit on a height. They settled on a human voice from a rooftop. That choice made the summons a person speaking rather than an instrument sounding. It meant the words themselves, not just the signal, carried across the town.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions the call to prayer in only two places. Here, and in the short surah about the Friday gathering. That is a very small footprint for something so audible. The classical sources discuss how the call was set up. They treat it as a decision reached through consultation rather than as a matter settled in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Attaching mockery to a failure of reasoning rather than to malice changes what the passage asks of a believer. If ridicule comes from not connecting things, then neither payback nor grievance is the answer. The ayah also treats the call as a test of the hearer, not of the caller. That quietly moves the whole situation. What is measured is the reaction. It is not the summons.

crossReferences.why: Mentions the call to prayer again, in the passage about the Friday gathering.
Sets the criterion that this ayah illustrates, using the identical pair of words.
Describes hearts that do not reason, using the same verb for the failure named here.

studies.applyIt: The next time you hear the call, whether from a speaker, a phone, or your own memory of the hour, stop what you are doing for the length of it and listen to the words rather than treating it as a timer. It takes under a minute. Most of us have heard it thousands of times and never once listened.
studies.explainEasier: When you call people to prayer, they laugh at it and treat it as a game. That is because they do not think it through. They do not use their minds.

studies.title: Do You Resent Us For This
studies.meaning: A question is put in the Prophet's mouth and it is close to disarming. Do you resent us for anything other than that we believe in God, and in what was sent down to us, and in what was sent down before? The list is the point. What is being objected to includes belief in their own scripture. The final clause is sharper. But the argument has already been made by the shape of the question rather than by what follows it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to communities of earlier scripture in the city. Early scholars do not tie it to one exchange. The setting is a series of arguments in which the new community's claims were being contested. The ayah's method is typical of this surah. It sums up the opponent's position back to them in the mildest possible terms and lets that summary do the work.

keyTerms.note: A verb for disapproval that leads toward retaliation, not mere dislike. It names finding fault with something and wanting it punished, which is why the mildness of the list that follows is so pointed.
The clause that makes the question work. It states that the belief being objected to includes their own revelation, so the objection turns out to be to an agreement rather than to a difference.
The same word used to close the earlier passage about judging by what was sent down. Its return here links the resentment described to the failure diagnosed only a few ayat before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Argument in that world was carried on in public and remembered afterwards. Disputes between communities happened at gatherings and in markets. A well-formed question, repeated by bystanders, could settle a matter better than an answer could. Skill with words was not decoration. It was the means by which positions actually moved. This ayah's method would have been recognised at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated here as resent occurs only three times in the Quran. In one of them it describes people who found fault with others for nothing except that they believed in God. The word carries the sense of taking revenge. So what it names is never merely a difference of opinion between parties.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the disagreement exactly. Then it shows how small it is at the point of contact. What is objected to is belief in God and in revelation. That includes revelation the objectors accept. The framing does not settle the dispute. But it changes what the dispute is about. The surah has been doing this throughout, moving arguments from identity onto conduct and content.

crossReferences.why: Describes people persecuted for nothing except that they believed in God, using the same verb.
States belief in what was sent to earlier prophets without distinguishing between any of them.
Repeats the same declaration of belief across every revelation it names in turn.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement, try stating the other person's objection back to them in the plainest words you can find, and then stop. Do not add your answer. Half the time they will correct you, which means you had it wrong. The other half, hearing it said flatly does more than any argument you had prepared.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet is told to ask them a plain thing. They hold it against us only for this. We believe in God. We believe in what He sent to us, and in what He sent before.

studies.title: Worse Than That In Recompense
studies.meaning: The question of the previous ayah is answered with a counter-question. It is about recompense rather than about people. Shall I tell you of something worse in its outcome with God? What follows is a list of conditions. Being cursed, drawing anger, the change the earlier scripture reports of a community that transgressed, and the service of false powers. The classical scholars differ over whether that change was of form or of state. They record both readings without deciding.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering an objection raised against the community. The episode hinted at belongs to the earlier scriptural history. The Quran refers to it in two other places. It never tells it in full. Early scholars treat it with care as an account of one past group. This surah's method is to name conduct and what follows from it. It does not label any living community.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to come back, the same family as the word for a reward. Applied to a bad outcome, it keeps the sense of something returning to its origin rather than being imposed from outside.
From a root meaning to exceed all bounds, as floodwater does. The word names any authority that has overflowed its proper place, which is why it can cover idols, tyrants and systems alike.
A comparative from the verb to lose one's way. The passage measures distance from a road rather than depth of guilt, which keeps the image spatial and matches the sentence's closing phrase exactly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories of communities destroyed for transgression were the common inheritance of the region. They were told at gatherings and along the trade routes. Ruined settlements in northern Arabia were pointed out to travellers. They were the remains of peoples who had been warned and had not listened. Such accounts were not exotic to this audience. They were part of the landscape, and they set the register for hearing a list like this.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran refers to this change in three places and never tells it as a scene. In each case it is mentioned in a single clause inside a larger argument. That is unusual for the text's handling of dramatic events. The classical commentaries note the restraint and generally read it as deliberate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given to an objection about a community is a list of conditions rather than a list of people. What is described is a path. Cursing, anger, change, and finally the service of what has overstepped its bounds. Placing that last makes it the destination rather than the starting point. So the passage reads as a warning about direction. That is how the classical commentaries generally handle it.

crossReferences.why: Refers to the same episode in a single clause, within the earlier Medinan surah.
Refers to it again, attached to an account of transgression concerning the sabbath.
Names the same false power, and sets rejection of it against holding fast to God.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing you serve that has quietly outgrown its place: a metric at work, a schedule, an opinion you need from someone. Not evil, just oversized. Name it out loud, and then do one small thing this week that would be unthinkable if it were really in charge. That is the whole test the word here proposes.
studies.explainEasier: The Prophet is told to point to something worse. Some people were cursed by God and made to face His anger. Some were changed into apes and swine. Some served false powers. They are further from the right road.

studies.title: They Came In And Went Out
studies.meaning: A short sentence with a symmetry inside it. When they come to you they say we believe, and they entered with rejection and left with it. The two verbs bracket the visit, so the declaration made in the middle is surrounded on both sides by what did not change. Nothing is inferred about them; the passage states what was carried in and out. The closing clause then moves the whole matter to God's knowledge of what is concealed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the section on people who presented one position and held another. Early scholars tie the description to particular visitors in the city without agreeing on which. They read the ayah as describing a posture rather than naming a group. The setting is a town where formal visits between communities were frequent. What was said at them was reported back and weighed.

keyTerms.note: Paired in this sentence with the verb for leaving, and both take the same object. The symmetry makes the visit a container: something was brought in and the same thing was carried out again.
To keep back something that others have a claim on, used in the Quran of withheld testimony and hidden scripture. It names suppression of what should be disclosed rather than ordinary privacy.

A comparative form used of God across the Quran. It does not merely assert knowledge but places it above the knowledge of everyone in the sentence, including the people being described about themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Delegations were how business between communities was done. A group arrived, greetings were exchanged in fixed forms, positions were stated, and everyone went home to report. The formality was protective. It let two parties who did not trust each other meet without incident. It also meant something else. Everyone present understood the meeting to be a performance as much as a disclosure.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence uses two ordinary verbs of motion, entering and leaving, to frame an entire inner condition. Both take the same object. The Quran often works this way. It carries a judgement through the arrangement of very common words rather than through vocabulary that announces itself as religious.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage declines to accuse and instead describes a shape, then hands the assessment to God. That is a consistent move across this section: conduct is stated plainly and the verdict is withheld from the reader. It also names concealment as the real subject, which implies the visit itself was not the failure. What was hidden during it was, and only one party to the meeting could know that.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same distance between what is said aloud and what the heart holds.
States that God will call to account for what is in the hearts, whether shown or hidden.
Describes people saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts, on a particular day.

studies.applyIt: Think about a meeting you have coming up where you already know what you will say and what you will not. That is normal. But check one thing before you go: whether anything you are withholding is something the other person has a right to know. If it is, decide about it now, not in the room.
studies.explainEasier: When they come to you they say they believe. But they walked in without belief and walked out the same way. God knows what they are hiding.

studies.title: Racing In Sin
studies.meaning: A single sentence of observation, and its verb is the striking part. You see many of them hurrying into wrongdoing, hostility, and the consuming of illicit gain. Hurrying is the same verb used a few ayat earlier. There it described those rushing toward alliances out of fear. So the surah applies one word to two very different failures. The closing clause is a formula of dismay rather than a sentence passed: how wretched what they have been doing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The passage sits in a stretch describing the conduct of some among the communities of earlier scripture. Early scholars note that the wording is careful: many of them, not all. The surah has already qualified two similar descriptions the same way. The setting is a market town where lending at interest, bribery in disputes and sharp practice in weights were all present and all profitable.

keyTerms.note: A form implying eagerness and competition, used elsewhere in the Quran of racing toward forgiveness. The same verb serves for hastening toward good and toward harm, so what it measures is appetite rather than direction.
From a root meaning to scrape away or to destroy utterly. The word occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah, which is one way the chapter marks out its subject.
From the verb to cross a boundary. Paired with the general word for wrongdoing, it separates the wrong done in private from the wrong that reaches across and takes something from someone else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A market in that world had no inspector. Weights were the trader's own, a debt could be rolled over with an addition each time, and a judge's favour could be secured with a gift that nobody called a bribe. None of it was hidden; it was simply how business ran for those who could get away with it. Everyone knew which houses had grown wealthy that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for illicit earnings appears three times in the Quran. All three are in this surah, within about twenty ayat of one another. Such concentration is rare. Early scholars treat repeated vocabulary of that kind as one of the ways a chapter signals what it is actually about.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verb chosen is the passage's argument. Wrongdoing is not described here as weakness or as a slip. It is described as eagerness. People move toward it fast, and they race each other there. That makes it a matter of appetite, not of a struggle lost. The same verb is used elsewhere for racing toward forgiveness. So the energy itself is neutral. Only its object decides what it becomes.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for hurrying toward forgiveness and a garden, pointing that energy the other way.
Asks immediately why the scholars among them do not restrain exactly this behaviour.
Names consuming others' property wrongly, and using the authorities in order to do it.

studies.applyIt: Watch your own speed this week. There is something you get to quickly and something you approach slowly, and the gap between them tells you more than any list of intentions. Pick the one you are slow to and start it ten minutes earlier once. Speed is habit, and habit is what this ayah is measuring.
studies.explainEasier: You see many of them racing into sin and bad feeling. They take money they should not take. The ayah says what they keep doing is truly bad.

studies.title: Why Do They Not Restrain Them
studies.meaning: The question turns from those doing wrong to those who watch them do it. Why do the teachers and the scholars not restrain them from their sinful speech and their consuming of illicit gain? The closing formula is the same one used of the wrongdoers in the previous ayah, with a single verb changed. Early scholars notice the change. The doers were described by what they do, and the scholars by what they produce, which is the harsher of the two.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the description of wrongdoing in the ayah before, and read with it as one unit. The setting is a city where scholars held real authority. They gave rulings, settled disputes and taught. Their silence on a practice worked as permission. The passage addresses that authority rather than the practice, which is the shift the two ayat perform together.

keyTerms.note: A particle that both asks a question and expresses reproach. It is not a neutral enquiry; the form already contains the judgement, which is why the ayah needs no accusation after it.
The verb of forbidding, but its root sense is reaching a limit. What is asked for is the placing of an end point, which in a society without enforcement was largely a matter of speech.
A verb of craft and deliberate production, replacing the plainer verb for doing used one ayah earlier. The change makes the scholars' silence a thing constructed rather than merely a thing done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A scholar's word travelled. He was consulted at weddings and funerals. He was consulted at the settling of estates and the drawing of contracts. What he declined to object to was recorded by everyone present as acceptable. His household was supported by the community he advised. That meant objecting to a wealthy family's practice carried a direct cost. The passage names that pressure without excusing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat end with formulas differing by a single word. One uses the ordinary verb for doing. The other uses a verb meaning to craft or fabricate. Classical scholars reading the pair together generally take the second as the graver. Their ground is that silence in the face of a wrong is something a person builds rather than something that happens to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is extended from the act to the permission around it. The passage does not accuse the scholars of doing the wrong. It accuses them of not placing a limit on it. It treats that omission as a form of making. That is a claim about how communities decay. Not through the number of wrongdoers, but through the number of people who decide that saying something is not their part.

crossReferences.why: Describes an earlier community that did not restrain one another from the wrongs they committed.
Names the practices this question is about, in the ayah immediately before it.
Describes a community defined by enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

studies.applyIt: Think of a thing said or done regularly around you that you have decided not to object to. You have reasons, and they are probably good ones. This week, in one instance, say the smallest possible version of the objection: not a speech, one sentence, without heat. Notice whether anything you feared actually follows.
studies.explainEasier: The ayah asks why their teachers and scholars do not stop them. They see the wrong talk and the money taken wrongly and say nothing. What they are making is bad too.

studies.title: His Hands Are Outstretched
studies.meaning: A saying is quoted and answered in the same breath. Someone said that God's hand is tied. The reply reverses it word for word: their own hands are tied. Then comes the correction. Both His hands are outstretched, and He spends as He wills. The image of two open hands is among the most striking figures in the Quran. The early scholars handle it as they handle all such pictures. They keep the generosity it carries without picturing a form.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars give the saying to particular people, not to a whole community. Their reports differ over who said it and when. The wider setting was a time of hardship. A remark about God's provision drying up would have had an obvious occasion then. The ayah answers the idea rather than chasing the speakers.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle used of a hand chained to the neck. The Quran uses the same image elsewhere for miserliness. The saying accuses God of the very thing this word usually accuses a person of.
A dual form, so two hands. The early scholars read the dual as heightening generosity rather than describing a body. Arabic uses open hands for giving as naturally as English uses an open door.
The verb of putting out a fire, used here of a war that has been kindled. It describes not a battle won but a fire that fails to take. That is a quieter kind of help than victory.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A closed fist and an open hand were the standard Arabian signs for a mean man and a giving one. The poets used them all the time. A chief was praised as one whose palm was never closed. A tight man was described as having a hand bound to the neck. The saying quoted here was not a fine point of doctrine. It took the plainest insult in the language and pointed it upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The same image of a hand chained to the neck turns up in another surah. There it is advice to a person about their own spending. It warns against the closed fist and against the hand opened until nothing is left. So one gesture covers human balance. The dual form covers a giving from God that has no limit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply does not argue that God is generous. It turns the charge back on the accusers first, in the grammar of the sentence, before making any claim at all. Then it states the positive side in the widest terms. He spends as He wills. The passage also shows how the tradition reads picture-language about God. It keeps what the image says and refuses to turn it into a description of a form.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of a hand tied to the neck, as advice about a person's own spending.
Records another saying attributed to some, that God is poor and that they are rich.
Says that God withholds and gives in abundance, and that to Him is the return.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk about your own resources when you are anxious. There is a way of saying we cannot afford it that is accurate, and a way that is a small theology. Say one true, specific sentence about your situation this week instead of the general one. The general one is usually where the tied hand creeps in.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said that God's hand is tied, meaning He has stopped giving. God answers that their own hands are tied. His two hands are open wide. He gives to whoever He wants.

studies.title: Had They Believed
studies.meaning: A conditional sentence, and its whole force lies in the mood. Had the people of the scripture believed and been careful of God, We would have covered over their wrongs. And We would have brought them into gardens of delight. Nothing is denied to them and nothing is promised. A door is described as open, and not walked through. The turn is abrupt after a long stretch of criticism. The early scholars note that the surah interrupts itself this way again and again.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, placed right after some of the surah's sharpest material about conduct. The early scholars read the sudden turn as typical of the chapter. Criticism is followed by an opening rather than by a verdict. No specific occasion is reported. The people addressed were neighbours in the city. The community traded with them, argued with them and shared a street with them. They were not a distant idea.

keyTerms.note: From the root for covering, the same used earlier in this surah for atonement. Wrongs are described as buried rather than as never committed, which keeps the record honest while removing its weight.
From the verb to guard oneself. Paired here with believing, it names an ongoing wariness rather than a single act of assent, so the condition described is a way of living rather than a declaration.
An intensive noun from the root for a soft and pleasant life. Attaching it to gardens describes the quality of the place rather than its features, which is unusual in the Quran's garden imagery.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A garden in Arabia was a walled plot with running water and shade. It was the most valuable property a family could hold. It was also the clearest picture of ease that anyone had. Owning one meant you stopped worrying about the season. So the audience heard a specific and envied thing, not a symbol. It was the difference between a life of counting and a life of enough.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one after it are both built the same way. Each describes what would have followed from something that did not happen. The Quran uses that construction sparingly. Here it gives two sentences in a row that criticise and invite at the same time. Neither one does either thing directly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage keeps the future open while describing the past honestly. Nothing in it shuts a door. The criticism before it is not withdrawn, and it is not allowed to settle into a verdict. That pairing is a shape this surah returns to. It says something about how the Quran wants a disagreement held. What is said about conduct is final. What is said about people is not.

crossReferences.why: Continues with a second conditional, about what upholding their scriptures would have produced.
Ends a similar passage of correction with an invitation rather than with a conclusion.
Names a standing community among them who recite the signs of God through the night.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have quietly written off. Not an enemy, just a person you have concluded will not change. Say to yourself the sentence this ayah models: if they did, what would follow. Then behave for one week as though that were still available. The change, if there is one, will show in how you speak to them.
studies.explainEasier: God says that if these people had believed and been careful, He would have wiped away their wrongs. He would have let them into beautiful gardens. The door is still open. Nobody has been shut out.

studies.title: Eating From Above And Below
studies.meaning: A second conditional follows the first. This one is about food rather than the hereafter. Had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to them, they would have eaten from above them and from under their feet. Rain and harvest, named as directions rather than as things. Then the sentence does what the criticism around it has not. It names a balanced community among them, before it turns back to the many.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars read above and below as rain from the sky and crops from the ground. Those were the two sources of every living in a farming society. They also note the clause that names a balanced group among them. They read it as a deliberate limit on the criticism. It matches similar notes elsewhere in this surah and in the one before it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something stand, used across the Quran for establishing prayer. Applying it to a scripture means putting it into practice rather than merely possessing, preserving or reciting it.
From a root meaning to aim straight for something and to keep to the middle of a road. It names a group that neither exceeds nor falls short, and the same root gives the word for economy.
A direction rather than a substance. Pairing it with beneath the feet covers the two sources of food in that world, rain and soil, without naming either, which makes the promise total.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabia depended on two directions. Rain came or it did not, and the wells and the date palms answered accordingly. A year's whole prospect could be read in the sky within a fortnight, and villages sent watchers to high ground for the first clouds. To describe abundance as eating from above and below was to name every possible source at once, in the only terms that mattered.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause naming a balanced community is one of several places where this surah narrows a broad criticism at once. The chapter does it again and again. It says many of them rather than all of them. The classical scholars treat those words as binding. They shape how the material around them should be read.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Food is presented as tied to conduct. The Quran does this elsewhere, and always with care. The claim is about a community over time. It is not about one person's luck in a given year. What makes the ayah notable is the limit it sets. It has just described a large failure. Then it stops to name those the description does not fit. The commentaries treat that clause as decisive.

crossReferences.why: Says belief and God-consciousness would have opened blessings from the sky and the earth.
Names a standing community among the people of scripture who are not like the rest.
Describes provision arriving from a direction the person had not reckoned on.

studies.applyIt: Look at where this month's provision actually came from. Not the salary line, the whole chain: the person who hired you, the rain that grew the food, the health that let you work. Write down three links you had no part in arranging. It takes five minutes and it changes what the word earning means.
studies.explainEasier: God says that if they had lived by their own books, food would have come to them from the sky above and the ground below. Some of them do keep to the middle path. Many do not.

studies.title: Convey What Was Sent Down
studies.meaning: A short instruction with the largest possible stake attached. Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message. The condition is absolute: partial delivery counts as none. Then a promise of protection follows. That tells you what the instruction was up against. The early scholars record more than one account of the occasion and do not agree. They set the reports out without ranking them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources keep several accounts of when this ayah came down and what it was about. They differ. The commentaries record the range rather than settling it. What they agree on is the setting. Delivering the message carried real physical risk at the time. That is why the ayah pairs its instruction with a promise of protection rather than with a warning.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to reach a destination, in a form meaning to make something arrive. What is asked is not speech but arrival, so the measure of success lies with the hearer rather than the speaker.
From a root meaning to hold something back from falling or from harm, the same family as the word for a bond or a firm grip. Protection is described as a holding rather than a covering over.
The word for a message sent and, by extension, for the office of the one who carries it. Using the singular makes the whole commission one thing, which is why leaving out a part fails all of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia carried words he was not allowed to edit. Delegations learned what they were sent with by heart. They recited it back word for word, sometimes to a hostile crowd. A messenger who softened a message on arrival had failed at his only task. The custom protected the sender and put the carrier at risk. Everyone in that society knew which of the two was exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for conveying gives its name to a whole field of Arabic study. That field looks at how speech is shaped so that it reaches its hearer. The same root also gives the word for coming of age. So the language treats delivery, arrival and growing up as versions of one idea.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction defines a messenger wholly by what he passes on. It leaves no room for judging what an audience can bear. That is a demanding standard. The promise of protection is attached to the task, not to the result. So the risk was expected to be real and the welcome uncertain. The passage also treats revelation as something held in trust rather than owned.

crossReferences.why: States that nothing rests on the Messenger except the delivery of the message itself.
Describes those who deliver the messages of God and fear no one except Him.
Says the Messenger's charge is what was placed on him, and yours is what was placed on you.

studies.applyIt: There is something you have been asked to pass on and have been softening: a decision, a diagnosis, a colleague's honest view. Deliver it once this week in the words you were given, without your own cushioning. You can be kind about the manner. This ayah's whole subject is the difference between kindness and editing.
studies.explainEasier: God tells His messenger to pass on everything he has been given. If he leaves part of it out, he has not done the job at all. God also promises to keep him safe from people.

studies.title: You Stand On Nothing
studies.meaning: The instruction to convey is followed at once by what is to be conveyed, and it is blunt. You stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what was sent down to you from your Lord. The demand is that they apply their own scriptures, not that they drop them. Then the ayah grants that the message will increase many of them in defiance. It closes by telling the Prophet not to grieve over that.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to communities holding earlier scripture. The early scholars read it together with the ayah before it. They take the instruction to convey and this content as one movement. No specific occasion is reported. The setting is the running argument in the city about what each community's scripture asked of it. This ayah takes a position that is demanding and generous at once.

keyTerms.note: Literally standing on no thing, an idiom for having no footing at all. The image is spatial: what is denied is a place to stand rather than a claim to be right, which is a sharper accusation.

The verb for making something stand, used across the Quran of establishing prayer. Applied to scripture it means putting the text into practice, and its choice here answers the image of having no footing.
From the root for water overflowing its banks. What increases is not disbelief alone but a spilling past limits, which the Quran treats as a failure distinct from denial itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was the posture of a claim. A man rose to speak in a dispute. Where he stood in the assembly showed what backing he had behind him. To tell a group they were standing on nothing borrowed from that setting directly. It did not say their argument was weak. It said there was no ground under them at all. That was the most complete dismissal the idiom allowed.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about the revelation increasing many of them in defiance appears twice in this surah. The wording is nearly the same both times, four ayat apart. Repeating at that distance is one of the surah's habits of structure. The classical scholars mostly read the second use as closing a section that the first one opened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The demand made of another community is that it be true to its own revelation. That sets the pattern for how this surah handles difference. The ayah also grants something unusual. The arrival of guidance can make some people worse. It says so without embarrassment, then tells the Prophet not to grieve. So the passage builds the failure of the message into the message's own account of itself.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same clause about the revelation increasing many of them in defiance.
Instructs the people of the Gospel to judge by what God sent down within it.
Says the revelation is healing for believers and increases only loss for wrongdoers.

studies.applyIt: Take the tradition you belong to and ask what it actually asks of you this week, in its plainest terms, rather than what you enjoy about belonging to it. Do one of those things on Thursday. This ayah's whole demand is for footing, and footing comes from practice rather than from possession.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people who follow earlier books that they stand on nothing until they live by those books. Many of them will only push back harder when they hear this. God tells His messenger not to be sad about that.

studies.title: Nothing To Fear, No Grief
studies.meaning: Four communities are listed by name. Then the sentence starts again with a condition that cuts across all of them: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, and acts rightly. Early scholars discuss the grammar closely, since a singular relative clause takes over the list. What is promised is stated as an absence: no fear and no grief. Those are the two directions worry runs. One goes forward to what may come, the other back over what is gone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah addressed largely to communities holding earlier scriptures. The passage has just told them their books do not stand on nothing. A nearly identical sentence appears earlier in the Quran, at 2:62. Early scholars treat the repetition as deliberate. They note that here it follows an appeal rather than a rebuke.

keyTerms.note: A community named three times in the Quran and never described. Classical scholars offer differing identifications and several say plainly that the group is not certainly known, so the name is left standing as given.
Anxiety directed forward, at what has not yet happened. Across the Quran it is paired with a word for grief over what already has, and the two together cover the whole timeline of distress.
The verb for working, joined to a word meaning sound or fit for purpose. Right action is described as repair, making something work as it should, rather than as obedience to an instruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religious identity in Arabia was inherited and public. It was tied to which shrines your people kept, and which oaths they swore by. Communities lived side by side in Medina. Each had its own courts, festivals and burial grounds. A person's group showed in their name. This sentence names four of those communities. Then it says the same thing about individuals inside them. That cut against the grain of how everyone was sorted.
studies.didYouKnow: In this verse the word for the Sabians stands in the nominative case. The construction would normally call for the accusative, as it does at 2:62. This is among the most discussed points of grammar in the Quran. The classical grammarians explained it as a deliberate suspension. It sets the word slightly apart from the list around it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sentence puts the decisive weight on what a person believes and does rather than on the label they carry, without dissolving the labels: the communities are named, not merged. The promise is framed as removal rather than addition, which is a specific kind of comfort. It does not say what such people will be given. It says what will not be there, and names the whole of what human beings are usually afraid of.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sentence with the communities in a different order, and a reward clause added.
Gives the same promise to whoever submits and does good, in the singular.
Explains why the communities differ, and tells them to compete in good works.

studies.applyIt: Write down the fear that has been running underneath this week, and the regret that has been running alongside it. One sentence each. The verse names those two and only those two, which suggests that almost everything heavy you are carrying is one or the other, and it helps just to see which.
studies.explainEasier: God names several different groups of people. Then he says the same thing about all of them. Anyone who believes in God and the Last Day, and does what is right, has nothing to fear and nothing to be sad about.

studies.title: Whenever A Messenger Came
studies.meaning: A covenant is recalled and messengers are sent. Then a pattern is stated, not a set of events. Whenever a messenger came with what their souls did not want, one group they called liars and another they killed. The word whenever makes it a repeated shape rather than a list of incidents. The two responses are not treated alike. The grammar keeps them apart. One is stated as finished, the other in a form that keeps going.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section reviewing covenants made and broken. The Quran names no individual messengers or episodes here. It gives the pattern and leaves the instances to an audience that partly knew them. The early scholars supply names from the older tradition. They treat those names as material beside the text rather than as part of it.

keyTerms.note: A construction of repetition rather than of a single instance. It converts a set of events into a habit, which is why the ayah reads as the description of a mechanism rather than an accusation about particular occasions.

From the root for falling or inclining downward, the same word used for the desires the Prophet is warned against following. The criterion for rejection is named here as appetite rather than as evidence.

An imperfect verb where the clause before used a past tense. So the killing is described as ongoing while the denial is complete. The early grammarians read the shift as making the second response the more vivid.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who told a tribe something it did not want to hear had two things to fear. Neither of them was argument. He could be discredited, which cost him his standing and his chance to trade or marry. Or he could be dealt with more directly on a road somewhere. Both outcomes were common. Anyone bringing unwelcome news worked them out in advance.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah shifts tense between its two clauses. The charge of lying is in the past. The killing is in a form that keeps going. The early grammarians treated such shifts as deliberate rather than loose. The commentaries on this ayah discuss the change at length. Most read it as bringing the second act before the listener's eyes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test for rejection sits in desire rather than in evidence. That is the passage's real claim. Messengers were not refused because their case was weak. They were refused because of what their message asked. That makes the pattern portable. Any community can be measured by how it treats what it did not want to hear. The surah has been building toward exactly this point.

crossReferences.why: States the same pattern in the earlier surah, naming the same two responses in order.
Continues with what they assumed would follow, and with what happened twice over.
Describes messengers sent one after another, each denied by the community he came to.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last time someone told you something true that you did not want to hear. Did you argue with the content or with the person? Most of us go for the person, because it is quicker. Find that conversation again, and go back to whatever the content actually was. It is probably still waiting.
studies.explainEasier: God made an agreement with the Children of Israel and kept sending them messengers. Every time a messenger brought something they did not like, they called some of them liars. Others they killed.

studies.title: Blind And Deaf, Then Again
studies.meaning: A calculation is described and then its consequence. They reckoned there would be no reckoning, so they went blind and deaf. Then God turned toward them. Then many of them went blind and deaf again. The structure is the point: a failure, a mercy, and the same failure returning, with the mercy placed in the middle rather than at the end. The closing clause adds nothing except that God sees what they do.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the review of an earlier community's history. The Quran presses centuries into one sentence with three turns in it. The early scholars note that this is how the surah handles the past. It gives a pattern rather than a chronicle. No specific episodes are named. The classical commentaries fill them in from the older tradition where they can.

keyTerms.note: The verb of accounting and arithmetic, used for forming an expectation. It shares a root with the word for the final reckoning, so the sentence has them miscalculating the very thing they are calculating about.
Two verbs in a form describing something that happened to them, not a condition they were born with. The early scholars read the pair as a loss that follows a choice rather than coming before it.

The same verb used for a person's own repentance, with a preposition that reverses its direction. Placing it in the middle of the sentence makes mercy an event within the history rather than its conclusion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness and deafness were common, and they carried real consequences. A man who could not see could not travel alone or judge a beast at market. A man who could not hear was cut out of the poetry and the news. Those were the whole information system of a tribe. Using the two together named a person shut off from every way anyone learned anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs for blindness and deafness appear in the same order twice inside this one ayah. A sentence of mercy stands between them. That kind of exact repetition inside a single ayah is uncommon in the Quran. It lets the shape of the sentence carry the argument before any of its words do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's turning sits in the middle of the sentence, not at its close. That says something about how the passage understands mercy. Mercy is not the end of a history. It is an event inside one. The same failure can follow it. That is a sober picture. It refuses two easy readings at once. A community is not finished. And having been forgiven does not settle anything.

crossReferences.why: Describes hearts hardening after signs were shown, in a review of the same history.
Gives the pattern of rejection that this ayah says they assumed would carry no consequence.
Describes those God has made deaf and whose sight He has blinded, after turning away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a change you made after something went wrong, and then let slip back. Not a failure of resolve; almost everyone's list is long. Pick one and restart it today rather than waiting for the next thing to go wrong. This ayah's whole shape is about the stretch that comes after relief arrives.
studies.explainEasier: They thought nothing bad would happen to them, so they stopped seeing and hearing. Then God turned to them in mercy. Then many of them went blind and deaf again. God sees everything they do.

studies.title: Worship God, My Lord And Yours
studies.meaning: A claim is named, and then answered by quoting the one it is made about. The Messiah himself said: children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord. Setting his own words against the claim is the whole argument. The first possessive does the work. My Lord places him among the worshippers. What follows states what comes of giving God a partner. It is given in the Messiah's reported speech, not in the Quran's own voice.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to Christian communities. Such communities were spread across the peninsula, and delegations reached the city. So the passage had real people on the other side of it. The early scholars do not tie it to one meeting. The wording it answers is specific. Through this section the Quran names a statement rather than describing everyone who might hold something like it.

keyTerms.note: The first possessive is what carries the argument. By naming God as his own Lord, the reported speech places the speaker inside the same relation as his listeners rather than anywhere above it.

From the root for sharing or partnership, as in a business venture. The word describes giving something a share in what belongs to God alone. That is why the early scholars treat it as a matter of what is credited to whom.
A place one comes back to for shelter. Using the word for refuge of the fire is deliberate and bleak: what should be a return to safety turns out to be the destination itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reported speech was how authority worked in that world. A claim was strong or weak according to whose words stood behind it. A saying from a respected figure could end an argument outright. Chains of transmission were tracked with care in poetry and family lines long before they were used for anything else. Answering a claim about someone with that person's own words was the strongest move available.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah carries the longest reported exchange between God and Jesus anywhere in the Quran, near its very end. Every quotation of his speech in the chapter places him in one of two roles. He is a servant speaking to God, or a messenger speaking to his own people. He is never quoted here speaking about himself in the third person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works by quotation rather than by assertion. The ayah does not simply deny the claim. It sets the claim beside words reported from the figure it concerns, and lets the two stand together. That method respects the sources of the community being addressed. It also makes the clash plain. The same move runs across this whole section of the surah.

crossReferences.why: Gives Jesus saying he told them only what he was commanded, to worship God his Lord and theirs.
Reports the same statement, that God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.
Reports it once more, within the account of his call to his own people.

studies.applyIt: When you next want to know what someone thinks, go to what they actually said rather than to what is said about them. It takes longer and it is nearly always different. This ayah's whole method is to set a claim beside a quotation, and most disagreements you are in would not survive ten minutes of that.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say that God is the Messiah, the son of Mary. But the Messiah told his own people to worship God, who is his Lord and their Lord. He was asking them to worship the same God he did.

studies.title: Will They Not Turn Back
studies.meaning: A formulation is named and denied, and then something unexpected follows. There is no god but one God; and if they do not stop saying it, a painful punishment will reach those among them who reject. The qualification is careful, those among them, not all of them. And then the very next sentence is not a threat but a question. Will they not turn to God and seek His forgiveness. The passage moves from denial to invitation in a single step.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It addresses a particular statement rather than a community. The early scholars discuss what exactly is being denied, and they state it with care. The setting is the same run of meetings with Christian communities in and around the city. The classical commentaries single out one feature above all. In the second ayah the passage turns suddenly toward invitation.

keyTerms.note: A construction meaning one of a set of three. The early scholars note that the Arabic names a counting rather than a relation. That is why they take such care over what statement is being reported and denied.

From the root for reaching a limit, the same used earlier in the surah for scholars restraining others. Here it is intransitive: reaching one's own limit and stopping, which is a description of turning back.

A question with a particle of gentle reproach rather than accusation. Placing it directly after a warning changes the register entirely, and the sentence that follows names God as forgiving and merciful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Argument about doctrine came into Arabia along the trade roads, and it came unsettled. The churches of Syria, Egypt and Abyssinia disagreed with one another. Traders repeated those disputes without fully following them. Wordings that had taken whole councils to settle were boiled down to a sentence by the time they reached a market in the peninsula. The Quran takes up the wording it names with care.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat is one of the shortest in the surah. It is almost entirely a question. The Quran often follows a severe statement with a short opening of exactly this kind. The shortness is part of the effect. Nothing is added to the invitation, and no condition at all is attached to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies a statement, names what follows from it, and then offers a way out at once. All of that happens in two sentences. The order matters. The invitation comes after the warning rather than instead of it, so neither one cancels the other. And God is named as forgiving and merciful at the exact point where a reader expects the argument to close. This surah ends its hardest passages that way again and again.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same formulation and closes with an instruction to say what is better for you.
Names the related claim and answers it with the Messiah's own reported words.
Tells those who exceeded against themselves not to despair of the mercy of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you end an argument you believe you have won. Most of us stop at the point of being right. This passage does not: it states the disagreement and then leaves a door open in the next breath. In your next disagreement, say the door sentence out loud, whatever yours is, before you walk away.
studies.explainEasier: Some people say God is one of three. The Quran says there is only one God. Then it does something gentle. It invites them to turn back to God and ask Him to forgive them. God forgives.

studies.title: They Both Ate Food
studies.meaning: The argument is made with the plainest possible fact. The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers had passed before him; and his mother was a woman of complete truthfulness. Then the sentence everyone remembers: they both used to eat food. Nothing about doctrine, nothing about miracles. A daily necessity is named, and the necessity is the argument. The ayah closes by pointing at the clarity of the signs and the strangeness of what is done with them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the address to Christian communities in and around the city. No specific occasion is reported for it. Through this section the Quran argues from what both sides already accept. The choice of eating as the meeting point shows that. It is the one thing nobody disputes. It needs no scripture at all to establish.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for truth, used in the Quran of a small number of figures. It names someone whose truthfulness is constitutional rather than occasional, and it is the highest description the text gives her.
The verb for a place becoming empty or a stretch of time going by. Applied to the messengers before him, it says only that they came and were gone, which is exactly the point being made.
A dual verb in a continuous form, so habitually and both of them. The grammar insists on the ordinariness: not that they once ate, but that eating was a regular feature of their lives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food was the mark of a creature in that world's thinking. The Quran mocks idols for not eating. Stories of extraordinary beings usually had them needing nothing at all. Everyone knew what depending on a meal meant. A body weakens. A household has to provide. A season can fail. Naming eating was the shortest way to place someone inside the created order.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran. The description given her here, a woman of complete truthfulness, is used elsewhere in the text of a prophet. It ranks her by a quality of character rather than by a role. That is the pattern the Quran keeps to when it describes her.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues from the body. Whatever is claimed about a person, a person who needs food depends on something outside himself. The ayah lets that do all the work. It also honours Mary in the same breath. That is typical here. Correcting a claim about her son is not allowed to make her smaller. Both moves happen inside one sentence.

crossReferences.why: Says the messengers sent before all ate food and walked about in the markets.
States that they were not bodies which did not eat, nor were they immortal.
Describes Mary as chosen and purified above the women of all the worlds.

studies.applyIt: Eat one meal this week slowly, with your attention on the fact of needing it. Not gratitude exactly; just the plain observation that you stop working without this, several times a day, for your whole life. This ayah builds an argument out of that fact, and the fact is available to you three times daily.
studies.explainEasier: The Messiah was a messenger, like the messengers who came before him. His mother Mary was a truthful woman. They both ate food, the way everyone does. That is the whole point the verse makes.

studies.title: Neither Harm Nor Benefit
studies.meaning: Two questions, and then an instruction. The first asks whether people worship, beside God, what has no power to harm or help them. The test offered is power rather than doctrine. The second speaks to the people of scripture directly. Do not go to excess in your religion beyond the truth. Do not follow the leanings of a people who went astray earlier and led many others astray. Excess, not shortfall, is named as the danger.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long address to communities of earlier scripture. The early scholars read the warning against excess as aimed at one particular pattern. It is not aimed at devotion in general. The pattern is the raising of a figure beyond what was ever claimed for him. No particular occasion is reported for either ayah. The passage sits at the end of the section as its summary.

keyTerms.note: The standard pair the Quran uses to test a claim to power. Naming harm first is deliberate: something that cannot even hurt you has no leverage at all, which is a lower bar than being unable to help.
From a verb meaning to boil over, also used of prices rising past what a thing is worth. The image is of something exceeding its measure, so what is warned against is inflation rather than intensity.

The same word used earlier in this surah for what a judge is warned against following. Its return here puts excess in doctrine and pressure on a judge under one description. Both are things wanted rather than things concluded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia was full of powers that could not act. People asked stones at shrines about journeys and marriages. They left offerings at them. The standing of those stones rose and fell with events nobody could trace back to them. So the question about harm and benefit was not a puzzle for thinkers. It named the plain uselessness of things their own families had relied on.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning against excess in religion appears twice in the Quran. It comes in this surah and in the surah before it. Both times it is addressed to the people of scripture, in almost the same words. It is one of very few instructions in the text that guard against going too far rather than against not going far enough.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a failure that devotion produces on its own. Nothing here is about neglect. The danger named is warmth running past what is true. The Quran treats that as a way of losing a religion, not of deepening it. Pairing it with the question about harm and benefit is pointed. Excess and idol worship stand in one passage as two ways of putting power in the wrong place.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same warning against excess in religion, in almost exactly identical words.
Describes worshipping besides God what neither harms nor benefits, using the same test.
Makes a parallel argument about the Messiah from an entirely ordinary human need.

studies.applyIt: Look at a practice you are proud of, and ask whether any part of it has grown past what it was for: a rule you added, a strictness nobody asked for, a hill you now defend. Trim one inch off it this week. Excess is the harder failure to see, because it looks exactly like commitment.
studies.explainEasier: God asks why people pray to things that cannot hurt them or help them. He also tells those with earlier books not to go too far in their religion. They should not follow people who went wrong before.

studies.title: They Did Not Restrain One Another
studies.meaning: A curse is reported as having come through the tongues of two prophets, and then the reason is given in the next sentence, which is the passage's whole point. They did not restrain one another from the wrongdoing they were committing. Not that they did wrong, which is stated separately, but that they let it stand among them. The closing formula repeats the one used earlier in this surah for scholars who kept silent.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a review of an earlier community's history. The Quran names David and Jesus as the tongues through which the curse came. It does not describe the episodes at all. The early scholars supply accounts from the older tradition. This sits right after a long section on conduct inside the community being addressed. The classical commentaries note the placing. The warning was not meant to stay in the past.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for something spoken through someone rather than by them. It keeps the words as God's while identifying the human voice that carried them, which is how the Quran often describes prophetic speech.

A reciprocal form, so the restraining runs in every direction rather than downward from an authority. What is described as missing is mutual correction among equals, not the enforcement of a rule from above.
From the verb to not recognise. A wrong is named as something a healthy community fails to recognise as its own, so the word already contains the reaction the passage says was missing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe policed itself through speech. There were no officers, so a man was restrained by knowing that an uncle or a neighbour would say something at the next gathering and that the remark would be remembered. When that stopped happening, nothing else took its place. Everyone in the audience had watched a family let something go and had seen how quickly the next thing followed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for restraining one another is reciprocal in form. That is unusual for this root in the Quran. Elsewhere the forbidding of wrong is described as something a person or a community does to others. The reciprocal form makes it something a group owes to itself, in every direction at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage spreads the guilt rather than gathering it in one place. The wrongdoing is named once. The silence around it is named separately and given a whole ayah. That puts the two on much the same footing. It is a claim about how a community is judged. Not by its worst members, but by what the rest of it put up with. The surah has already used the same measure on scholars.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same measure to scholars who did not restrain those around them.
Describes a community defined by enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.
Warns of a trial that will not strike only those among you who did the wrong.
