studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to that has one thing everyone privately dislikes and nobody names. You are probably waiting for someone better placed to say it. So is everyone else. Say the mildest possible version at the next opportunity, and notice how many people agree with you afterwards in private.
studies.explainEasier: Some people in an earlier community were cursed by God through the words of David and Jesus. They broke the rules. Worse, they watched each other do wrong and said nothing to stop it.

studies.title: What Their Souls Sent Ahead
studies.meaning: One sentence of observation and one of consequence. You see many of them turning for support to those who reject faith. Then a formula of dismay: how wretched is what their own souls have sent on ahead of them. The verb is the striking part, because it makes the alliance a shipment rather than a decision, something despatched forward to a destination. The closing clauses name what arrived there: God's displeasure, and a punishment they remain in.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the stretch describing conduct during a time of unsettled alliances. The early scholars tie the description to particular people. They are careful about the wording, which says many of them rather than all. The passage belongs to the same discussion as the earlier ayat on protection pacts. The classical commentaries read the whole run together as one argument about allegiance.

keyTerms.note: The verb of sending something on ahead of you, as goods were despatched before a traveller set out. Deeds are pictured as freight already in transit, which makes the outcome an arrival rather than a sentence.
A word for displeasure stronger than the ordinary term, and the direct opposite of the word for good pleasure used earlier in this surah. The two frame the same relation from either end of it.

The self named as the agent, exactly as in the account of the first murder earlier in this surah. Both passages make the interior the actor, which keeps responsibility from being displaced outward onto anything else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Merchants sent goods ahead of themselves. A caravan carried a man's consignment to a market he would reach weeks later, and by the time he arrived the goods were already there, already sold or already spoiled. Nothing could be recalled once it had left. The image behind this ayah's verb was a commercial routine every trading family understood in their bones.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the language of sending something on ahead for deeds in a number of places. It is one of the text's most persistent images. The present is a place from which things are sent out. The hereafter is the place where they are collected. The words are drawn entirely from trade.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence is described as an arrival rather than a verdict. Nothing in the sentence has God reacting to the alliance. What is named is displeasure and a state of remaining. The cause runs from what was sent ahead. That framing comes up across the Quran and changes the register of judgement. It is less a courtroom than a delivery. And the person receiving it made the shipment.

crossReferences.why: Says every soul will know what it sent on ahead and what it held back.
Instructs a soul to look carefully at what it has sent forward for tomorrow.
Sets out the instruction about allegiance that this ayah describes being disregarded.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you sent ahead this week. Not what you meant, what actually left: the message you sent, the money you moved, the hour you gave someone. Make a short list on Friday. It is a strange and clarifying exercise, and it takes the question of character out of the realm of intention.
studies.explainEasier: You will see many of them siding with people who reject God. What they have sent ahead of themselves is terrible. God is angry with them, and they will stay in punishment.

studies.title: Belief That Changes Nothing
studies.meaning: A test is proposed, and it is a test of behaviour. Had they believed in God, and the Prophet, and what was sent down to him, they would not have taken those others as protectors. The reasoning runs backward from conduct to conviction. That is the reverse of how belief is usually weighed. The closing clause states the conclusion in the surah's usual register. Not all of them, but many, have stepped outside the boundary.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about alliances formed during a time of conflict. The early scholars read this ayah as the summary of an argument begun several ayat earlier. They note that it supplies reasoning the earlier ayat had only hinted at. The setting throughout is a city where everyone knew whom a person stood with. That could not be separated from what they claimed to hold.

keyTerms.note: A verb of adopting or acquiring, used across the Quran for taking something as a protector, a god or a friend. It describes a deliberate acquisition rather than a relationship a person drifted into over time.
The term used here rather than the word for messenger. The early scholars note that the surah moves between the two. This one stresses the office itself rather than the act of carrying a message.
From a root describing a date leaving its skin. Its repeated use across this section keeps naming one failure: not denial of a boundary but movement past one that is still acknowledged as real.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in that society was private. A visit, a gift, a marriage talk, a shared meal with a rival house: all of it was watched and discussed. A man's side could be read from a season's ordinary movements. So reading belief from conduct was not a fine claim about doctrine to that audience. It was simply how everyone sized up everyone else.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names God, the Prophet, and what was sent down as three objects of one verb for believing. That triple construction turns up in a handful of places in the Quran. It always joins the source, the carrier and the content together. So no one of the three can be held on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reasons from action back to belief, and treats that step as sound. It is a demanding standard. A stated conviction can be checked against a record. It is not checked only against a person's own sense of themselves. The surah applies the test to the community it is addressing. The commentaries read it as open to anyone looking honestly at their own alignments.

crossReferences.why: Describes the conduct that this ayah then reasons backward from to its cause.
Sets a person's attachments against God and His Messenger and asks which is more beloved.
Says you will not find people who believe in God taking as friends those who oppose Him.

studies.applyIt: Take one belief you would say you hold firmly, and find the calendar entry from last month that reflects it. If there is not one, that is information rather than a verdict. Put one in this month. The ayah's method is to read conviction from conduct, and it works just as well turned inward.
studies.explainEasier: If they really believed in God and His messenger, they would not have taken those people as friends. But many of them did. What people do shows what they truly believe.

studies.title: Because They Are Not Arrogant
studies.meaning: An observation is made about who stands closest and who stands furthest. Then the ayah does something unusual. It gives its reason. Those nearest in affection are described as saying we are Christians. The reason offered is that among them are priests and monks, and that they are not arrogant. What is named is a way of being rather than a label. The ayat that follow describe one encounter instead of a general rule.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars connect this passage to particular Christian communities in the Prophet's lifetime. Those include the people who received emigrants from Mecca, and delegations that reached the city. They read the ayat that follow as describing one such meeting. The reports differ in detail. The surah has kept qualifying its descriptions of every community. It does so again here by giving a reason.

keyTerms.note: A word for love carrying closeness and goodwill rather than passion. It is from the same root used for what God places between spouses, so what is described is a settled warmth rather than a political alliance.
From a root meaning to fear or to hold in awe. The word names people defined by a posture toward God rather than by an office, which is why it sits so naturally beside the clause about arrogance.
A form meaning to make oneself great, so what is denied is self-inflation rather than pride felt. The Quran uses this exact verb for refusing to accept truth from someone regarded as beneath one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Monks' cells dotted the trade roads through Syria and northern Arabia. Travellers relied on them. A monk gave water and shelter to a caravan and asked for nothing. In that economy such a thing was remarkable enough to be remembered and retold. Traders coming back to Mecca described these men. So the audience had heard about this picture from people they knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The reason in this ayah is stated in the grammar of the sentence as a cause. That is uncommon. The Quran usually describes conduct without saying what produces it. Here the reason is spelled out, and it comes in two parts. Among them are people given over to worship. And they do not make themselves great.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage roots a difference in how open people are, not in who they are. It names the obstacle exactly: making oneself great. That is what closes a person to what they hear. It matches the Quran's wider account of why arguments fail to land. The reason is given openly, so the description travels. Any community can be measured by the same two markers.

crossReferences.why: Describes the encounter this ayah introduces, with eyes overflowing at what they heard.
Describes monasticism among the followers of Jesus and how it came about among them.
Describes those who make themselves great being turned away from the signs.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you can accept a correction from someone you consider less qualified than you. That is the exact test this ayah names, and it is easier to fail than to detect. The next time it happens, take the correction on its merits and say thank you before you have finished deciding whether they were right.
studies.explainEasier: God says the people hardest on the believers are some who reject Him. The closest in warmth are those who call themselves Christians. That is because they have priests and monks, and they are not proud.

studies.title: Eyes Overflowing With Tears
studies.meaning: A physical response is described before any decision is reported. When they hear what was sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears. The cause is what they have recognised of the truth. Recognition is the word used, not discovery. They are seeing again something they already held. Only then do they speak. Their request is not for entry or for reward. They ask to be written down among those who bear witness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars connect this passage to a delegation that came to the city and heard the Quran recited. Reports name more than one such occasion and do not agree on which is meant. The surah has just explained why some listeners are open. This ayah supplies the instance. Recitation was the ordinary way anyone met the text, so this scene shows the standard first contact.

keyTerms.note: The verb of a vessel filling past its edge, used of a river in flood. It describes the tears as a consequence of something else being full, which locates the cause inside the person rather than in the eyes.

To know something again, distinct from the verb for coming to know a thing for the first time. The word implies earlier acquaintance. That is why the early scholars read the scene as recognition rather than discovery.
People who testify to what they have seen. The request is to be entered on a list of witnesses rather than of believers, which is a specific and notably modest thing to be asking for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was recited aloud at fairs and gatherings. Audiences wept at it openly and without embarrassment. Arabia had a highly trained ear. People could tell within a few lines whether something was ordinary or extraordinary. A strong recitation could silence a market. The reaction this ayah describes was one everyone could read. That is part of why it is offered as evidence.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes weeping at hearing revelation in more than one place. Each time the physical response comes before any statement of belief is quoted. The order is steady enough that the classical scholars remark on it. They treat the tears as evidence rather than as decoration in the scene.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats recognition as evidence and puts it in the body. Nothing is argued and nothing is given up. Something is heard, and the eyes fill. That says something about how the Quran understands its own effect. It also sets a standard the argument around it cannot reach. A case can be resisted. A recognition is hard to talk yourself out of once it has happened.

crossReferences.why: Gives the words they say next, arguing with themselves about why they should not believe.
Describes those given knowledge falling on their faces in tears at the recitation.
Describes those who fell down weeping when the signs of the Merciful were recited to them.

studies.applyIt: Listen to a recitation once this week without following a translation and without treating it as background. Five minutes is enough. You are not trying to feel anything in particular. This ayah describes a response that arrives before understanding, and most of us have arranged our listening so it never gets the chance.
studies.explainEasier: When they hear what was sent down to the Messenger, their eyes fill with tears. They know it is true. They say: our Lord, we believe, so write us down with those who tell what they saw.

studies.title: Why Should We Not Believe
studies.meaning: The speech continues, and it is framed as a question they put to themselves. What is it with us that we should not believe in God and in the truth that has come to us? The second half names what they want, and the verb is not certainty but longing: we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous. Nothing is claimed. A reason to believe is stated as the absence of a reason not to, and the outcome is left as a hope.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of a delegation's response. The early scholars read this ayah as the reasoning behind the tears in the ayah before it. They note that the Quran quotes the speakers at length rather than summarising them. The surah does this again and again, with refusal and with acceptance. It gives each its own words and lets the two stand against one another.

keyTerms.note: An idiom asking what could possibly be the matter, used when a course of action needs no defence at all. The phrasing puts the burden of explanation on refusal rather than on assent.

A verb of eager desire that can also carry the sense of coveting. Used of God's mercy it names hope that reaches without presuming, which is why the classical commentaries treat it as the fitting posture.

keyTerms.gloss: the righteous, those who are sound
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be in good repair, the opposite of the word used elsewhere for corruption. The request is to be included among people who are whole rather than among those who are rewarded.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Joining a group was a formal matter. A person entered a tribe by an act of alliance. He was named in front of witnesses. After that he carried its protection and its duties. So asking to be counted among a body of people was the natural way to phrase a request. It was more natural than asking for a benefit. This speech uses that form twice over.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for hoping runs across the Quran for a longing that reaches upward with no assurance attached. It is used of prophets and of ordinary people alike. It is one of the few words in the text that expresses desire toward God while not claiming a right to what is desired.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech models a posture the surah has been circling for many ayat. There is confidence about the truth and no confidence at all about one's own standing. Belief is stated as obvious. The outcome is stated as hoped for. The two sit in one sentence without strain. That combination is hard to hold, and the passage presents it without comment.

crossReferences.why: Records Abraham hoping his faults will be forgiven on the day of judgement.
Gives the tears and the first request that this speech continues on from.
Records Joseph asking to be joined with the righteous, using the same phrase.

studies.applyIt: Try asking for something this week the way this speech does: state plainly what you believe, then name what you want as a hope rather than as an expectation. Most of our requests are either demands or apologies. This one is neither, and the difference is audible when you say it out loud.
studies.explainEasier: They ask what could stop them from believing in God and in the truth that has reached them. They hope their Lord will count them among the good people. They do not claim it. They hope for it.

studies.title: Rewarded For What They Said
studies.meaning: The response to the speech is a reward, and the ayah is precise about what is being rewarded: what they said. Not what they did, and not what they believed in the abstract, but the words just quoted. Gardens with rivers running beneath, and they remain there. Then the contrasting sentence arrives with no transition at all, naming those who rejected and denied. The two are set side by side and left without any comment joining them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the account of the delegation. The early scholars note that the reward follows straight on from the quoted speech. That is unusual. Elsewhere the Quran ties outcomes to belief and to action. Here it ties one directly to something said. The classical commentaries read the speech as evidence of what lay behind it, not as enough on its own.

keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to return, so a reward is something coming back to its origin. The same root gives the word for a garment, which is put on and returns to its wearer. The early Arabic dictionary writers note the link.
The preposition marks cause. Attaching a reward to speech rather than to deeds is rare in the Quran. The early scholars are careful to read the words as evidence of a state rather than as a trade.
From a root meaning good and beautiful at once. It names doing something well rather than merely correctly, which is a higher standard than the word usually rendered as righteous.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A spoken declaration carried legal weight in Arabia. A man became a member of a tribe, freed a slave, divorced a wife or accepted a debt by saying so before witnesses. There was no document behind any of it. Words were the instrument, not the record of one. A reward attached to what someone said would have read as natural rather than as unusually generous.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat is word for word the same as an ayah much earlier in this surah. There it closes an entirely different passage. The Quran repeats fixed formulas this way at the ends of sections. The classical scholars treat such repetition as a marker of structure rather than as emphasis.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a reward on speech says something about how the Quran understands a sincere utterance. It is not treated as separable from the person who produced it. The abruptness of the contrasting sentence matters too. Nothing softens the turn. The effect is to keep the generous half from being read as a general pardon. The specific promise is left entirely intact.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same closing sentence word for word, ending a different passage in this surah.
Contains the speech that this reward is attached to as its stated cause.
Describes people of earlier scripture who believe, and names their reward with their Lord.

studies.applyIt: Say the thing you actually believe out loud to one person this week, in your own words rather than in borrowed ones. Not an argument, a statement. This passage attaches a great deal to an utterance, and most of us have never once put ours into a sentence we composed ourselves.
studies.explainEasier: God rewards them for what they said. They will have gardens with rivers running under them, and they will stay there. Those who refuse to believe and call the signs false will end in the Fire.

studies.title: Do Not Forbid The Good Things
studies.meaning: An instruction to believers about their own strictness. Do not declare off limits the good things God has made lawful for you. Do not overstep. The early scholars report that some in the community had begun giving up food, rest and marriage as a form of devotion. The passage stops it. What follows is positive. Eat of what God has provided, lawful and wholesome, and be conscious of Him. Being conscious sits beside eating rather than against it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars report that a group had agreed among themselves to give up meat, marriage and ordinary comfort in the name of devotion. These ayat came in answer. The reports vary in their details and in who was involved. The wider setting is a community full of eagerness, still working out what shape that eagerness should take.

keyTerms.note: The verb of making something inviolable, in a form meaning to treat it as such. The instruction concerns the act of declaring rather than the act of holding back. That is the distinction the early scholars build on.

The verb of crossing a limit, used earlier in this surah of hostility toward others. Using it here for excess devotion places both under one description, as transgressions of a measure that was already set.
The same adjective this surah has used for permitted food and for clean earth. Its return here ties eating, purity and provision together through one word carrying pleasantness and cleanness at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Giving things up was a known path in the region. Monks in the Syrian cells lived on very little. Hermits were spoken of with awe. The idea that closeness to God meant subtraction was in the air along every trade road. A community forming its own practice would naturally reach for the model it could see. This passage answers that reach directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this same verb for declaring something off limits when it criticises an older Arabian practice of setting certain livestock aside. So the instruction here joins two opposite errors under one verb. One is superstitious restriction. The other is pious self-denial. Both take a decision that was never the person's to make.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line around one religious impulse. Eagerness that narrows what is permitted is named as overstepping. The word used is the one this surah applies to aggression. That puts the two in one category. Both take a measure belonging to God and adjust it. The positive instruction that follows keeps the correction from reading as leave to be careless.

crossReferences.why: Asks who has declared off limits the adornment and good provision God brought out for His servants.
Addresses declaring off limits something God had made lawful, in an entirely different setting.
Answers a question about what is permitted with a category rather than with a list.

studies.applyIt: Find one good thing you have quietly cut out of your life for reasons that sounded spiritual at the time: a food, a rest, a pleasure, a friendship. Take it back this week, deliberately and with thanks. This passage treats that reclaiming as obedience, which is not how most of us were taught to think about enjoyment.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers not to make the good things He allowed off limits for themselves. He tells them to eat what He has given them, so long as it is lawful and good. Being careful of God fits alongside enjoying it.

studies.title: The Oaths You Did Not Mean
studies.meaning: A line is drawn between two kinds of oath. The idle ones, sworn without meaning them, carry nothing. The ones deliberately tied do. Then an atonement is set out, and it is given as a set of choices rather than one requirement. Feed ten needy people at the level you feed your own family, or clothe them, or free a person from bondage. Whoever can manage none of these fasts three days. The closing instruction is to guard your oaths.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars connect this passage to the ayat just before it, in which a group had bound themselves by oath to give up ordinary comforts. They read it as providing the way out of an oath that should not be kept. Reports about the specific occasion vary. Oaths in Arabian life were sworn constantly and casually, and the first clause addresses that practice.

keyTerms.note: Words carrying no weight, used elsewhere for chatter in a gathering. Naming a category of speech that does not bind is unusual, and it concedes that people talk without meaning what they say.
From the same root as the word for contracts in this surah's opening ayah. The image is a knot deliberately tied, so what makes an oath binding is an act rather than a particular form of words.

The middle of a range, and by extension the balanced or the best of it. Setting the standard at what you ordinarily feed your own household ties the atonement to the giver's actual life rather than to a fixed amount.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs swore constantly. An oath ran through ordinary speech the way emphasis does in English. Most of it meant nothing beyond insistence. But a formal oath, tied deliberately in front of witnesses, was among the strongest instruments in the society. Telling the two apart was a practical need rather than a fine point. Everyone produced both kinds inside a single conversation.
studies.didYouKnow: The atonement is offered as three choices. There is a fourth for anyone who can manage none of them. The standard for feeding is whatever the person usually feeds their own household. So the amount is tied to the giver's own life, not to a fixed sum. The Quran handles atonement that way again and again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats speech as consequential and then immediately limits the consequence. Words that were not meant do not bind, which is a concession to how people actually talk; words that were tied do bind, and there is a way out of them that costs something. Both halves are needed. Without the first, ordinary conversation becomes a trap; without the second, a bad oath would have to be kept.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same distinction between idle oaths and what the hearts have deliberately earned.
Warns against making God a pretext in oaths against doing good and reconciling people.
Opens this surah with the instruction to fulfil what is tied, using the very same root.

studies.applyIt: Count how many times you say I swear or I promise in a day when you mean only that you are serious. Then, once this week, replace it with the plain sentence underneath. The passage takes both kinds of speech seriously enough to separate them, and separating them yourself takes about a day of noticing.
studies.explainEasier: God does not hold you to oaths you did not mean. He does hold you to the ones you meant. If you break one of those, there is a way to make up for it. Feed ten people in need, clothe them, free a slave, or fast three days.

studies.title: Set It To One Side
studies.meaning: Four things are named together in one sentence. Intoxicants, games of chance, the altars, and the divining arrows. All four are described as defilement belonging to the adversary's work. The instruction given is to keep clear of them. Then the next ayah supplies the reasons, and they are social rather than abstract. One is the sowing of enmity and hatred among you. The other is being turned away from remembrance of God and from prayer. The passage closes as a question rather than as a command.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical scholars describe a series of passages on this subject sent down at intervals, of which this is the last. They note that the community's practice changed in stages. Reports about the immediate occasion vary. Wine and games of chance were woven into Arabian social life and into its poetry. That is why the passage argues from consequences rather than simply naming the thing.

keyTerms.note: A word for filth, used of what is physically and morally repellent at once. Applying it to all four items in the list places a drink, a game and a shrine practice under one single description.

From the word for a side, so literally to put something to one side of yourself. The verb asks for distance rather than for struggle, which is a different instruction from resisting something at close range.

A participle inside a question rather than an order, placed at the very end of the passage. The early scholars note that the community treated the question itself as decisive. The form leaves the answer to the hearer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wine and the arrow game were social institutions. The game shared out a slaughtered camel by lot. It was thought generous, since winners fed the poor from their portions, and poets praised men for playing it. Drinking gatherings were where alliances were made and verse recited. Withdrawing from both meant withdrawing from the ordinary machinery of Arabian social life.
studies.didYouKnow: The reason given in the second ayah is entirely social and devotional. It names enmity between people, and distraction from remembrance and from prayer. No physical harm is mentioned anywhere in it. The passage argues from what these practices do to a community and to attention. That is an unusual line of reasoning for its subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the harm rather than only the thing, and both harms it names are about relationships. Something that sets people against one another and something that pulls attention away from God are treated as two sides of one damage. Ending on a question rather than an order is also striking. The case is set out in full. Then the decision is handed back to the listener.

crossReferences.why: Says there is benefit in them and greater harm, weighing the two against each other openly.
Addresses approaching prayer while not knowing what it is you are saying.
Names the divining arrows earlier in this surah, inside a quite different list.

studies.applyIt: Identify the thing that most reliably takes an evening from you and gives nothing back. You know which one. Put it physically to one side for a week, out of reach rather than resisted, and notice what fills the hours. This passage asks for distance rather than willpower, and distance is much easier to arrange.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers to stay away from drink, gambling, idol altars and arrows used to tell fortunes. These things come from Satan. They stir up hate between people and pull you away from God and from prayer.

studies.title: Only Clear Delivery
studies.meaning: A short instruction closes the passage. Obey God, obey the Messenger, and be on your guard. Then a conditional that lifts weight rather than adding it: if you turn away, know that all that rests on Our Messenger is clear delivery. The sentence is addressed to the community, and its effect is to separate two responsibilities. What is conveyed is one person's charge; what is done with it afterwards belongs to everybody else.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on intoxicants and games of chance. The early scholars read the placing as deliberate. A hard instruction is followed by a reminder that the Messenger's part ends at delivery. The community was being asked to change a deeply rooted social practice. The ayah addresses the pressure that puts on the one doing the asking as much as on those being asked.

keyTerms.note: The verb of wariness before a known danger, with no object supplied. Leaving it unstated makes the warning general. The early scholars read it as caution about one's own slipping rather than about anything outside.
The noun from the verb used earlier in this surah for conveying the message. It names arrival rather than speech, and pairing it with the word for clarity sets the whole standard for the office.
An active participle, so not merely clear but clarifying. Attaching it to delivery means the message must be made plain rather than simply issued, which places a real demand on the one carrying it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The difference between carrying a message and enforcing it was familiar. A herald sent between tribes announced terms and withdrew. Whether the terms were accepted was not his affair. Holding him answerable for the reply would have seemed absurd. That custom protected messengers. The ayah calls on it at a moment when a very unwelcome message had just been delivered.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about clear delivery being all that rests on the Messenger appears in several places across the Quran. It comes back at the end of passages where a demand has just been made. Its work is always the same. It closes a section by saying what the one delivering the message is and is not answerable for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah lifts weight from the messenger without lifting it from the audience. Nothing is taken back from the instruction before it. What is removed is any idea that compliance was the messenger's to secure. That protects the office from being judged by results. It also closes off a way of dodging the instruction, since nobody else is going to carry it for you.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle a few ayat later in almost identical terms.
Says that if they turn away, only clear delivery rests upon you.
Divides the charge in two: his part is to deliver, and yours is to respond.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have said clearly to someone once and are still repeating. Say it a final time, plainly, and then stop. The repetition is usually about your discomfort rather than their understanding. This ayah draws exactly that line. Delivery is your part. The rest was never yours.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to obey Him and obey His messenger, and to stay careful. If they turn away, they should know one thing. The messenger's only job was to pass the message on clearly.

studies.title: No Blame For What They Ate
studies.meaning: A question the last passage left open is answered here. Those who believed and did good are not blamed for what they had already eaten before the instruction came. Then the condition is stated three times, each time a step higher. Conscious and believing and doing good, then conscious and believing, then conscious and doing beautifully. The repetition is the ayah's structure. The early scholars read the stages as one ongoing state seen from three angles rather than as three separate demands.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, right after the passage about intoxicants and games of chance. The early scholars report that a question came up in the community about people who had died before the final instruction was given. This ayah answers it. Reports about the particular occasion vary. The general point is one any community faces when a practice changes. What becomes of what was done beforehand.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to lean or tilt to one side. Blame is pictured as a departure from upright, which is why the Quran uses this particular word for what is not held against a person.

The verb of eating and drinking together, wider than either alone. Its generality keeps the answer from being tied to one substance. The early scholars note that the ayah answers a category rather than an instance.
From the root for good and beautiful at once. It arrives at the end of the ascending sequence, so the passage closes on doing well rather than on merely believing or merely avoiding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Practice changed in stages in that community, and people died in between. A man who had fallen at one of the early battles had lived under different guidance from someone alive ten years later. Families asked what that meant for their dead. The question was not academic. It was asked by people naming a brother or a father. That is why the answer is so direct.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah states its condition three times in a rising sequence. The classical scholars counted the elements with care and disagreed about how the three stages map onto one another. What they generally agreed on is that the repetition is deliberate. They also agreed that the last term, doing beautifully, stands highest among them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage settles the past without loosening the present. Nothing done before the instruction is charged. The condition attached is stated three times, to make clear that this is no general exemption. It also says something about how change works. What matters is the direction a person is facing when an instruction reaches them. The record from before it arrived is not the measure.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction that this ayah answers a lingering question about.
Answers a similar question about prayer performed before a change of direction.
States that what has already passed is excepted from a newly given instruction.

studies.applyIt: There is a standard you hold now that you did not hold five years ago, and someone in your life is still being judged by you against it retroactively. Stop, once, deliberately. This ayah is careful to separate what was done before an instruction arrived from what is done after it, and most of us are not.
studies.explainEasier: People who believe and do good are not blamed for what they ate before the rule came. What counts is what they do now. They keep believing. They stay careful. They keep doing good.

studies.title: Game Within Reach
studies.meaning: A test is announced in advance, which is unusual. God will test you with something of the game your hands and your spears can reach. The specification matters: not distant game but game close enough to take easily. The stated purpose is that God may know who fears Him unseen, and that phrase means fear when nobody is watching. Announcing a test does not weaken it. It moves the whole difficulty inside the person being tested.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to a community travelling toward the sanctuary. The early scholars describe conditions in which game came unusually close to the camps. The pilgrims were in a state where hunting was set aside. So the temptation was continuous and physical, not an imagined case. Reports about the particular journey differ. The setting is a company on the road with limited food and animals within arm's reach.

keyTerms.note: The verb of testing by trial, from a root meaning to wear something out through use. A test in this sense reveals what is already there rather than adding anything, which is why announcing it changes nothing.
The clause specifies proximity. Something within arm's length is a different test from something requiring effort, and the ayah is precise about which of the two kinds is meant here.

A phrase covering both what is hidden from a person and what a person is hidden from. Here it means fearing God where nobody is looking, which is the only condition under which such fear can be measured.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan lived close to hunger. Provisions were counted for a fixed number of days, and a gazelle standing within a spear's throw was several days of food for a family. Passing it up was not a matter of principle held at a distance; it was a decision made with an empty pot and children watching. The passage names a temptation that had a taste and a weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about fearing God in the unseen appears in a dozen places across the Quran. It is always attached to what a person does when nothing outside is holding them back. It is one of the text's standard formulas for sincerity. It works by naming the absence of witnesses rather than the presence of good intention.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Announcing a test is the passage's most striking move. Once a person knows they are being tested, external motives become useless: nothing is proved by passing a test you know you are taking, unless you would have passed it anyway. That is exactly what the clause about the unseen measures. The test is designed to be transparent, and the transparency is part of its mechanism.

crossReferences.why: Continues with what follows if the boundary named here is crossed deliberately.
Announces testing with fear, hunger and loss, also stated openly in advance.
Names those who fear their Lord in the unseen as having forgiveness and a great reward.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing this week that would be easy to take and that nobody would ever count: an extra minute, a small overclaim, a corner cut. Leave it, deliberately, once, and do not tell anyone that you did. The whole subject of this ayah is what a person does in the absence of an audience.
studies.explainEasier: God says He will test the believers. Game will come close, within easy reach, while they are on pilgrimage. He wants to see who fears Him when nobody is looking. Anyone who goes too far will be punished.

studies.title: Its Equal In Livestock
studies.meaning: The boundary announced in the last ayah is stated. Then the passage sets out what follows a deliberate crossing. A matching animal from the herds, valued by two people of integrity from among you, brought as an offering to the sanctuary. Or feeding those in need. Or a matching amount of fasting. Three routes, and the stated purpose is that the person taste what their act brought. Then a clause changes the register entirely. God has pardoned what is past.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed to a community in the state of pilgrimage. The early scholars discuss how the matching animal was valued and record differing views. The setting is a sanctuary system much older than the mission. Certain months and a certain territory were held inviolable. Hunting inside them was set aside by custom as well as by instruction.

keyTerms.note: Literally two possessors of justice. The assessment is handed to people rather than to a table of values, so equivalence becomes a judgement made by named individuals who can be held responsible for it.
From a root meaning heavy or indigestible, used of food that sits badly. The word describes an outcome that has to be carried and digested rather than a penalty imposed from outside the person.
The verb of effacing a trace, as wind erases footprints in sand. Its placement here is deliberate: the past is described as wiped away rather than as counted up and then forgiven.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary was the one place in Arabia where a man could stand beside someone whose brother he had killed and not be attacked. That truce was the basis of the pilgrimage economy and of the great fairs. Extending the peace to animals was not sentiment. It was the logic of the sanctuary carried to its edge. Everyone who traded at those fairs knew what that peace was worth.
studies.didYouKnow: The valuing is given to two people rather than to a fixed table. The classical commentaries record long discussion of what counts as a match between a wild animal and a farmed one. It is one of the places where the Quran leaves a judgement to human beings. It also names the quality those people must have.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The stated purpose is that the person taste what their act brought. That is a specific claim about what such a response is for. It is not the restoring of a balance, and not the protecting of a population. It is an experience the person actually has. The pardon clause that follows keeps the whole thing looking forward. The surah's usual movement appears again, from severity to an opening in one breath.

crossReferences.why: Announces the test whose failure this ayah then sets out the consequence of.
Names the same boundary in the surah's opening ayah, within a single clause.
Describes the sanctity of the sacred month and equivalence in any response to a breach.

studies.applyIt: Think about how you make amends when you have broken something small. Most of us apologise and move on. This passage builds in something that costs a little and is felt. Next time, add one concrete thing to the apology, chosen so that you notice it. Not as punishment, but so the repair is something you have actually done.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers not to hunt while on pilgrimage. If someone does it on purpose, he makes up for it. He gives an animal of equal worth, or feeds people in need, or fasts. God has forgiven what happened before.

studies.title: The Catch Of The Sea
studies.meaning: A permission and a restriction are set side by side in one sentence. What the sea yields is open, described as provision for you and for travellers; what the land yields by hunting is set aside while a person is in the state of pilgrimage. The distinction is not about the animals but about the setting: the sanctuary's peace covers ground and not water. The ayah closes by naming God as the one you will be gathered to.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the passage on the state of pilgrimage. The early scholars discuss at length what counts as the catch of the sea and record differing views. The mention of travellers reflects a practical fact: preserved fish was among the few foods that survived a long journey, and pilgrims crossing to the sanctuary from coastal regions carried it. The permission had a specific practical use.

keyTerms.note: The same noun is used for hunting on land two clauses later, so the sentence turns on one word with two different fields. The early scholars build their whole discussion on that deliberate symmetry.
A word for goods and for temporary benefit at once. It names something to be used up on a journey rather than possessed, which suits a permission framed around people on the move.

A caravan or a group on the move, from the verb to travel. Naming them separately from you indicates that the provision was understood to serve people passing through as well as those already settled.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fish reached inland Arabia dried and salted. It was carried from the Red Sea coast and from the Gulf. It kept for months and weighed little. That made it caravan food in a way fresh meat never could be. A pilgrim travelling for weeks with hunting set aside still had to eat. The sea supplied the one protein that could make the journey with him.
studies.didYouKnow: The same Arabic noun serves for the catch of the sea and the game of the land inside this one ayah. Only the following word tells them apart. The Quran often builds a distinction this way. It repeats a word and changes one element beside it, so the difference between two cases becomes audible in the sentence itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a boundary and makes it precise rather than wide. Something is set aside, and something next to it is opened on purpose. That stops the restriction from spreading into everything nearby. The precision is itself a mercy. This surah has already warned against the opposite instinct, the one that declares more off limits than was ever asked.

crossReferences.why: Warns against declaring off limits what God has made lawful, earlier in this same surah.
Opens the surah with the same restriction stated inside a single short clause.
Describes the sea as subjected so that fresh flesh may be eaten from it.

studies.applyIt: Find a rule you follow that you have quietly widened past what it says. Most of us have one, applied to a whole category when it was written for a case. Read the actual wording once this week. This ayah takes the trouble to open the thing next door, which suggests the widening is not a safe error.
studies.explainEasier: God allows people on pilgrimage to eat what the sea gives. Travellers may eat it too. Hunting on land is set aside for that time. The verse ends by asking people to be careful of God.

studies.title: A Standing For The People
studies.meaning: Four things are named as appointed: the Sacred House, the sacred month, the offerings, and the garlanded animals. The word used for what they were appointed as means an upright support, something that holds a structure standing. Then the purpose given is not about worship but about knowledge. It is that you may know God knows what is in the heavens and the earth. The connection is left for the reader to draw. The early scholars offer more than one way of drawing it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the close of the surah's material on the sanctuary. The four items named were already settled in Arabian practice long before the mission. That is part of the point. The passage describes them as appointed by God rather than as new. The early scholars note that the surah's opening named the same elements. So the chapter returns at the end to where it began.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to stand, so what is named is a prop that keeps something else upright. The early scholars read it as covering both the economy the sanctuary supported and the wider order it made possible.
The adjective means forbidden in the sense of protected, from the same root as the state of pilgrimage. What is described is not a prohibition but a sphere within which certain things are suspended.

Beasts marked with a collar to show they were destined for offering. The garland made an animal untouchable on the road, so a mark of cloth functioned as protection across otherwise hostile territory.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary made the Arabian economy possible. During the sacred months weapons were laid aside. The great fairs opened, poetry was judged, debts were settled and marriages arranged. Tribes that would fight in any other season traded side by side. Remove that arrangement and the peninsula loses its markets, its news network and its only reliable place for peace.
studies.didYouKnow: The sacred month, the offerings and the garlanded animals are named together here. They are named again near the opening of this surah, in the same order both times. The chapter closes its material on the sanctuary by returning to a list it started from. The classical scholars note that as deliberate framing rather than repetition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purpose clause is the ayah's difficulty. It is not obvious why a sanctuary should teach that God knows everything. The early scholars read it in more than one way. An arrangement of this precision implies a knowledge behind it. Or a place where nothing may be taken teaches that everything is already seen. The ayah does not choose, and the commentaries keep the range.

crossReferences.why: Names the same elements near the opening of this surah, framing the section that ends here.
Describes the House as a place of return and of security for the people.
Names the first house appointed for people, and describes the guidance in it.

studies.applyIt: Think of an arrangement in your life that holds everything else up and that you never notice: a standing agreement with a relative, a fixed evening, a rota someone maintains. Name it this week and thank whoever keeps it running. This ayah's word for the sanctuary is simply the thing that keeps the rest standing.
studies.explainEasier: God set up the Sacred House, the sacred month and the animals brought as offerings. They hold things up for people. He did this so people would know that He knows everything in the sky and on the earth.

studies.title: Severe, And Also Forgiving
studies.meaning: Two statements about God are put in one sentence with nothing between them but a conjunction. Know that God is severe in consequence, and that God is forgiving and merciful. Neither qualifies the other and neither is given precedence; the grammar holds them level. Then the next ayah turns to the Messenger and says his charge is delivery alone, adding that God knows what you show and what you keep back.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's long instructional section. The early scholars note that this pairing of two descriptions is a recurring formula in the Quran. It usually appears where a stretch of instruction ends. No occasion is reported for either ayah. Coming after the material on the sanctuary and on keeping oaths, the pair sums up rather than opens a fresh argument.

keyTerms.note: The second word comes from a root meaning to follow behind, so the consequence trails the act. Severity is described as the closeness of that following rather than as the intensity of anything inflicted.
The same noun used a few ayat earlier for what rests on the Messenger. Its repetition within one surah at short distance is among the ways this chapter marks the limits of the office.
A pair of opposites covering the whole of a person's conduct. The construction leaves no third category available, which is how the Quran usually closes a sentence about the reach of God's knowledge.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruler in that world was known by which of the two he was. Some chiefs were remembered for never letting an offence pass. Some were remembered for forgiving everything. A tribe knew which kind it had. Holding both descriptions of one authority at equal weight in a single sentence cut against how that society thought about power. There, a steady temperament was the mark of a leader.
studies.didYouKnow: This pairing of severity and forgiveness occurs several times in the Quran, and the order changes between passages. Neither one is fixed as the closing term. The classical scholars discuss that. Reading a pair of divine descriptions means holding both at once rather than treating whichever comes last as the final word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two statements are placed at equal weight, and the reader is left to hold them. That refuses the two shortcuts most people take with God. One is assuming the severity is decoration. The other is assuming the mercy is a technicality. The next ayah then takes the Messenger out of the picture. Nothing stands between the reader and the pair except what they show and what they hide.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same pair in the reverse order, announcing mercy first and the punishment after.
Names God as forgiving of sin and severe in consequence within one sequence of names.
States the same principle about the Messenger's charge a few ayat earlier.

studies.applyIt: Take whichever of the two you habitually forget. Some of us live as though only severity were real and some as though only mercy were. Say the half you neglect out loud once a day this week, in a plain sentence. It is a small correction and it usually shifts something within a few days.
studies.explainEasier: God is hard on wrongdoing, and God forgives and shows mercy. Both are true at the same time. The messenger's only job is to pass the message on. God knows what people show and what they keep hidden.

studies.title: Abundance Is Not A Measure
studies.meaning: A short statement with a concession built into it. The foul and the wholesome are not equal, even if the abundance of the foul impresses you. The concession is what makes the ayah useful. It admits that quantity really is impressive rather than pretending nobody feels it. Then the address changes to people of understanding. That suggests seeing past a large number is a matter of reasoning. It is not a matter of managing to feel differently about it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the close of the surah's instructional material. No occasion is reported for it. The early scholars read it as a general principle summing up much of what comes before. The chapter has often described majorities behaving badly. It has just as often limited those descriptions with the phrase many of them. This ayah gives the reasoning behind that habit.

keyTerms.note: A word for what is spoiled or noxious, used of bad soil, bad speech and bad earnings alike. It names something that has gone wrong in itself rather than something merely disapproved of.

keyTerms.gloss: it impresses you, it pleases you
keyTerms.note: The verb of causing wonder or admiration, and in another form the root yields the word for self-satisfaction. The ayah concedes the reaction rather than criticising the person who has it.
Literally possessors of the inner core, from the word for the kernel inside a shell. Understanding is named as what lies beneath a surface, which suits an ayah about looking past appearance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Quantity was the measure of everything. A tribe's strength was counted in men, a man's in camels, and poets recited numbers as praise. Standing in a market and seeing which stall had the larger heap told you which trader was winning. In a society without written accounts, visible abundance was the only accounting anyone had, and it was very hard to argue against.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for people of understanding occurs sixteen times across the Quran. Nearly always it comes where a judgement is asked that runs against appearance. It is the text's standard address to a reader being asked to think rather than to look. And it is built on the word for a kernel.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates two things people habitually merge. One is how common something is. The other is whether it is good. That distinction is simple to state and very hard to hold. So the passage names the impression before denying its authority. It also puts the correction in the register of intelligence rather than of piety, which makes it something anyone can check.

crossReferences.why: Names a balanced community among a majority described otherwise, in this same surah.
Says that following most of those on earth will lead you away from God's path.
Says only people of understanding take heed, using the identical phrase for them.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing you are doing mainly because a lot of people do it. Not a bad thing necessarily; just something whose only real argument is the crowd around it. Write down the actual reason, if there is one, in a sentence. If you cannot, that is this ayah's whole content, delivered by you rather than to you.
studies.explainEasier: God says that bad things and good things are not equal. A lot of something bad can still look impressive. So people who think should stay careful of God. That is how they do well.

studies.title: Do Not Ask About Things
studies.meaning: An instruction that runs against the usual encouragement to enquire. Do not ask about things which, if disclosed to you, would trouble you. The reason given is not that the answers are hidden but that they would land badly. Then a note about timing: asking while the Quran is being sent down will get them disclosed. The next ayah supplies a precedent, a people before who asked and then rejected what they were given.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars report a setting in which people pressed the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with questions. Some were about matters deliberately left unspecified. Some were designed to test him. Reports of the particular occasion differ. The general situation is a community receiving revelation in real time, where one question could produce an answer that then bound everyone.

keyTerms.note: The verb of causing distress or displeasure. What is warned against is not an unanswerable question but an answer that would sit badly, which locates the problem in the asker rather than in the subject.
The verb of effacing a trace. Silence is described here as a deliberate omission rather than an oversight, so what has not been specified is presented as an act of mercy.
A name for one who does not respond immediately to provocation. Pairing it with forgiving at the end of this ayah suits a passage about people pressing for answers they should not want.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Questions were a competitive form in that culture. Poets and orators tested one another in public. A question designed to trap was a recognised move with its own prestige. Delegations arrived carrying prepared difficulties. In a society where a public answer could not be taken back, asking was an exercise of power. This passage addresses that use of it directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran contains a series of ayat that begin with the phrase they ask you, and each of them supplies an answer. This passage stands against that pattern. The classical commentaries read the two together. Some questions are answered at length. Some are described as better left unasked in the first place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats revelation as having deliberate silences, and calls them mercy. That is a large claim about scripture. It means an absence in the text is not a gap waiting to be filled. The passage also treats the asker's motive as relevant to whether a question should be asked at all. That shifts the ethics of enquiry from the subject onto the person asking.

crossReferences.why: Answers one of the questions the community did ask, about the phases of the moon.
Describes a messenger who clarifies much and deliberately passes over much else.
Describes a question about the Hour and the answer that its knowledge rests with God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a question you keep wanting to ask someone, where you already suspect the answer and know it would not help. Leave it unasked this week. That is difficult and it is exactly what this passage describes. Some knowledge changes nothing except your ability to be at ease with a person.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers not to ask about things that would upset them if they were told. Some things are left unsaid on purpose, and that is a kindness. People before them asked, and then turned away from the answers.

studies.title: God Did Not Appoint These
studies.meaning: Four practices are named and denied in a single clause. God did not appoint any of them. Each was a category of livestock set aside from ordinary use by custom, marked and released, and each carried an assumed religious sanction. The ayah does not argue about whether the animals should be released; it denies the attribution. What is being corrected is a false ascription to God, and the closing clause names most of those who do it as not reasoning.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, though the practices described belong to older Arabian religion. They are addressed for what they were: an inherited system with no source anyone could name. The early scholars describe the four categories in detail and differ over the specifics, since the customs were already fading. The point being made does not depend on those details. The ayah states it as a matter of who is credited.

keyTerms.note: One of four categories of livestock set aside by custom and marked so that nobody would use it. The early scholars describe each one differently. That suggests the practices were already receding when this ayah was given.
From a root meaning to cut or split, so inventing is pictured as cutting cloth to shape. The verb is used across the Quran specifically for attributing to God something that He did not say.
The same phrase used earlier in this surah of those who mocked the call to prayer. In both places the failure named is a joining of things together rather than a shortage of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The four categories were visible in every herd. An animal with a slit ear or a particular mark was known to be untouchable. The rules about which offspring triggered which status were passed down without anyone remembering why. Real wealth was tied up in these releases, sometimes a great deal of it. Nobody could name a source for the system. Nobody questioned it either.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah names four older Arabian livestock customs. Three of the four terms occur nowhere else in the Quran. The classical scholars had to rebuild the practices from reports. Their descriptions of each one differ from one another. That is itself evidence of how quickly the customs disappeared.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The correction is aimed at who is credited rather than at the practice. That focus is the passage's substance. Something can be harmless in itself and become serious once God is named as its author. Inventing a rule and pinning it on God is treated across the Quran as its own kind of wrong. This ayah gives the clearest ordinary example of it.

crossReferences.why: Describes similar practices with livestock and the claims that were attached to them.
Asks who gave permission for declaring some provision off limits and some lawful.
Warns against the tongue describing falsely, saying this is lawful and this is not.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you attach religious weight to something that is really a family habit or a local custom. There is nothing wrong with the habit. The question is whether you present it as more than it is, to yourself or to children. Separate the two once this week, out loud, and see what changes.
studies.explainEasier: Arabs used to set certain camels aside and treat them as holy. God says He never set up any of that. People made it up and said it came from Him. Most of them do not think it through.

studies.title: What We Found Our Fathers On
studies.meaning: An invitation and a refusal, quoted exactly. Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger; and the answer given is that what we found our fathers upon is enough for us. The refusal is not an argument against the content, because the content was never examined. Then the ayah asks a single question that does all the work: even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided. The precedent is not disputed. Its authority is.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the denial of the inherited livestock customs in the ayah before it. The early scholars read the two together. The practices are denied, and this ayah quotes the defence that was actually offered for them. The setting is a society in which inherited practice carried more authority than argument. In that world the phrase quoted here was a complete and respectable answer.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to reckon or to count, so what is claimed is sufficiency in an accounting sense. The word appears elsewhere in the Quran with God as its object, which sharpens its use here for inherited custom.
The verb of coming upon something, with no implication of having chosen it. The refusal is honest about its own basis: what is defended is not what was concluded but what was simply already there.
A particle combining a question with a concession. It grants the premise entirely and then attaches a condition that empties it, which is why the ayah needs no further argument after asking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Precedent was the legal system. With no written law, a dispute was settled by what had been done before. Whoever remembered furthest back recited it. Genealogy carried authority for the same reason. In that world, saying we found our fathers doing this was not stubbornness. It was the strongest citation available, and appealing past it to anything else was the unusual move.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase quoted here, that we found our fathers upon this, comes back in several places across the Quran. It is put in the mouths of different communities addressing different prophets. The Quran presents it as the standard reply rather than as one people's particular failing. That is part of why it appears so often.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not attack inheritance itself. It asks what the inheritance is worth. The question raised is whether the people being followed had access to anything the follower does not. If they did not, the chain has no starting point. That test is available to anyone and works in every direction. It applies to a person who inherited something true and never examined why.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same reply in the earlier Medinan surah, with a different verb for finding.
Gives the same refusal and adds that they follow even a caller inviting to the fire.
Presents the reply as the standard answer given to every warner sent to a town.

studies.applyIt: Take one practice you inherited and have never examined, and find out this week why it is done. Not in order to abandon it. Most of what you find will be worth keeping, and you will hold it differently once you know. The ayah's question is only whether the people you got it from knew.
studies.explainEasier: When they are told to come to what God sent down, they say that what their fathers did is enough for them. But their fathers may have known nothing at all. Then the old way is not a reason.

studies.title: You Are Responsible For Yourselves
studies.meaning: An instruction that is easy to misread, and the early scholars say so. Take care of your own souls. Whoever has gone astray cannot harm you if you are guided. Read alone it sounds like withdrawal. The classical commentaries treat the condition as the key. Being guided includes what this surah has already required, restraining wrongdoing among those around you. The last clause moves everything to a shared return, which keeps the instruction from becoming isolation.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars record that this ayah was sometimes quoted to justify staying out of a community's affairs. The classical commentaries answer that reading directly. They set it against the passages in this same surah about failing to restrain one another. Reports of a specific occasion vary. The instruction arrives where the surah has been describing other communities at length.

keyTerms.gloss: take care of your own selves
keyTerms.note: A construction of obligation with no verb in it, an idiom meaning attend to this. It marks something as being on you, so what is assigned is a responsibility rather than a boundary around your concern.

A reflexive form, so accepting guidance rather than merely receiving it. The early scholars read the whole conditional through this word, since what counts as being guided determines what the ayah permits.
A noun of place from the verb to return. Its plural possessive matters: everyone returns to the same place, which is why the ayah cannot be read as separating one person's fate from another's.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe answered for everything its members did. It paid their debts and carried their offences. One man's wrongdoing could bring a raid down on his cousins. Against that background, telling a person to tend his own soul was new. It was easy to hear wrongly. Nothing around them treated a person as answerable on his own.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical commentaries on this ayah spend more space arguing against a misreading of it than explaining it. That is unusual. They record that it was quoted early on to justify staying out of communal affairs. They answer by pointing to the condition attached, and to what this surah has already said about mutual restraint.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Each person answers for what they do. But nobody is let off from the life around them. One conditional clause does both jobs. Nobody carries another's record. And nobody is on the right path while ignoring what goes on nearby. Holding those two together is the hard part. The tradition reads the ayah as a guard against despair, not as leave to walk away.

crossReferences.why: Condemns a community that did not restrain one another, within this same surah.
States that no bearer of burdens carries the burden of anyone other than itself.
Instructs guarding yourselves and your families, joining the two responsibilities together.

studies.applyIt: There is a situation you cannot fix and are still carrying. Name the part of it that is genuinely yours, in one sentence, and set the rest down for a week. Not permanently and not with indifference. This ayah is a relief for people who overreach, and it is not addressed to people who have stopped caring.
studies.explainEasier: God tells believers to look after their own souls. If they are on the right path, someone else going wrong cannot harm them. In the end everyone goes back to God. He will tell them what they did.

studies.title: Two Witnesses At The End
studies.meaning: A procedure is described for a specific and difficult moment. A person is dying away from home, on a journey, with a bequest to make and nobody from their own community present. Two people of integrity are called, or two from outside the community if that is all there is. They are held back after the prayer. They are asked to swear that they will not sell their testimony for any price, even for a relative, and will not hide what they saw. The oath's wording is quoted in full.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars report an incident in which a man died on a journey among people not of his community, and part of his estate went missing. They connect this ayah and the two that follow to it. The reports differ in their details. Travel deaths were common and the practical problem was real. A bequest was witnessed by strangers in a place with no record and no recourse.

keyTerms.note: An idiom built on the verb to strike, used across the Quran for journeying. The image is of feet striking the ground, and it carries the sense of a hard trip rather than a pleasant outing.

The early scholars differ over whether this means outside the family or outside the community. Both readings are recorded, and both point to the same practical situation: no ideal witness is available at all.
Testimony is described as something that could be sold, which names the temptation exactly. The same commercial image is used earlier in this surah for selling the signs of God cheaply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dying on the road was ordinary. Caravans buried people where they fell. Whatever a man carried passed through the hands of whoever happened to be travelling beside him: his goods, his money, his instructions for his family. There was no way to check anything afterwards. The oath in this passage was the only tool available. That is why its wording is so exact.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the longest procedural passages in the surah. The oath it sets out is quoted in the first person rather than summed up. The Quran gives the exact words to be said, which it does only rarely for a procedure. The classical scholars remark on how precise the wording is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage builds a safeguard for a moment when no safeguard is possible. It does so by placing the whole weight on an oath sworn before God after prayer. That is a statement about what holds a person when nothing outside can. It also expects failure honestly. The ayat that follow set out what to do if the oath turns out to have been false.

crossReferences.why: Sets out what happens if the first testimony is afterwards found to be false.
Gives the longest passage in the Quran on recording and witnessing a debt.
Requires standing firmly in witness for God even against oneself or near relatives.

studies.applyIt: Write down what you would want done with the things you leave behind. Tell one person where the note is. It takes twenty minutes and almost nobody does it. This passage exists because a man died on a road with his instructions in his head. The people who loved him had no way of finding out what they were.
studies.explainEasier: When someone is dying, two honest people should watch him say what he wants done with his things. If there is any doubt, they swear by God that they are telling the truth and hiding nothing.

studies.title: If The Oath Was False
studies.meaning: The procedure continues by expecting its own failure. If it comes to light that the two witnesses had earned a wrong, two others take their place. They come from among those with the stronger claim. They swear that their testimony is truer and that they have not overstepped. The design is symmetrical. An oath is answered by an oath rather than by an inquiry, because in that setting there was nothing to inquire with.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing straight on from the previous ayah's procedure for a death on a journey. The early scholars discuss the mechanics at length. They record differing views about who exactly the replacement witnesses are. The passage assumes a world without documents and without officials. There was no way to examine what happened in a place weeks away, and it builds accordingly.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the verb to trip over something. Discovery is described as accidental, which is honest about how such things actually came to light in a society with no means of investigation.
The verb means to become deserving of something, so the wrong is described as acquired rather than merely committed. The phrasing keeps attention on what the two now carry with them.

The verb of crossing a boundary, used across this surah for aggression and for excess in religion. Its appearance inside a sworn formula makes the oath a promise about limits rather than about facts alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world was settled by oath because nothing else was available. There were no records and no officials. There was no way to check a story told about a camp three hundred miles away. An oath sworn by God before a community was not a formality added to evidence. It was the evidence. A man who swore falsely was gambling his standing and a great deal more.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage and the two around it form the longest continuous procedure in the surah. The classical commentaries record more disagreement about their details than about almost anything else in the chapter. The difficulty lies in the Arabic itself. The early scholars say so rather than smoothing it over.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage designs for dishonesty rather than assuming honesty. That is a particular kind of realism. It provides a remedy without providing certainty. Two oaths are set against two oaths, and the matter is left there. So the final settling is handed elsewhere. The next ayah says as much by naming what the procedure is actually for.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the original procedure that this ayah supplies the remedy for.
States what the whole arrangement is actually for, immediately afterwards.
Gives another procedure in which oaths are answered by oaths where witnesses are lacking.

studies.applyIt: When you next design something that depends on people behaving well, spend five minutes on what happens if they do not. Not out of suspicion. This passage builds its own failure case into itself, and arrangements that skip that step tend to break on the person least able to absorb the damage.
